In massive machine-type communications (mMTC), granting numerous users low-latency connections is made possible by non-orthogonal grant-free access with low signaling overhead. This research proposes a novel two-stage approach using a genetic algorithm (GA) to generate user-specific sequences for low-latency grant-free uplink access. First, the initial GA finds a subsampling strategy to map a two-dimensional grid onto a one-dimensional sequence space. Subsequently, a second-stage GA is employed to produce sequences under practical RF constraints. These genetically designed sequences are optimized within mutual information boundaries using a mutual information calculator, which is based on orthogonal matching pursuit and the alternating minimization algorithm. Simulated results verify that the proposed sequences outperform traditional widely-linear sequences in terms of target sequence space hit rate across diverse channel environments. This approach holds promise for efficient, automated sequence design. Further development of the genetic algorithm is suggested for scaling up to larger systems. Additional ideas to integrate the proposed methods into practical mMTC grant-free protocols are also presented. Simulation results indicate that with these optimized sequences, it is feasible to achieve an 87% reduction in pilot overhead in low-snr scenarios and improve user throughput by 53% in moderate snr conditions compared to conventional two-dimensional code-based methods. This sequence design can be integrated into existing grant-free uplink access schemes to enhance performance. Simulation results of this integrated method show that with these sequences, it is possible to achieve a 67% higher target hit rate in low-snr environments and 42% higher target hit rate in moderate snr conditions compared to using conventional sequences in single-user systems. Moreover, this integrated method can also achieve 86% reduced pilot overhead in low-snr environments and improve user throughput by 50% in moderate snr conditions compared to conventional two-dimensional code-based methods. This research aims to provide a scalable and practical solution for low-latency grant-free uplink access sequences in mMTC systems. Nevertheless, incorporating all possible ASR interpretations could facilitate more accurate understanding of the user's intended message. This work aims to transmit the full range of possible interpretations to a subsequent module via a confusion network, which represents the various connections between spoken words and intended concepts. While some confusion networks are generated internally by speech recognition systems, others can be produced via post-processing of the initial predictions. To enable accurate training and inference with these confusion networks, our model calculates the most probable concept combinations based on the interconnections between speech sounds and intended meanings, effectively translating the confusion network into a structured representation of the conversation. We present a new framework for the dialogue management component, which is flexible enough to work with both the standard top-prediction outputs and the more comprehensive confusion networks, thus providing a smoother link between speech and computer code. Following the success of pretraining techniques in learning representations, various methods utilizing pre-trained models in continual learning have been developed. Some of these approaches build upon the pre-trained representations by implementing mechanisms for continual learning with minimal or no updates to the backbone models. In this study, we challenge the necessity of complex models by comparing a basic alternative we devised. We propose that a pre-trained feature extractor can achieve high performance in continual learning tasks, including the Split-CIFAR100 and CoRe 50 benchmarks. To test this, we conducted a straightforward comparison: a single-headed, task-free baseline uses the frozen pre-trained model to extract image features and calculate their corresponding mean features for every encountered class. It then determines predictions by computing the Euclidean distance between query features and mean class features. This simple baseline delivered impressive results, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on the Split-CIFAR100 benchmark and challenging the preponderance of recent continual learning research. Furthermore, we extended this simple approach to tackle the more demanding Continual Repeated Learning (CoRe) 50 benchmark, where the tasks follow a curriculum of increasing difficulty. We found that this simple baseline performed competitively, earning second place among all submitted methods at the 2022 Challenge: Repeated Learning (CoRe) 2022 (https://corechallenge2022.github.com/leaderboard/). Our work aims to promote skepticism towards continually updating pre-trained models and to encourage the community to develop even simpler yet more effective approaches for continual learning without model fine-tuning. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) in a parallel optimization (PAROP) framework, with sampling points adjusted based on prior data holding (PDH) principle. Initial sequence parameters such as data sampling rate and PDDH factor are determined through a T2 relaxation time-weighted four-dimensional (3D+respiration) map, with optimized values leading to motion compensation in-line. Following model-based reconstruction, the final reconstructed image is a static T2-weighted image, free from respiratory effects. As this method does not require a respiratory sensor, test studies were conducted to evaluate its robustness in cases where signal intensity variations arise due to changes in SNR, reconstruction parameters, sample datasets and contrast mechanisms. Furthermore, functional parameters of the pancreas and liver were compared with those generated using a conventional, free-breathing sequence. Evaluation of clinical applicability was also demonstrated through an in vivo study of liver lesions. Using a 1.5T MRI scanner, the research shows that rCASPR-PAROP method produces images with high quality, rendering them suitable for clinical procedures involving radiotherapy and treatment planning guided by MRI. This approach is compatible with existing imaging software and can be used to generate a comprehensive spatial data set for treating liver lesions and understanding their location in relation to vital organs. Using a model for optimizing sequence design has significant implications, opening up a wide array of possibilities for the development of novel MRI sequences in the future. We propose InDistill, a novel model compression approach, combining the principles of knowledge distillation and channel pruning to effectively transfer critical information flow from a powerful teacher model to a more efficient student model. Unlike previous techniques that collapse this information, InDistill leverages layer-wise pruning of the teacher's intermediate stages, aligning their widths with those of the student, thereby enabling direct information distillation without an intermediate encoding step. To facilitate knowledge transfer, we employ a curriculum learning strategy that prioritizes layer-wise difficulty and critical learning periods. Through these advancements, InDistill significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving enhanced results on a range of benchmarks, including ImageNet and CIFAR-100. The implementation of InDistill is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ziplab/Indistill. Our findings indicate that model compression can effectively preserve the critical information flow, thereby improving the efficiency of knowledge transfer and model compression. The underlying code for InDistill is written in PyTorch and can be accessed at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=I1R4jIr0kKc with a related video presentation. Two submersion functions from the plane to the line can be rescaled to match each other based on the coefficients of their linear components, resulting in equivalent foliations. Furthermore, two linear submersion functions are topologically equivalent if and only if they share equal cross ratios. By using these cross ratios, a topological equivalence metric can be defined for linear submersion functions, enabling the calculation of their distinct topological equivalence levels. We demonstrate that the space of linear submersion functions, subject to specific constant summation constraints, has a dimension determined by the number of unique cross ratios involved. Consequently, a specific algorithm can be applied to find the topological equivalence of linear submersion functions, as well as their foliations, through iterative computations of successively larger sets of cross ratios. Moreover, our method enables the solution of abstract word equations by employing an algorithm that formulates each word as a linear submersion function's system of partial derivatives. Results and findings from our experiments conducting random searches on specific cases are presented. Ultimately, further research is suggested on extending these findings and concepts to non-linear submersion functions. To confirm our theoretical conclusions, the software code used for these experiments and demonstrations is included in the appendix. Using these techniques, interesting solutions to specific cases of word equations can be found, resulting in novel conclusions about their space. Existing methods for topological classification, such as continuous deformation, are found to be less efficient even in simple cases, resulting in interesting geometric visualizations of the connection between words and specific geometric figures, such as triangles and triangles with an interior triangle. Interestingly, the relationship between words and specific geometric bodies can also be visualized through color images. Ecosystems that naturally thrive in dry environments have become increasingly vulnerable due to the rising threats of degradation and declining productivity. One notable aspect of these ecosystems is the spontaneous formation of plant patterns that can visually appeal and help regulate their response to stress. Research has shown that herbivory is a critical mechanism behind the creation of these patterns and the functioning of the entire ecosystem. Despite this, many mathematical models aimed at understanding this process are limited to their local scope, which neglects the significance of grazing animals' movement and sight range in shaping the dynamics of plants. This study introduces a novel cellular-automaton model that takes into account the way grazing animals move and feed on plants, thereby providing a more accurate representation of the interactions between these living beings and the plants. Our research uncovered various features, such as the emergence of plant patterns, which could be adjusted by modifying parameters related to grazing animals' movement and sight. Unlike previous local models, our non-local grazing model exhibited more intricate and nuanced behavior, such as the emergence of cyclical patterns, which were absent in earlier studies. Our results also suggest a significant relationship between the length of grazing animals' movement and the development of animal-favoring strategies, such as the formation of circular patterns that benefit grazing animals, which was absent in earlier studies. These findings highlight the complex interplay between the movement of grazing animals, plant growth, and the emergence of plant patterns. They also imply a critical role for non-local grazing in understanding the development of mechanisms that benefit grazing animals and the emergence of characteristic features in these ecosystems. One such feature, namely, hexagonal arrangement of plants, was absent in earlier studies. Our model provides an innovative approach to understanding the complex interplay between the movement of grazing animals and the development of patterns. It also opens up new avenues for further advancement in this field. It is worth noting that while our model is theoretical, it can offer insights that could benefit practitioners working in rangeland management. They can adjust parameters, such as those governing grazing pressure, to improve the health and maintenance of these crucial ecosystems. A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to the traditional approach. Our paper sheds light on the fundamental limits of safety for Dimensionality Reduction by Counting by demonstrating that both sketches are essentially the most secure when considering both query efficiency and sketch size. Moreover, we show that CountSketch sketches when compared to support-recovery focused ones, possess notable query efficiency advantages of up to 20 times. Finally, we expand our findings to related estimators such as those employed in influence assessment. An accompanying demonstration allows the comparison of estimator performance. A python-based program, ipie, has been developed for auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo simulations, along with its implementation on central and graphical processing units and interfacing with PySCF. Preliminary timing benchmarks compared to existing C++ codes show ipie performs equally well or better on both CPUs and GPUs. AFQMC results for the isomerization of [Cu$_2$O$_2$$]^{2+} were achieved using ipie with selected configuration interaction trials, achieving convergence for small basis sets. Additionally, results for a quadruple-zeta basis set with an estimated error of less than one kcal/mol were reported, involving 52 electrons and 290 orbitals with $10^6$ sampled configurations. Discussions on future enhancements, including parallelization and linear scaling capabilities, are explored.

Quantum Monte Carlo methods, renowned for providing ab initio electronic wavefunctions without requiring computational enhancements through the determinant of a fermion lattice, have been in extensive research since the 1960s, with the most prominent technique being auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC). Since its inception in the 1980s, progress in applying AFQMC has been slow due to its inherent nature of computing ground states using the sum of many-electtron Slater determinants, usually exceeding billions. This has been overcome with the development of the first mini-program in the late 1990s at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, using compiled Fortran, as well as more recent implementations on graphical processing units at the University of California, Santa Barbara and the University of Texas, Austin. These innovations have brought quantum chemistry simulations with the theoretical scalability of $O(N^{\frac{3}{4}})$ in both computational resources and energy truncations.

Despite these breakthroughs, there remained limitations in the computational and efficiency of these simulations: 1) the dependence on a C++ compiler, which hampers portability to other systems and causes inconsistencies in the program's usability, and 2) the inability to parallelize simulations on multi-core CPUs and GPUs due to the unavailability of a general, easy-to-use interface. This has constrained simulations and analyses of electronic wavefunctions using the theoretical and computational capacities of modern computing systems. This work addresses these shortcomings by presenting a Python-based AFQMC program, ipie, designed for ease of use with the computational power of both CPUs and GPUs, as well as the development and implementation of a general, easy-to-use interface for parallelization.

We examine a mechanism design problem for selling $k$ items to unit-demand buyers with private valuations for each item, who can choose between participating directly in the auction or being represented by an intermediary. The aim is to develop robust auction designs that don't rely on the buyer-demand distribution and work well across diverse contract scenarios between intermediaries and buyers.

Initially, we focus on the case of $k$ identical items where buyers draw private valuations independently from a specified, non-degenerate probability distribution 't', and analyze the performance of two mechanism designs - the single auction and intermediaries-enabled mechanism designs. In the case where intermediaries are precluded, we prove that the single auction achieves a revenue loss of at least $\Omega(\sqrt{\mathsf{SDP}_\mathrm{gap}(t) \cdot k})$ compared to the optimal revenue. When intermediaries are allowed, we develop a general technique to prove that the enabled mechanism achieves a significantly lower loss, specifically, a much smaller loss bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{\mathsf{SDP}_\mathrm{gap}(t)^{1+\delta_o/t'} \cdot k})$ where $\delta_o$ is a positive constant determined solely by the distribution 't', in contrast to the optimal revenue. Furthermore, when considering the distribution 't' uniform or normal, we show that a larger exponent $1+\delta_o/t'$ can be attained. In order to tackle this problem, we extend the existing techniques in robust mechanism design, particularly by introducing new black-box techniques for removing the assumption of independent demand and by generalizing robust mechanism design to the scenario of simultaneous auctions, which had previously been studied only in independent value contexts. We show the optimality of our results against independent value distributions by proving lower bounds on the loss in robust mechanism design, both for single and multiple auctions. In order to study robust mechanism design, we examine the behavior of the sum of optimal mechanisms under various distributions. In particular, we identify a distribution-independent lower bound on the loss of robust mechanisms in terms of the sum of optimal values in the Plummer-Young conjecture. By utilizing this conjecture, we prove robust lower bounds for both single and multiple auctions. We also evaluate the performance of multiple auctions in distinct scenarios and find that non-trivial robust lower bounds exist only for specific distributions 't'. To facilitate abstractive summarization, we've introduced an efficient planning mechanism that enables the generation of grounded summaries. This method involves pre-annotating summaries with entity chains, and training transformer models to predict these chains, and subsequently generate summaries conditioned on them. In our experiments, which included pre-training and fine-tuning with the planning objective, we found that incorporating entity chains led to better summarization performance and entity accuracy on four diverse datasets. Specifically, we observed significant performance gains of 2.3 and 3.6 points in ROUGE-L on the CNN/DailyMail and NewsRound datasets, respectively. Furthermore, our method excelled compared to a top-performing baseline that leverages abstractive copying, and demonstrated efficacy on datasets that require precise entity extraction, such as the FactV2 dataset where it achieved a 19.6 point increase in F1 score. We've also made our implementation publicly available. For related work and technical details, please refer to the accompanying paper. For a deeper analysis, including multimodal extensions of our method, please see the follow-up study. The code can be accessed via this repository. This research presents new sufficient conditions for differentiating a function with n real variables, where these conditions are grounded in the differentiability of a related function with n-1 variables and are less restrictive than traditional criteria. We have also discovered a novel inequality related to these conditions. We have derived specific outcomes for functions within two variables. Moreover, our findings have been applied to establish the differentiability of particular integral functions, encompassing logarithmic, exponential, power, and arctangent functions, as well as functions described by integrals, such as the Cauchy principal value and the Mercator series. Human vocal synchronization in social interactions provides valuable information about a person's cognitive behaviors, suggesting the importance of understanding entrainment patterns in conversations. To measure this synchronization accurately in two-person dialogues, we developed a dynamic approach that combines convolutional networks and transformer architecture to capture both immediate and long-term conversation contexts. By incorporating attention layers for analyzing both internal and external factors, our model can learn meaningful patterns in social exchanges across various domains. Through classification experiments, we verified the effectiveness of our approach in identifying authentic and inauthentic conversations. Moreover, when testing our model with individuals having Autism Spectrum Disorder, our results indicate a strong statistical link between our entrainment measure and relevant clinical symptoms, both internally and within relationships. Our study highlights the value of vocal synchronization as a significant indicator of an individual's well-being. Furthermore, we believe that our approach can facilitate the development of innovative technologies that recognize and benefit from people's natural social behaviors. A recent study applied a realizability technique to establish the meaning of a quantum lambda calculus, which results in a multitude of acceptable typing rules, all of equal standing. Building upon this concept, we present a significant subset of typing rules, which formulates a versatile quantum calculus, accompanied by a corresponding categorical interpretation. Specifically, we outline a semantics based on an adjunction between the categories of spaces with linearly combined values and the category of sets with distributed values. Furthermore, we present a semantics for the quantum lambda calculus that utilizes a mapping between these two categories. The proposed quantum lambda calculus is shown to effectively capture the essence of quantum control methods, which we illustrate through the creation of several non-trivial examples. Moreover, we will discuss how this theoretical framework can be used to provide a theoretical basis for quantum algorithms programming competition, which was held in 2019 as a part of the NISQ challenge initiative. The competition's program and outcomes can be found at https://niscchallenge.org/. In addition to its theoretical significance, the adjunction-based semantics of the lambda calculus offers technical utilities that facilitate the translation of quantum algorithms into a mixed prefix notation, which simplifies the process and makes it more efficient than methods that work solely with matrices. In particular, we will highlight the case study of the Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm, which we will represent using the quantum lambda calculus and illustrate with a simple linear category-based representation. In contrast to other approaches, we will demonstrate that our method yields a manifestly linear version of the algorithm that incorporates a re-reading of the quantum control methods in terms of the adjunctions and mappings involved. Lastly, we will also outline a corresponding linear semantics for the quantum lambda calculus in the style of the lambda calculus itself, which is shown to correspond to the categorical semantics through a translation inspired by the Gentzen-Annexation Theorem. This linearity principle is shown to imply the decidability of the pre-type pre-consistency and the pre-type type soundness for the quantum lambda calculus. Interestingly, we will show that the underlying linearity principle does not preclude the computational expressiveness of the quantum calculus. In fact, even within the manifestly linear version of the calculus, which is shown to be equivalent to the original calculus, we will identify non-deterministic properties. Analytical calculations have been performed for two types of quasiparticle excitation energies per particle in systems of up to seven electrons within both the Laughlin theory and composite fermions theory, accounting for the comprehensive jellium potential consisting of electron-electron, electron-background, and background-background interactions. The findings support that the composite fermions wavefunction outperforms the Laughlin wavefunction in energy for two quasiparticle configurations, albeit the difference in their energies diminishes with growing system size. For small system sizes, though the composite fermions wavefunction is energetically favorable, its ground state is disfavored due to unphysical properties. The energy per particle of the composite fermions wavefunction scales better with system size, exhibiting a more desirable size dependence. The energies obtained via analytical calculations of the two quasiparticle excitation costs on top of the ground states are complemented with numerical data for both wavefunctions. The findings suggest that the two quasiparticle excitation cost serves as a reliable indicator of ground state quality only in systems of a considerable size; for smaller system sizes, other energy scales besides this cost influence the ground state properties greatly. The composite fermions wavefunction is found to predict a systematic deviation of the two quasiparticle excitation cost from the pinching point at halving the quasiparticle excitation cost, developing theory is necessary to rectify this discrepancy. The phenomenon is analogous to a charge parity anomaly identified in the ground state of composite fermions, implying that the composite fermions wavefunction fails to describe properly the two quasiparticle excitation properly. The analytical calculations for energies, encompassing electron-electron, electron-background, and background-background interactions, reveal the significance of these components for two quasiparticle configurations, implying a substantial contribution from electron-background interactions in systems of a small number of particles. The composite fermions wavefunction is found to be insensitive to electron-background interactions, but with size and density correlations yielding a substantial effect. The position distribution of electrons in the ground state of a composite fermions system is discovered to be unstable under a perturbation removal and causes the system to be attracted to an electron, much like an impurity. The findings are available in a graphical format for the analytical energy per particle of the ground states and their differences with varying system size, electron background coupling, and electron-electron interaction type. In the context of glaciology, particularly when modelling contact-related issues in marine ice sheets, Stokes variational inequalities come into play. This research focuses on a specific scenario involving a 2D marine ice sheet with a grounding line, though the approach can be extended to other contact issues like subglacial cavitation. A primary challenge arises from the analysis due to ice's nonlinear rheology, the implementation of a power-law based friction boundary condition, and the presence of rigid modes in velocity space, resulting in a semicoercive variational inequality. To tackle this complexity, a mixed formulation is explored that incorporates a Lagrange multiplier, followed by a finite element approximation analysis. This research derives error estimates by employing a specially constructed projection operator to account for rigid modes, leveraging a Korn-type inequality, under the condition that rigid modes do not exceed one dimension. To corroborate these findings, numerical results are provided. This study is a development of previous work, described in [ arXiv:2104.11324, arXiv:2101.01495 ], which focused on second-order cone programming and Lagrange multiplier methods. A complementary numerical investigation can be found in [ arXiv:2107.07594 ]. This work is part of the author's Ph.D. research. Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, we found reduced gas fractions and increased ratios of molecular to atomic gas within the galaxy. By analyzing outflow properties, we found they originate from the galaxy's disk at relatively moderate velocities and there is no clear relationship between outflow occurrence and disk distance. These findings suggest outflows in this galaxy are primarily driven by star formation, influencing the gas's molecular fraction and usage rate. However, we did not detect the expected occurrence of outflows in the galaxy's disk due to limitations of our data. Our results are generally consistent with what has been observed in nearby galaxies, indicating outflow-driven feedback can regulate the galaxy's star formation process. Due to the low signal of outflows in our NOEMA and KCWI data, we cannot determine if outflow occurrence is correlated with disk instability. To address this question, we require spatially complete and high-resolution UV data with sufficient continuum sub-beam sensitivity. Our model simulations suggest that in this galaxy, outflow occurrence should be 100% in our NOEMA and KCWI fields of view, and the cloud cradling model can explain the observed relationships between outflow mass and star formation and gas usage times. However, the cradling model does not replicate the relationships between outflow mass and gas usage time and gas fraction in a physically meaningful manner. Consequently, a more complex feedback mechanism may be required to explain these relationships. Our findings imply that in this galaxy, outflow-driven feedback has reduced the galaxy's star formation rate, but that in the observed fields of view, we do not see the expected occurrence of outflows due to limitations of our data. In order to investigate the prevalence of cloud-scale outflow occurrence in this galaxy using NOEMA and KCWI, we require to measure the star-forming surface density with either Integrate to the Edge or Rotating Disk constraints. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. Our findings suggest triangular flow to stem from similar initial sources to elliptical flow. Consequently, we expect triangular flow to serve as a valuable indicator of the initial system's anisotropic geometry at the level of partonic density. Furthermore, we believe the ratio of $v_3/\epsilon_3$ to $v_2/\epsilon_2$ may facilitate the detection of geometric flow influences at varying transverse momentum levels. Our research enables a more substantial understanding of anisotropic flow origins and allows for the utilization of specific flow ratios as sensitive probes of initial conditions and partonic flows. Ultimately, we intend to enable data analyses by comparing theoretical predictions with experimental measurements. Such comparisons will allow us to quantitatively assess initial anisotropic geometry. Furthermore, we plan to investigate transport characteristics by analyzing experimental data through the lens of the multiphase transport model. By doing this, we will be able to study various transport properties in intermediate states of extreme matter. Notably, we will be exploring the behavioral patterns of dynamic properties in lab-created matter, as well as assessing whether the rules governing normal matter apply to the matter in lab conditions. In addition to these key areas of study, we are also working to bridge the theoretical and experimental gaps by comparing theoretical and experimental results on anisotropic flow influences and parton energy loss. By bridging these gaps, we will be able to study the theoretical and experimental properties of anisotropic flow and determine if there are any distinguishing features of anisotropic flow influences at various momentum levels. In addition to these key areas of study, we are also working to bridge the theoretical and experimental gaps by comparing theoretical and experimental results on parton energy loss. achieve this goal, we developed SyROF, an innovative testbed that features a
synchronized robotic platform enabling researchers to concentrate on robotic
coordination and synchronization without the need to delve into the underlying
mechanisms. Our testbed consists of a modular robot design, leveraging
incidental motion to improve coordination and efficiency. Additionally, we
integrated an original vision processing algorithm to enhance robustness and
precision, and developed a centralized controller to streamline coordination
efforts. Our experimental assessments of the testbed's various components were
successful, and we showcase three practical applications as case studies. By
overcoming key hurdles encountered during the development process, we provide
insights that can be applied to other robotic platforms. Ultimately, we demonstrate
how SyROF enables researchers to expedite their progress in creating robotic

Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable effort,
so many researchers opt for pre-training their model on a different task before
further refining it using a smaller annotated dataset. Top-notch methods for
monocular depth estimation have caught their attention. Although using depth
estimation for pre-training has yielded benefits, it's unclear whether using
classification under the same setup would be equivalently beneficial. Our study
offers an in-depth explanation for why depth pre-training outperforms
classification pre-training and suggests that employing supervised learning
with paired images for both tasks can help clarify the underlying causes. We
also present a simple yet effective approach, based on cross-entropy, that uses
paired images to improve segmentation results and can even work well with weak
annotations. Our experiments demonstrate that the cross-entropy loss can
surpass current standalone segmentation techniques. Moreover, when integrated with
other segmentation methods, it can help boost their performance and aid model
generalisation after training on limited annotated data. Our code is available
at https://github.com/auriculote/depth-loss-semseg/ and the findings have been

Our objective is to quantify the magnitude of off-shell and non-resonant influences on the forms of various differential distributions that will be crucial for top quark mass determination via template fitting techniques. These distributions require special handling to ensure accurate top quark mass extraction. The susceptibility of facial recognition systems to fraudulent presentations restricts their adoption in high-stakes applications. Effective countermeasures against these deceptive attempts are vital for the safe integration of facial recognition technology. Current approaches have shown limitations, often becoming overly specialized in training datasets and struggling to adapt to unseen attack methods and environments. In this research, transfer learning is applied from the vision transformer model to tackle the challenge of detecting unknown anti-spoofing attacks. Experimental results conducted on widely accessible datasets showcase the superiority of our proposed solution, outperforming state-of-the-art methods significantly in zero-shot scenarios within the HQ-WMCA and SiW-M datasets, while also achieving substantial improvements in cross-database evaluations. Additionally, our model exhibits impressive performance when faced with novel attack techniques and environments derived from the AIST-SPOOF database. Our findings along with the implemented code are openly available for review at this link: https://github.com/IndigoPurple/ZSSP-ViT. Our model's online demonstration can be accessed at https://zsspindiep.herokuapp.com. Evolutionary algorithms have seen significant advancements in recent years through parallel computing, resulting in Parallel Evolutionary Algorithms (PEAs). However, a major limitation in Asynchronous PEAs (APEAs) arises from idling computing nodes until the next evaluation can be completed, causing a bias towards generating solutions with shorter computation times. As a result, despite giving more opportunities to optimize, APEAs often exhibit a subpar performance. To overcome this drawback, a novel parent selection technique has been proposed to counter the effects of evaluation time bias in APEAs. According to the introduced concept of Frequency-based Parent Selection (FPS), a parent is selected not only based on its performance but also an adaptation factor that differences between parent and offspring qualities. By introducing the FPS, a modified Non-dominated Sorting Multi-objective Evolutionary Algorithm with Pareto Front (NSGA-II) was proposed, demonstrating the efficacy of the proposed approach in decreasing the gap between synchronous and asynchronous algorithms. Experimental results conducted across 8 multi-objective optimization test problems revealed that the modified NSGA-II (NSGA-II-FPS) yields better results compared to the original NSGA-II, especially in terms of non-dominated solution set size and spread. Performance validation also demonstrates that NSGA-II-FPS outperforms leading C++ implementations of mainstream MOP pareto-front search algorithms including CDES-M2, MOPSO, and RILS-M2. Observations gathered from experiments point to FPS being a versatile technique capable of enhancing the performance of a comprehensive search. Therefore, its effectiveness can be extended to a comprehensive search without parallelization, providing an additional improvement in search outcome. Moreover, an important quality factor for acceptance was identified through experimental analysis, that parents with high adaptation factor offspring are more valuable than their counterparts. Subsequent experiments conducted to establish a parent selection rule based on offspring quality categories revealed that some classes are acceptable while others need be prohibited. Consequently, a detailed search for such acceptable classes using detailed analysis between high and low quality parent-offspring pairs was proposed as part of an algorithm improvement in search outcome. The proposed improvement in search outcome has shown efficacy in a comprehensive search without parallelization, and its effectiveness can be verified at top-level management decision-making process. Above all, the proposed improvement in search outcome has significant theoretical value at highest computational complexity level. Therefore, its effectiveness can be extended to a comprehensive search without parallelization, providing an additional improvement in search outcome. The recent microlensing event OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 involved a cold super-Earth planet located among a group of eleven planets where the mass of the host star compared to its planetary mass is less than 0.0001. We used the Keck/NIRC2 telescope's near-infrared adaptive optics to create more precise data on the mass of the lensing star's host, enabling us to establish that the observed light excess, with an amplitude of 16.96 plus/minus 0.11, most probably originates entirely from the lensing star itself. This conclusion is driven primarily by the low probability of an unresolved companion with a mass ratio calibrated to be less than 0.67 at 90% confidence level. Combined with recently announced OGLE-2017-BLG-1434's mass radius observations, our current understanding confirms the mass of the super-Earth planet, with a mass of 4.2 plus/minus 0.5, in solar masses, completing a very clear picture of a cold super-Earth with a mass of 6.6 plus/minus 0.9 solar mass units, located within the 2.5 kilometer radius orbit of its 0.29 solar mass host. We used the mass of the host to establish the current velocity of the super-Earth planet, with a mass of 67 plus/minus 4.6 km/h, placing it among the planets with the lowest speeds observed so far. We further used our newly found information to plot a resolved picture of our solar system's surrounding planets within the mass-range of 1 to 30 solar mass units, located within 2 to 11 kilometer radial distances, and with current velocities ranging from 35 to 67 km/h, thereby serving as a vital component in our attempt to understand our solar system's overall movement. Finally, using an enlarged picture of observed super-Earths, we have been able to identify an overall correlation between their mass and their orbital distance, thus providing crucial insights into super-Earth formation processes. Furthermore, we observed an overall shift towards lower mass host stars who had the chance to form super-Earths within more compact mass systems. However, current data is still too limited and further detailed observations are required in the mass-range of 10 to the power of minus 1 to 3 solar mass units and with orbital distances spanning approximately 2 to 12 kilometer radial distances in order to reliably establish super-Earth movement patterns within our solar system

The concept of an effective, time-independent Floquet Hamiltonian underpins the Floquet engineering of isolated systems, describing their evolution over driving periods and often obtained through analytical series in the driving frequency. However, extending these ideas to open quantum systems, modelled by Lindblad master equations, poses a significant challenge. In systems with only two states, unique Floquet operators can be derived, but this is generally not possible in more complex systems. Instead, we develop a different high-frequency approximation for time-dependent Lindblang generators, which accurately captures key properties. Leveraging this approximation, we demonstrate the existence of unique, high-frequency expansions for time-periodic Lindblang generators and semidefinite metrics in small parameter regimes. Furthermore, we derive explicit formulas for the leading terms of these expansions and show that they satisfy key consistency conditions. Finally, we outline the numerical protocols necessary to compute these high-frequency expansions and apply them to the Floquet engineering of open quantum systems. By engineering bound-like mixed states, we achieve experiments that verify the high-frequency expansions and evaluate the accuracy of Floquet engineering methods for Lindblang generators. As a result, we establish high-frequency expansions for Lindblang generators as a viable approach for open quantum systems and confirm the applicability of Floquet engineering in such systems. Additionally, we develop explicit formulas for the leading terms of expansions for key properties in various open system models, significantly expanding the scope of Floquet engineering in these systems. Moreover, we derive new high-frequency expansions for time-dependent observables and apply these to the implementation of non-destructive measurements in both static and dynamic systems. In particular, we perform measurements on dynamical systems with periodic driving, enabling us to extract time-resolved data that complements the results obtained with time-independent systems. The distinction between these two approaches allows us to perform measurements on distinct parameters, thereby increasing the flexibility of experiments that aim to achieve specific goals. Ultimately, we apply our developed protocols to the implementation of quantum teleportation in systems with time-dependent coupling, effectively replacing the integrity of vital system elements. By exploring the interplay between driving, system dynamics, and the structure of open quantum systems, we establish a fundamental framework for the implementation of sophisticated quantum technologies, addressing a core challenge of high-frequency engineering in the process. The numerical protocols presented have potential applications in the engineering and optimization of quantum systems, potentially contributing to the growing repertoire of quantum engineering tools. Our recent studies of the effects of Rh content in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ reveal the emergence of magnetic clusters due to the mixing of 4$f$ and 5$d$ moments in Ce and Pd sublattices. As the Rh ratio increases, the material undergoes a transition from ferromagnetism to a state known as the spin-freezing phenomenon, characterized by the presence of localized Pd moments. Using neutron polarizatio experiments, we found that the analysis relying on simple ferromagnetic models significantly overestimates the Pd moments, by more than 50%. A more accurate picture emerges when incorporating the concept of spin freezing and appropriately adjusting the moment values. Our research demonstrates that a detailed understanding of the effects of Rh content in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ requires a refined analysis of the material's magnetic properties. Based on these findings, we recommend a revised set of magnetic parameters for further study. Moreover, our study indicates that the spin-freezing effect can be realized within a broader composition range of Rh content in Rh and has significant implications for the formation of magnetic clusters in this system. Utilizing a cluster variation algorithm and incorporating the effects of dispersion and spin freezing, we can accurately predict the material's magnetic properties across a wide range of compositions. Notably, our analysis for $x$ = 0.2 reveals a nonuniform distribution of moments within specific clusters, which might explain the material's susceptibility to magnetic excitations. A proposed explanation for this phenomenon involves the resonance-like coupling between the Ce and Pd moments. A more in-depth investigation of this effect is warranted. Our study of the effects of Rh content in CePd and related systems has far-reaching implications and offers valuable insights for the continued study of these materials using neutron scattering and other techniques. Current methods primarily address the interpretation of individual cases (inspiration from Deep Learning), but fall short in offering three key aspects essential for effective explanation: the ability to pinpoint crucial graph elements (such as nodes and edges) contributing to the prediction; the capability to generate explanations for distinct parameter settings of the same model; and the ability to measure explanation importance objectively. The resulting PE-GNN can generate graph explanations to reveal the impact of different feature types (self-attention, node, and edge) and predict their importance. The peculiar system, RXCJ0232.2-4420, at $z$ = 0.28, contains a unique radio halo surrounding its central cluster core. To explore its development and composition, we examined archival X-ray data from Chandra and XMM-Newton, examining the dynamic cluster state and searching for gas substructures. Its X-ray brightness surface density lies within the expected range, but the X-ray temperature exceeds the estimated cluster redshift scale. We discovered two distinct gas substructures with temperatures of approximately 3.26 and 4.34 keV, each indicating mass scales around $1.4-2.2 \times 10^{44}$ erg s$^{-1$. We found temperature contrasts of around 32% and 13%, along with projected separation distances of 330 and 480 kpc, characteristic of dynamic systems. The possible merger of these substructures may have influenced the formation of the central radio emission, though its initiation and primary energy source remain unclear. It's also possible that the primordial formation of the halo from accreted gas may be due to accretion streams that formed the surrounding large-scale environment. We consider a dynamic system most likely to explain the observed halo characteristics. The observed morphological uniformity of the halo might result from interactions between the streams and the surrounding environment that influenced the formation stream. We also suggest further observations to determine the observed merger scale. The observed X-ray properties were more closely related to systems of a much lower redshift scale, indicating possible density enhancements or ambient environments that influenced the observed cluster. We consider the observed halo as an example of a more widespread phenomenon, or perhaps an exceptional case. We also propose the need for more detailed observations of similar systems to further our understanding. The paper includes further detailed figures for clarity and reference.

Recently introduced, the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU) is a novel type of recurrent neural network designed to consolidate information and is highly effective at training. However, the complex mathematical nature of its memory module makes it difficult to optimize, resulting in training times that are prohibitively expensive for the high cost in computational resources required. In an effort to improve performance, we developed a novel parallel training method for LMUs, designed to overcome optimization challenges presented by the complex nature of its model. This method, in combination with utilizing the HOGWILE experimental framework, facilitated the successful implementation of the LMU on GPUs, resulting in notable improvements in training times of up to 3.5 times for small and medium-sized networks and up to 8.6 times for larger networks. In addition, we accomplished a $2.5$ times speedup in inference times of the LMU, achieving real-time capabilities on various benchmark datasets such as MNIST and IMDB. This achievement marks the first successful implementation of LMUs on modern CUDA architecture and resulting in substantial time savings, opening up the possibility of successful implementation of the model to tackle more complex datasets. This paper presents a detailed description of the innovative parallel training method, its inherent mechanics, and the implications of its design, in addition to our optimized implementation of the LMU. One challenge of this work is the difficulty in optimizing the model's nature, addressed by the author via the innovative parallel training method. This research aims to enable the successful implementation of the LMU on various architectures and accelerators, addressing a long-standing open issue. As the next decade unfolds, the field of particle physics is driven to unravel the enigma of dark matter, the universe's imbalance of matter over antimatter, the seemingly calculated balance of the electro-weak scale, and various fundamental physics aspects.  A significant challenge lies in exploiting the Standard Model's strengths to detect the feebly interacting components of dark matter and matter-antimatter imbalance candidates.  In this review, we will concentrate on particles like neutrinos, the dark matter candidates (either as a whole particle or a part with a very small mass), and the possible Proton decay indicators, all of which interact feebly with matter.  A variety of experiments and observations have been discussed to search for these particles, and the anticipated results of the searches conducted between 2015-2021 will also be examined.  Furthermore, we will look at the plans and anticipated findings of the search for feebly interacting particles in the upcoming experiments and analyses.  A particular emphasis will be given to NEOS, the search for faint nuclear excitations, and the potential search for light sterile neutrinos.  It's worth noting that the enigma of dark matter and the matter-antimatter imbalance candidates has not seen significant progress during this period of time but we are anticipating some hopeful signs and outcomes in the near future.  This review is based on the report submitted to the U.S. National Academy of Sciences in December 2021.  A separate document has been prepared for the theoretical aspects of the feebly interacting particles, particularly the dark matter candidates. We examine a two-wave system in the interval (-1,1), where one wave absorbs energy and the other does not, with partial damping that mimics a viscoelastic material's behavior. Prior research showed that with damping throughout the entire domain, the system's energy decreases at a rate proportional to $t^{-\frac{1}{2}}$. We've developed an all-optical technique for producing and measuring non-reversible properties. We discovered that when applied to a fiber Bragg grating, squeezing a coherent light source induces a one-way direction for light transmission, which we verified by recording spatial light patterns. This non-reversible effect can be fine-tuned by adjusting the parameters of the squeezing process. Notably, our technique has the advantage of not relying on the presence of light-absorbing components, making it suitable for integrated photonic applications. We also measured the greatest degree of non-reversible properties induced by any all-optical method so far, which equals 8.16 dB. This breakthrough has potential for advancing many photonic technologies that rely on optical non-reversible properties. Furthermore, we demonstrated the possibility of generating a laser using the combination of a non-reversible device and a laser reservoir site. This achievement contributes significantly to the field of optical non-reversible properties, ultimately paving the way for applications in quantum computing and information processing. The process of squeezing coherent light can be described in detail by two linear equations that define the relationship between variables. Based on these linear relationships, we developed a model that explains how non-reversible properties are produced in our Bragg grating setup. We discovered that the presence of frequency-shifted light only marginally affects the width of the frequency distribution of light transmission, which mainly depends on the distribution of amplitude. In contrast, the width of the frequency distribution of light frequency, on the other hand, is influenced by both the distribution of amplitude and frequency. We also verified that a particular type of frequency distribution containing only the second frequency has the greatest degree of non-reversible properties. This finding suggests that the width of the frequency distribution of light frequency might be a suitable metric to quantify the degree of non-reversible properties. We explored various experimental scenarios using the width of frequency distribution to quantify the degree of non-reversible properties and compared them with theoretical predictions. Blind Image deblurring attempts to estimate a latent sharp image and the blur kernel that produced a given blurry image. Several extensions of the classical Richardson-Lambert algorithm have been developed for this purpose. We introduce Kernel Mixture (KM), a novel algorithm for blind image deblurring. By employing the mixture of two Kernel Regularized Expectation Minimization (KREM) procedures, KM fulfills the strong convexity requirement, allowing for the minimization of the chordal distance between the image and its reconstruction. Our simulation studies demonstrate that KM surpasses alternative methods in restoring clarity and accuracy. Additionally, KM is presented as a unified framework by first analyzing its potential pitfalls and limitations in generating blurry images. We further extend the applications of KM to the correction of image distortions. Our paper provides comprehensive step-by-step instructions for its implementation. Moreover, KM is shown to be effective in correcting geometrical and lens distortions in photographs. We provide practical demonstration of these applications. Lastly, KM is embodied in a plugin called Blurry for the Adobe Photoshop image processing software, showcasing its practical usability.

particularly vital in systems requiring safety and security assurances.
Hoare logic serves as a widely employed formal methodology for thoroughly
examining software adherence to specifications through precondition/postcondition
declarations. The improvement of semantic parsing methods and increasing
computational capabilities enable the extraction of formal logical structures from
natural language inputs with growing precision and breadth.
  This research outlines a formal framework for utilizing Hoare logic in the
formal verification of imperative code through logical structures derived from
compositional semantic parsing of declarative language assertions.
Our proposed method, dubbed Natural Hoare Logic, enables direct software
verification against domain-specific, natural language statements obtained from
parsing declarations.
  Effective program specifications often incorporate domain-specific terms,
which are typically omitted in translations derived from logical forms.
  To address this, we employ a two-layered Hoare logic structure.
  The inner level verifies assumptions about and effects on domain-specific states
while the outer level validates the functional correctness of imperative code
using general logical expressions for pre/post-conditions.
  We apply this model to various imperative programs and compare the
objectivity and expressivity of NHL against traditional Hoare logic.
  Our comparison reveals a generalisability advantage in utilizing a formal
structure for specification rather than translation, offering improved
expressivity through domain-specific terms.

extract logical structures, specify imperative code, and prove its specifications

demonstrations presented in this paper, supported by its online repository with

to the field, our method outperforms existing approaches with its scalable
extractability, enabling the specification and verification of more complex
programs than prior research. Moreover, our proposed model retains desirable
attributes such as correctness, expressivity, and objectivity without any loss.

encouraging formal verification of software from increasingly sophisticated
logical structures derived with growing precision and breadth from natural language
specifications through the employment of semantic parser. The structure of this

paper proposes a novel three-phase training approach based on expressivity 
criteria, consisting of global network reduction, weight refinement, and targeted 
weight reorganization. To streamline the network, we incorporate Shrinkage 
Skeleton, a versatile reduction method, to condense the graph weight-coarse 
structure. Subsequently, we improve weight precision through an adaptation of 
Pyramid Coarse Graining. Lastly, we improve the graph topology by implementing 
a Local Topology Rewiring scheme. Our experiments with models of varying 
complexity across multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this 
training strategy in maximizing the expressivity of deep graph neural networks. 
Empirical analysis reveals that each phase's contribution can be precipitated 
and visualized, and we identify the key limitations of this framework, 
particularly its sensitivity to the initial phase, which may necessitate further 
research. You can find more details about this work at https://github.com/microsoft/dgnn-design.

Program analysis through Abstract Interpretation involves simulating the behavior of a program in a simplified environment to approximate its true behavior. This simulation traditionally has two steps: the upward phase uses approximation to ensure the analysis stops, followed by the downward phase which uses interpolation to mitigate the loss of accuracy resulting from approximations. This paper suggests an alternative by temporarily switching from an approximation to an exact model of the program's behavior, effectively "healing" the approximations in a more precise way than traditional interpolation could. The idea is implemented in a commutative property, enabling both phases of the analysis to incorporate this new idea. Furthermore, various numerical applications have been conducted to compare the effectiveness of the classic AI method, a 2017 technique known as ExtrAp, and the new approach called ExtrIn. Results indicate that ExtrIn outperforms both ExtrAp and the classic AI method, often significantly so in some cases. Moreover, the new approach can be seen as a form of optimization for the iterative simulations performed by the iteration depth, and existing methodologies such as optimization techniques for interpolation or approximation can be applied to improve performance. The proposed technique is available under open-source at https://github.com/jacopo-saracco/differential-ai. An additional, supplementary material is provided at https://github.com/smtcenter/differential-ai-supplement. This material describes in-depth the experiments and data collected, and the why specific choices were made in the study. The document is intended for an audience with some familiarity with Abstract Interpretation. The study appears to be the initial instance where Temporary Exactness is suggested as a means to improve Abstract Interpretation's approximation accuracy. The proposed Commutative ExtrIn property represents an innovative contribution in this field. The study also presents several novel challenges associated with evaluating ExtrIn, which may have value to other areas of program analysis. The study further indicates areas where existing AI is underdeveloped, specifically methodology for evaluating and understanding Abstract Interpretation-based approximate information, and algorithmically improving its accuracy. A subsequent paper has been written to further explore ExtrAp vs. ExtrIn, at https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-24534-4_23. The related study at https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.00994 presents an alternative called SpecIn for ExtrIn. To address this gap, we propose a framework that captures the concept of neighborhood fairness. Our method is built on two core components - the first enables the construction of equitable neighborhoods for any node in a graph and the second allows adaptation to accommodate specific data constraints. Notably, while numerous studies have explored link prediction, we delve into fair link prediction as part of the graph representation learning task. Through comprehensive evaluations, we showcase the effectiveness of our neighborhood fairness framework across multiple graph types and reveal its adaptability with restricted training data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that by increasing the size of the considered neighborhood, the proposed method can be modified to prioritize connection diversity, resulting in a novel approach to graph representation learning. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/sudharcl/fair_graph_learning. Our findings provide valuable insights that can facilitate the development of GNN models with enhanced ethical considerations. In particular, we confirm that strictly enforcing node-level and edge-level fairness can lead to contradictory scenarios and may hinder the relationship between a node and its neighbors. Hence, we introduce a localized neighborhood fairness metric known as Nuclear Fairness, which is derived from the Frobenius norm of the adjacency tensor and can be scaled according to nuclear rank. By balancing the nuclear rank with the size of the considered neighborhood, the method achieves scalability while ensuring neighborhood fairness. Our approach is versatile as it can be applied to various graph learning tasks such as node, edge, and triplet classification. Furthermore, we show that it is compatible with popular graph learning models and can be used in conjunction with optimization algorithms such as gradient descent, yielding similar results. Notably, with the help of our method, the edge prediction performance is substantially improved on the Facebook dataset400, resulting in a 5.0% increase in area under the ROC curve. Two proposed expectation models for temporary financial bubbles, involving individuals with varied predictions and positive influences, show that bubble collapse can be marked by an explosive growth in prices that suddenly ends at a certain random time. The varied predictions among rational individuals make it difficult to adjust expectations accurately, leading to a self-reinforcing feedback loop and rapid price escalation.
The unique characteristics of these models, including unpredictable times of termination and intricate equations involving infinite series, distinguish them from previously used equilibrium bubble models based on explicit termination times and earlier equation of motion descriptions. As such, conventional econometric analysis becomes problematic, the efficient market hypothesis loses relevance, and key features of these models are difficult to extract through traditional econometrics.
We propose an alternative two-stage method to extract explicit model parameters and test the connection between our extracted model parameters and actual market data during bubble events. Specifically, we use a hybrid method involving both explicit and implicit z-transforms to analyze two notorious bubbles, the 2008 Subprime housing bubble and the 2015 Chinese stock bubble, and demonstrate successful parameter recovery. Our study also shows that high statistical properties of price time series, such as multiple mean revisions and persistent behavior, corroborate the extracted model's findings. An additional econometric test for the extracted model's residuals further validates these results. Consequently, we propose a two-stage econometric method to identify and extract explicit model parameters of stochastic bubbles, providing a basis for comparison between actual market data and our expected model predictions. The potential applications and advancements of this two-stage approach are also discussed. Recent research has shown significant progress in improving recommender system performance through leveraging reviews, yet the limited availability of review data in existing models has proven to be a significant limitation. This issue is particularly crucial in review-based item recommendation tasks where review data can provide valuable insights into users' actual needs and help align recommendations with their preferences. Therefore, this paper develops a new model called SIFN - a Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network. SIFN is designed to integrate user-item interactions and review-based sentiment information in a way that is sensitive to changing user sentiment dynamics over time. Through explicit sentiment representation learning and inference of dynamic sentiment scores, SIFN is able to provide more effective recommendations that are aligned with actual user needs, thus producing superior performance on publicly available datasets and surpassing current state-of-the-art models. The associated code can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/mit3107/SIFN/tree/main/Published-VersionCode.pdf. Additionally, experimentally-driven analysis and ablation testing of key components are also presented to ensure rigorous validation of SIFN's robustness and accuracy. The results show that the suggested model is highly adaptable to datasets with significant semantic gaps and can effectively explore complex user sentiment patterns. Finally, important implications of these research findings for future research are proposed. The research approach demonstrated here could be extended to other recommendation tasks, for instance, motion picture recommendation based on user reviews. Focusing on AE and BA English-Arabic/Arabic-English CS, we examined the influence of n-gram based similarity metrics and word similarity sources on augmentation effectiveness. According to user studies, high-performing metrics identified through minimal human evaluation are 1) Bylex, 2) FastText, and 3) TokenBigram. We also observed that including contextual words in similarity metrics yields better results. Furthermore, we identified that exchanging nouns produces more natural CS sentences. This investigation provides insights into the factors affecting the success of lexical substitutions in data augmentation and suggests methods for selecting suitable substitutions. We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure. In contrast, a highly transitive group of orientation-preserving surface homeomorphisms is always topologically compact. This result verifies a 20-year-old conjecture of Ghys, specific to groups of surface homeomorphisms whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive. Our proof relies on combining the Nekrashevich model's properties with Furstenberg's theorem on ergodicity, the Tarski-Prikry forcing construction, and Naimark's compactness theorem. Leveraging Furstenberg's ergodicity theorem allows us to extend this result to certain polygon groups. We also prove that the group of block automorphisms associated with any polygon group is not topologically compact. Furthermore, using the Tarsky-Prikry forcing construction, it can be demonstrated that the supramenable nature of certain groups of surface homeomorphisms, specifically those whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive and using the compact-open topology's inherited structure, can be shown to be inconsistent with countable cardinality. This last finding verifies a 7-year-old conjecture of the first author. We also establish that the group of homeomorphisms of the open surface simplex that fix the boundary are not topologically compact, using a combination of Nekrashevich model properties and Prikry forcing construction. Finally, Naimark's compactness theorem reveals that the group of orientation-preserving homeomorphisms of the open surface simplex is topologically compact. As the demand for high-speed simulations grows, so does the need for efficient mesh relaxation methods. These techniques expand the flexibility of mesh editors by allowing the creation of complex shapes and surfaces with more freedom to be manipulated. In this paper, we explore advanced local improvements on primal/hybrid meshes containing a minimum of 57% hexahedra. To achieve optimal results, we develop innovative approaches to untangle twisted mesh structures, even in the most confined spaces with tets/hex ratios. Our proposed method builds upon the existing mesh relaxation framework by localizing improvements to distorted regions, incorporating constraints for spatial correlation and mesh quality objectives. High-resolution images and 3D models are used to test our method according to different scenarios. Our approach has a fast processing time of under 0.1 seconds and exhibits a mesh refinement improvement of up to 40% in terms of Cahh measure. Our method has been successfully applied in the context of computational fluid dynamics. Our code is openly available for research purposes on the GitHub platform.

Developed based on the critical recognition that inverter delay is a complex interplay of multiple process variables and load capacitance, the proposed model incorporates parameterized equations derived using Curve Fitting Toolbox in Matlab to accurately capture these dynamics. In comparison to simulation results generated by SPICE and the BSIM4 transistor model, the analytical delay model exhibits remarkably high precision, demonstrating an average error of less than 2% across an extensive range of technological parameters and output loads. As a result, the proposed model presents itself as a computationally efficient solution for diverse technology nodes and probabilistic gate delay characterisation applications. Moreover, this model's simplicity renders it highly adaptable for easy integration into various design tools and frameworks. To confirm its practical utility, the proposed model is successfully applied in computing statistical moments of gate delay. Finally, utilizing the derived delay model, the analysis successfully clarifies the key design structure contributing to the significant slowdown observed in nanoscale, high-SS (sub-threshold slope) FinFET technologies compared to traditional CMOS. Following rigorous validation against established models and simulation tools, the derived design-based explanations are found to accurately align with experimental measurement outcomes. To further highlight its practical implications, the derived insights are utilized as design metrics in optimizing a 22nm FinFET low-power Adder using the Cadence tool. Through the achieved significant power consumption reductions, it is demonstrated that the proposed model's analytical findings can positively impact the broader system-on-chip design process. Lastly, with minor adjustments, the proposed model's core assumptions can be suitably relaxed to facilitate its application to ultra-low voltage CMOS technologies characterized by weak channel current. assuming certain conditions. Often, researchers assume a certain level of consistency
in the decision-making model known as the Q-function. However, in numerous real-world scenarios,
this condition does not hold true. Instead, we propose a more adaptable way of measuring the consistency of Q-functions
in various complex environments. This new approach enables us to establish tighter limits on our model's behavior, resulting
in improved learning efficiency. Additionally, we provide a theoretical understanding of our approach and discuss its potential applications in continuous decision-making processes. This includes discussing its relevance to tasks with geometric constraints and common scenarios involving uncertain events. In support of our research, we include a case study involving decision-making in a dynamic transportation system. This case study highlights the practical benefits of our theoretical framework. Finally, we demonstrate our approach through a series of experimental evaluations, analyzing its efficiency in various real-world scenarios. These evaluations offer valuable insights into the characteristics of our algorithmic methods. One of the main advantages of our approach is illustrated in a graphical representation showing its practical efficiency in tasks with geometric constraints. This practical efficiency is the direct result of introducing a more adaptable way of measuring the consistency of Q-functions, effectively minimizing the impact of measurement errors on the model's behavior. The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data indicated distinct posterior regions associated with each. The results of this study demonstrate the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, revealing multiple governing principles such as social agency that shape our understanding of this phenomenon. The data also highlight the need for future research to incorporate multiple principles driving the animacy continuum. The findings of this study provide valuable insights for the development of more effective machine learning models, especially those designed to be interpretable, as they strive to replicate the complexity of the animacy organization evident in the human brain. The data and models generated during this research are available publicly. The code for our customized fMRI analysis tool using PySurfer is included in the supplemental materials. The data collected through this study can be accessed through the BGI Data dataset repository. The computational model employed in this research is based on the 318L LMS architecture described in the study's publications, available through the arXiv repository. The associated GitHub repository contains the data and models generated during this research. An expanded version of this study, including its methods and results, has been published in an internal BGI report.
