In scientific simulation, achieving precise replication of physical phenomena is a top priority. The issue of numerical approximation error arises even in idealized environments. This study focuses on partial differential equations, specifically on recovering the exact convex gradient of a solution while preserving its properties. This is accomplished through the application of a convex optimization-based SPF, designed to replicate the characteristics of the original solution. In developing a numerical technique for this optimization, we utilized the Douglas-Rachford algorithm. Our research includes analyzing stability, convergence, and efficiency in multidimensional settings, demonstrating great reductions in approximation error with minimal computational expense in 2D and 3D simulations. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in preserving the structural properties of the solution. To facilitate efficient computations, we implemented a matrix-free approach to the algorithm. We tested the SPF in various physical simulations, including Navier-Stokes equations and the Poisson equation. We also provided a demonstration of its potential to enhance regression models. We evaluated the effectiveness of the SPF in preserving the convexity of the solution in a 2D Navier-Stokes simulation with a range of flow regimes from highly viscous to non-Newtonian. Using a mesh-independent metric, we found that the SPF preserves at least 99.5% of the solution's convexity. We also demonstrated that the SPF achieves a 30% reduction in approximation error in 2D and 3D scenarios. To further assess its performance, we tested the SPF in preserving other solution properties in a 2D Navier-Stokes simulation. These results showed an improvement of up to 61% in the approximation error with a 40% increase in computational expense. We also evaluated the SPF's performance in preserving non-negative solutions in a Poisson equation simulation. These results indicated an improvement of up to 100% in the approximation error reduction with a 100% increase in computational expense. We also verified that enhancing the optimization algorithm's performance leads to greater reductions in the approximation error. Finally, we tested the SPF in preserving other solution properties in a 3D Navier-Stokes simulation with a coarse mesh. In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly for tasks requiring cooperation and communication, MARL agents are prone to being overly reactive to their social environment. As a result, they often make'stupid' mistakes and are overly influenced by their partners, leading their performance to fluctuate based on the state of their social environment. We introduce a new method called transfer empowerment that addresses this issue by empowering MARL agents to effectively evaluate the value of actions and develop consistent strategies, independent of their social context. This is achieved by adjusting the actor-critic target objective to prioritize maximising the mutual information between actions and rewards, and incorporating intrinsic motivation that facilitates transfer from observed partners to the MARL agent. By focusing on the social learning paradigm, our approach differs from traditional second-order autonomous learning methods. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach enables MARL agents to robustly and accurately learn from each other, even in challenging scenarios. Furthermore, our approach can be combined with various state-of-the-art MARL methods, and has been successfully applied to multiple task types, including the classic matrix chain multiplication experiment. The code for our approach is available on GitHub at https://github.com/azhihn/transfer_empowerment/tree/v1.0.0.0.0.0/tae-marl. We hope this research to provide a new perspective for the MARL community and ultimately, lead to the development of MARL agents with more stable decision-making. approach designed to leverage computer vision for identifying and 
transferring similarities and transitions across materials and their visual 
appearances. MatSim enables one-shot learning and classification for any 
material representation through an efficient pipeline incorporating 
physics-based rendering, streamlined dataset curation, and contrastive 
learning, ultimately leading to accurate predictions even in minimal 
available observations. MatSim promotes material vision understanding and 
bridges the gap between computer vision and materials science through an 
open-source implementation and benchmarking of benchmarks for one-shot 
learning and classification across materials, settings, and observer 
perspectives. MatSim is accessible at https://github.com/Sicklebill92/MatSim.

available at https://github.com/Sicklebill92/mat_sim_ospc.

classification, particularly through integration with popular object 
detection frameworks such as the Fast R-CNN model. 

We successfully apply MatSim to various applications, including one-shot 
learning and classification for effective texture transfer in computer 
vision, as well as predicting material parameters through fast editing in 
materials science and design. 

Ultimately, MatSim facilitates the understanding of materials, enabling 
efficient communication between materials scientists and computer vision 
specialists. We outline multiple avenues for extension and application 
beyond the current implementation of MatSim.

We introduce a novel method for local image feature matching, where instead of a sequential process, we first identify pixel-wise dense matches at an elementary level and refine the good matches. Our approach, called LoFTR, stands out for its simplicity in the detection phase, where instead of using convolutional neural networks, we use self-attention mechanisms to directly capture cross-image features. Our dense matching phase utilizes a consistent coordinate framework, ensuring that matching coordinates are defined consistently across all images and their respective pixel distributions analyzed. Experiments show that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art local feature matching methods and achieves comparable performance to deep learning-based image matching methods. The generalized form of the Einstein theory, the Rastall theory of gravity, incorporates the law of conservation of energy and momentum. We derive a charged black string solution using the Newman-Janis approach in a Rastall theory background. For nonrotating charged black string, the Rastall theory yields negative branching points, and the horizon's radius is influenced by the Rastall parameter. We analyze the behavior of the black string's singularity, showing that the Rastall parameter affects the horizon's location. We then consider Hawking radiation from a charged black string and study the influence of the Rastall parameter on Hawking energy and momentum. Since Hawking energy and momentum have complex forms, we calculate their real parts, representing Hawking radiation. We find that Hawking energy and Hawking pressure exhibit oscillating behavior with varying Rastall parameter and black string charge. Additionally, we assess the impact of the Rastall parameter on Hawking energy and momentum for nonrotating and rotating charged black strings (with spin parameter $k=0$). We derive a charged black string solution using the Newman-Janis approach, and Hawking energy and momentum are analyzed. Due to complex expressions, we consider specific cases of charged black strings in the context of the Rastall parameter. We then discuss the effect of the Rastall parameter on Hawking energy and momentum for various values of spin parameter $k$. We observe that Hawking energy and momentum increase or decrease depending on the combination of Rastall parameter and spin parameter. Both the Newman-Janis approach and direct integration method yield black holes as solutions to the Rastall equation; however, we focus on charged black strings in this study. We hope this study contributes to the understanding of modified gravity theories and the complexity of deriving black hole solutions in these theories. (This is the last research paper by the author. The research on extremely old and metal-poor stars within our Galaxy is instrumental in grasping its chemical evolution and the origin of star formation. These stars are rare, and only five have been detected so far with a metal content below -5.0. Recent data release from Gaia, which covers 219 million sources, presents an immense opportunity to identify metal-poor stars. Our research involves utilizing low-resolution spectra from Gaia to identify metal-poor stars, focusing particularly on selecting elderly stars. Our algorithm is centered on three elements: selecting metal-poor stars, identifying extremely old stars, and integrating these selections. In doing so, 202 metal-poor star candidates were found with a metal content lower than -5.0, and these were cross-checked against known star databases. Out of 202 candidates, 160 were found to match stars with a metal content lower than -5.0 in the Heliocentric Galaxy, Han et al., and LAMOST databases. Additionally, 42 candidates were discovered with a metal content lower than -3.0, and three of these were known stars with a metal content lower than -5.0 in the Heliocentric Galaxy and LAMOST databases. Our research also demonstrates that selecting metal-poor stars with a high S/N ratio and effective temperature has the greatest significance. Moreover, selecting metal-poor stars with a high surface gravity and low helium content produces a smaller number of false positives. These candidates were cross-checked against the ZYGAIA model, and 11 were found with a metal content lower than -5.0 and an age of more than 10 million years old, indicating their likelihood of being genuine metal-poor stars. Although the research has its limitations, such as the absence of Fe, which affects low-mass stars selection, and contamination from dwarf stars, which needs to be reduced, it lays the groundwork for identifying rare metal-poor stars within Gaia's upcoming fourth data release. We've conducted a thorough examination of eight distinct methods for evaluating the morphological intricacy of languages. These measures have different prerequisites for data annotation, yet our study identifies both similarities and disparities among them. We compare the methods visually and statistically to ascertain how they correlate with typological characteristics. This investigation seeks to determine whether these metrics assess the same underlying aspect of language or, alternatively, measure different facets of morphological complexity. The results from principal component analysis suggest that a substantial portion of variation across the eight measures is linearly associated. Conversely, our regression analysis using the WALS traits for English languages demonstrates that only two of the measures are independent, whereas the others exhibit significant correlations with existing linguistics metrics or, in some cases, each other. Notably, our findings challenge the prevailing consensus that languages with inflectional systems derive minimal morphological complexity from them. Furthermore, as evidenced by our map of morphological complexity for languages worldwide, including varieties not typically included in standardized tests, there exist instances of increased intricacy compared to expected patterns informed by typological characteristics. This suggests opportunities to develop more effective learning methods for languages with complex inflectional systems. Building upon this insight, we outline a novel approach to crafting morphologically complex artificial languages, thereby advancing our understanding of what these measures truly measure. This study culminates in recommendations for English language varieties to enhance their morphological complexity, which could, in turn, inspire novel artificial languages to mimic natural languages more effectively. In particular, our analysis suggests that an artificial language could be `maximally human' by systematically utilizing suffixes to convey distinct meanings across word forms. Ultimately, our investigation sheds light on what these measures actually quantify within languages. In accordance with practical principles, our work is accompanied by a freely accessible data repository containing computed intricacy scores for over 2000 English varieties worldwide, as well as an interactive, web-based map allowing users to discover which English varieties possess unusually high or low morphological complexity given their inherent characteristics. In total, our findings answer a fundamental question regarding language, thereby inspiring further research into the underlying language mechanics. Identifying trending social media events in real-time across various geographical locations is crucial, particularly for anticipating incidents such as accidents, protests, or breaking news. The dynamic nature of social media data demands processing strategies that combine speed and accuracy while also accounting for the disparate structures present in such data - points, sequences, and graphs. In this study, we present a novel approach to uncovering spatio-temporally related events from social media data using a multi-stage framework. The framework leverages a pre-processing phase for data transformation, integrates a graph-based method for event extraction via sequence scanning, and employs a clustering algorithm for event aggregation, all of which are executed in parallel to enhance processing efficiency. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated through comprehensive quantitative analyses of real-world data from social networks like Twitter and Google+ in three distinct countries, covering a span of one year, an effort that we complemented with a qualitative examination of the results. Notably, our approach successfully detected 95.5% of anticipated events from Google+ data in advance, achieved a clustering purity of 87.3%, and accurately localized 60% of Google+ and 41% of Twitter data on a map, while accurately determining their respective publication times to a minute. Furthermore, our approach successfully detected 61.7% and 34.1% of anticipated events from Google+ and Twitter datasets, respectively, as seen in a recent Google+ outbreak. The observed outcomes of our experiments demonstrate the superiority of our proposed methodology in uncovering events in a timely and efficient manner. Nonclassical properties in continuous-variable quantum systems are often marked by quantum correlations and Wigner negativity. This study explores how these two nonclassical traits are connected in the context of Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen (EPR)-like scenarios involving measurements. Specifically, we uncover instances where Wigner negativity is guaranteed in the quantum state of the unmeasured subsystem, provided that certain quantum nonlocal effects are present during measurements. Additionally, we illustrate examples that establish a correlation between the necessary conditions for both quantum steering and Wigner negativity. Moreover, we demonstrate through numerical simulations that these connections remain relevant even in more complex scenarios with multiple degrees of freedom. Ultimately, our findings refine our understanding of the relationships between quantum correlations, Wigner negativity, and quantum steering in continuous-variable systems. Accurate secure boundary analysis is crucial for practical quantum key distribution systems, but the current approach overlooks a critical aspect – the randomness consistency of seeds used in privacy amplification. We introduce and prove a quantum leftover hash lemma that applies to non-uniform random seeds, leveraging min-entropy, and subsequently establish a detailed method for secure boundary analysis in general quantum key distribution scenarios. Utilizing an online QKD simulator, we test a real-world experiment involving light intensity attacks, observing a discrepancy between the actual random seeds used in QKD and the assumed uniform distribution in traditional secure boundary analysis methods. Our modified analysis closely estimates the actual secure boundaries, demonstrating its accuracy. Notably, our analysis method can accommodate various quantum key distribution protocols without modification. Although the analysis is previously formulated but not validated, our numerical results reveal that neglecting the random non-uniformity of seeds in secure boundary analysis leads to a noticeable underestimation of the actual secure boundaries by about one bit, which can cause concern in practical QKD systems, especially those using Shannon cipher since the QKD distance and Shannon bound show linear correlation. In order to ensure secure communication, standard deviation of the actual random seeds should be evaluated first, and a linear correlation coefficient should be calculated based on experimental data. If the standard deviation is less than the underestimation threshold (one bit in our experiment), and the linear correlation coefficient is within a specified threshold, then the actual secure boundary can be estimated by the classical QKD distance. Otherwise, an auxiliary post-processing procedure should be used to remove the linear dependence, and the corrected classical QKD distance can be used for actual secure communication. In our experiment, the numerical results show an average one bit underestimation, and a correlation coefficient of 0.9991, indicating that the actual secure boundary can be estimated by the classical QKD distance without additional measures. Furthermore, the numerical results show that the auxiliary post-processing method does not significantly affect the actual secure boundary in most cases. Due to the linear correlation issue and the underestimation threshold in the standard method, we propose that the actual secure boundary should be estimated by the QKD distance with a one bit correction instead of the previously assumed QKD distance, leading to an improvement of about two orders of magnitude in the practical range, thereby significantly enhancing the efficiency of secure communication. Our numerical findings are obtained using an online QKD simulator, and we expect that our method can be seamlessly transferred to real-world experiments due to the high correlation coefficient of 0.9991 found in our tests.

Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of its symbol template, followed by thresholding to determine the signal's sign. Nonetheless, this method's reliance on short templates and the presence of a differential encoding scheme to combat fading effects comes at a cost, resulting in suboptimal performance in scenarios with significant fading levels. To enhance its performance, various enhanced methods have been developed, such as the use of delayed decision differential encoding and multi-level signaling, among others. In this study, we present an alternative enhanced method that builds upon the standard technique's core idea by introducing a novel combined detector that incorporates both delayed versions of the signal template. By doing so, we achieve improved error rates without the need for additional encoding schemes or increased complexity. Our simulations indicate that this method outperforms the standard approach, demonstrating a significant performance boost, with gains of up to 2 dB possible under certain adverse conditions. What's more, this method's success is largely unaffected by the signal's complexity, with our simulations showing comparable gains for different signal bandwidths. In summary, this proposed method offers improved performance over the standard approach, with benefits extending to a wide range of signals, from those with basic properties to more advanced ones. As a result, this method can be effectively applied to various practical scenarios, with our simulations estimating that it could achieve a performance increase of: $ (i) $ up to 1.7, 2, and 2.3 dB gain for $B_T=6,~12,$ and $24$ bandwidths when considering square-shaped QPSK signals; $ (ii) $ a 2, 3, and 4 dB gain when considering rectangular QPSK signals of the Rayleigh fading type. Importantly, this method's performance surpasses that of several well-established techniques, such as the pre-filtering method, while also largely reducing its complexity. Along the same lines, this method's performance is similar to that of the widely used generalized Gaussian FIR filter, although our simulations show that it requires only $38\%$ of its complexity to achieve a performance increase of this nature. Ultimately, this method's simplicity and the significant performance improvements it achieves over the standard approach, as well as other established methods with similar or less complexity, make it highly suitable for practical applications. In response, we present TiWS-iForest, a weakly supervised version of the Isolation Forest algorithm, tailored for resource-constrained IoT devices. Moreover, the proposed system supports online learning and maintains an accurate detection rate of 83% with 1% false positive rate even with 10% labelled data, showcasing its efficiency and effectiveness in real-world applications. Recent photometric studies of the first population stars within the galactic globular clusters revealed heterogeneity in metallicity, contradicting their previously believed uniform initial composition. However, previous spectroscopic data produced mixed results, fueling further investigation. A thorough high-resolution analysis was conducted on five bright red giant stars within the NGC 2808 cluster, using atmospheric parameters sourced from the literature and resulting in precise iron, silicon, calcium, titanium, and nickel abundance measurements with low margins of error. Despite minimal uncertainties, these targeted stars demonstrated a notable 0.25 dex range of iron content. A striking pattern emerged, as the iron content directly correlated with the star's location in the cluster chromosome map - bluer stars contained less iron. In line with the expected metal spread observed in other clusters, this variation in iron content was found to be consistent with a normal distribution. The presence of elevated nickel abundance within the subgiant USC1, positioned at the blue edge of the cluster's chromosome map, further supports the hypothesis of distinct stellar populations within NGC 2808. However, the data also indicate that silicon, calcium, and titanium abundances remain uniform across the cluster. In combination with photometric data, these novel spectroscopic findings suggest the presence of multiple stellar populations within NGC 2808, characterized by distinct iron content variations. Ultimately, this study contributes to our understanding of galaxy evolution in the local Universe, particularly through the observation of metal dilution in dynamically relaxed clusters. A detailed discussion explores the implications of these findings, potentially related to the introduction of enriched enrichment material during the formation of the second population within NGC 2808. In addition, these results underscore the significance of spatially targeted phase-space sampling in achieving precise, high-recognition spectroscopic measurements - a theme particularly relevant for future studies of multiple population globular clusters in the galaxy. Image search algorithms that retrieve and identify copied images from large databases comprise two main components: a neural network that converts an image into a transformation-resistant vector, and a high-performance but imperfect search algorithm. This paper introduces active indexing to optimize the interplay between these components. By quickly examining a subset of stored images, the system learns which components are under-performing and where improvements can be made most efficiently. Multiple imaging tests are conducted to rapidly generate new image vectors and assess their effectiveness in the search algorithm. Notably, our method yields a 32-fold reduction in the database size required for a commercial system after one day of processing, and significantly boosts the search speed and accuracy after optimizing the system parameters through active learning. Furthermore, our technique adapts to new image variants better than a passive system, and outperforms state-of-the-art passive methods in the long run. After one week of development, our fully active system achieves a search accuracy of 0.00017, an improvement of 1000 times over the initial value of 0.1, and surpasses the best passive method, which achieved an accuracy of 0.165. We investigate the influence of a quantum field vacuum on the angular momentum of a charge q moving in a uniform magnetic field. The orbital angular momentum generated is due to non-resonant electromagnetic waves emitted by the charge q, which are produced through photon splitting in the quantum vacuum. The source of this orbital angular momentum is similar to the orbital angular momentum associated with the spin of the quantum vacuum, which is also referred to as "circular polarization of electromagnetic waves". Our results show that in the case of a charge q moving in a uniform magnetic field, the orbital angular momentum generated is twice the magnetic moment of the charge, which is induced as a result of the non-resonant electromagnetic waves, leading to the following relationship: $L_{\mathrm{EM}}=2\mu_B=2\mu_B s$, where $L_{\mathrm{EM}}$ is the orbital angular momentum generated, $\mu_B$ is the Bohm magneton and $s$ is the spin of the charge. Additionally, we found that this orbital angular momentum generated is equivalent to the Zel'dovich orbital angular momentum associated with the quantum vacuum, which is produced as a result of the non-resonant electromagnetic waves emitted by a moving charge in a quantum field under the influence of a uniform magnetic field. The quantity of Zel'dovich orbital angular momentum is directly proportional to the fourth order of the fine structure constant and is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between the charge and the point of observation. The primary goal of Fine-Grained Named Entity Typing (FG-NET) is to accurately classify various entity types, typically achieved by constructing a knowledge base and a training dataset including the target entities and their corresponding fine-grained labels. However, the growth in the number of existing entity types and their associated sub-types has made it increasingly difficult to efficiently construct such a knowledge base and train the model without significant computational costs. To address this challenge, previous research has applied various graph-based neural networks to FG-NET, but these attempts were ultimately met with limited success. Refining search in hyperbolic space has shown significant potential in reducing computational costs and improving accuracy, so we have incorporated this approach into FGNET-RH, a novel refinery-based hyperbolic search framework for FG-NET. FGNET-RH involves constructing an entity graph using the distilled entity knowledge and refining the search within the hyperbolic space using an optimized approach. By integrating our innovative search algorithm and refinery methods, FGNET-RH can accurately classify fine-grained entity labels while efficiently searching through vast datasets, and our experiments confirm the superiority of FGNET-RH over state-of-the-art models. Achieving efficient and sustainable operation in cloud data centers largely relies on load balancing, and virtualization makes it possible to apply load balancing at different levels, including the network, host, and virtual machine (VM) levels. Since fine-grained load balancing, especially at the VM level, requires detailed information about VMs and their workloads, it is typically applied last in the hierarchy. However, VM creation requests can arrive at the cloud management system at any time with varying levels of information available about the requested VMs. Therefore, the load balancing strategy must be able to transition from coarser to more refined approaches as needed. This work introduces a novel load balancing strategy, called prepartition, which operates at the host level but with a refined VM-based approach. When a new VM is created, the prepartition strategy initially places each VM on a different host. As more detail about the requested VMs becomes available, the loading strategy can adjust the placement of these VMs based on the expected resource usage of each VM. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the prepartition strategy in ensuring efficient load balancing in cloud data centers. Significant physical harm can result from cyber assaults on Industrial Control Systems. Although in-person assessments can reveal vulnerable system components, they may not be effective against covert attacks that bypass detection during prolonged operations. We present a predictive real-time monitoring method in this study to identify whether a monitored Linear Time-Invariant system is safe from stealthy attacks at any given time. Our method incorporates previous attack experiences, is not dependent on previous incident data, and requires the solution of a specific set of matrix equations. We also establish a mathematical guarantee that the proposed method has a computational complexity of O((nd^2)^(L+1)) with proper parameter choice, where n is the system size, d is the number of system states, and L is the number of previous attack experiences. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method on both attack simulation and real-world case studies. We show the proposed method has a high degree of accuracy for multiple sets of parameters and outperforms the state-of-the-art method in computational efficiency. Our research also highlights the relationship between computation time and the likelihood of attacks in the training data, revealing a practical trade-off for practical applications. You can find the related code at https://github.com/Fengxi-Zhan/EffPredictiveMonitoring.

A precise summary can be derived from lengthy written documents via deep learning models, but English language models often benefit from larger datasets and pre-trained tools, whereas summarization for lesser-known Indian languages is hindered by data scarcity and a lack of suitable tools. Our solution, GAE-ISumm, suggests combining GraphAutoEncoders with WordPiece Embeddings to develop powerful neural networks for these under-resourced languages, using small, specially created training datasets. Additionally, our models are designed to be compatible with the officially recommended annotation standard for Indian language summarization, thereby facilitating seamless integration with existing datasets. Evaluations conducted on Gujarati language datasets revealed that our proposed models successfully matched the performance of their more substantial English-based counterparts, achieving an F1-score of 38.68 on the test set. Our study also explores the versatility of the officially recommended annotation standard with nearby language summarization tasks. The full source code and implementation of our model can be found at https://github.com/jaysonn/gae-isumm. Our study contributes first-hand insights into developing and assessing under-resourced Indian language summarization models, along with several practical solutions to associated challenges. Furthermore, in accordance with best practices within the research community, our study provides detailed ethical considerations regarding data availability and a thorough analysis of our findings, including relevant results from an internal consistency check. Ultimately, our study promotes future advancements in under-resourced understudied language NLP tasks such as summarization by recommending the introduction of simpler transfer experiments. The findings of our study have significant practical implications as they successfully establish the feasibility of accurately extracting key points from lengthy written documents across various Indian languages employing similar neural network architectures as those used for English summaries. Moreover, our study demonstrates the potential for enriching the existing officially recommended annotation standard through enrichment by incorporating adjacent language summarization datasets. A novel approach to quantizing log-likelihood ratio storage utilizing neural networks is presented. It was discovered that average L-values of QAM symbols consistently adhere to an ordered relationship, rendering them suitable for representation through categorical information. A neural quantizer network capable of converting categorical representations back to the original fixed-point format was then proposed. For low-bitization applications, simple networks such as the Categorical 1D Convolutional Network (CAT-Net) were found effective. However, for more complex scenarios involving higher numbers of symbol bits, a more advanced architecture based on the Conditional Channel Distribution Quantizer (CCD-Q) was developed. A method for estimating the conditional channel distribution was also introduced. The proposed method demonstrates favorable performance in terms of spectral distance, and outperforms traditional method such as maximum-likelihood based quantization. It was observed that the L-values predicted by the CAT-Net are highly uniform, whereas those produced by the CCD-Q contain more nuanced information. Ultimately, combination of these two networks yields superior results. A comparison with conventional method in terms of error rate performance is scheduled for discussion. It is anticipated that this work will contribute to the development of practical low-bitization approaches for Gray-coded modulation schemes. We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs. We contrast our results with a new, parameterized intractability result concerning modifying primary links in a given upward planar layout to ensure upward planarity. Our analysis is based on the treewidth parameter, showing that even for treewidth-$k$ graphs, unless P equals NP, we cannot efficiently identify an upward planar layout with fixed link modifications in less than $2^{O(k)}$ time. However, if we restrict ourselves to treedepth parameterizations, we demonstrate that link modifications with fixed source link adjustments are tractable, even at the cost of exponentially large factors. Furthermore, we illustrate the practical applicability of our treedepth algorithm to applications such as controlling air traffic and data pipeline management. We believe that our new algorithms, along with our empirical evaluation, contribute significant value to continuing active research in upward planarity and graph layout design. Our provided Python code embeds the new XP algorithm and fixed-parameter algorithm for treedepth, which was implemented using the XLitchi graph library and planarity module. This code builds upon SPQR tree-decomposition infrastructure from the SageMath Computer Algebra System and the trupath library, a C++11 implementation of treedepth computation. For further details on our algorithms' execution in the airline scenario, see the airtraffic Python script, which integrates the upward planarity computation with Boeing's air traffic model. We hope that our design and implementation influence future upward planarity and graph layout design research, incorporating the increasing adoption of parameterized algorithmic techniques and computational experiments in the graph and combinatorics community. We conclude by listing 49 additional graph layout and planarity-related problems, many of which originate from our own research and may serve as future challenging problems for the community to solve. A copy of this list can be found in the Appendices. Crowdsourced image datasets, often marred by noise, pose a significant challenge for even the most sophisticated neural networks. This difficulty arises from class imbalance and uncertainties in labeling, issues that are particularly prevalent in datasets consisting of images of ancient Greek papyri such as AL-ALL and AL-PUB, where individual characters are closely cropped from these images. The application of ensemble modeling to datasets of this nature can aid in identifying and quantifying the reliability of images with uncertain labels. This can be achieved through ensemble modeling using stacked generalization, incorporating multiple networks. Specifically, this method involves utilizing two ResNets, with one employing cross-entropy and the other using Kullback-Leibler Divergence as its loss function. The combination of image datasets labeled uncertainly, namely the 'Human Softmax' and k-nearest neighbor models, constitutes a novel approach that utilizes ensemble modeling. Utilizing this method on the AL-ALL and AL-PUB datasets revealed increased consistency in labeling following the identification of reliable images, with the inverted Kullback-Leibler Divergence (inKLD) metric serving as the basis for decision-making prior to the fine-tuning of these networks. Notably, these findings also highlight the inherent limitations of these networks in addressing complex papyrological tasks. Furthermore, this method enabled the accurate classification of individual characters despite significant variability within the training datasets, effectively overcoming challenges posed by overfitting due to data augmentation. Lastly, the presented method also serves as a means to assess the uncertainty of model predictions, with the use of entropy measures providing insight into the level of confidence a network should have in its own predictions. Following preliminary testing, it was found that the selected dataset, consisting of images of individual characters, was relatively free from labeling imprecision in contrast to whole-papyri datasets such as AL-PUB. Consequently, the application of ensemble modeling with stacked generalization, employing ResNets and incorporating methods like inKLD and k-nearest neighbor, may aid in identifying and mitigating noisy data points that may be present in datasets of this nature. Nonetheless, additional research is required to fully assess the efficacy of this method in addressing decision-making uncertainties that may arise. One such area for future research could involve the development of methods to rectify noisy data points, either by identifying them or by correcting them. Similarly, the present method may also be applied in addressing decision-making uncertainties that may arise in other fields. This decay is independent of the choice of metric and can depend on the specific observables chosen. Furthermore, for semiflows with weak expansion that exhibit slow decay in correlations, we can prove a similar result. Additionally, for semiflows with globally expanding dynamics, we can prove the exponential decay in the supremum norm of transfer operators acting on bounded observables. This decay is then applied to understand the exponential decay in the supremum norm of invariant measures for semiflows with globally expanding dynamics. It is made up of different symbols and certain sub-matrices must include each combination of those symbols a set number of times. The best, or smallest, such matrices are known as optimal, and if they have uniform distribution of those symbols across all columns they're also referred to as uniform. Historically, optimal matrices had been constructed in only a few ways. However, a 1996 paper suggested a different method which had the potential to yield new, or "new-old", optimal matrices. However, for nearly 20 years after this suggestion, no one could figure out how to actually construct these matrices using this approach. However, our own attempts at combining techniques from combinatorics and graph theory have allowed us to construct many of these matrices, and even prove a couple of the statements related to their construction, showing the method from that 1996 paper is indeed effective after all. Our new method has also allowed us to cover previously unexplored cases in this field of optimization. Furthermore, we've also explored a related optimization problem known as the weak covering array, and using our own techniques has allowed us to gain a better understanding of this problem as well. A notable interconnection exists between the LH class and the 'NISZ' class of nonlocal operations using noisy isotropic states. In this work, all nonlocal games with noisy maximally entangled states are declared decidable. This declaration relies on two main findings - a characterization of 'truncated' two-player tensor products using unitary equivalence, and a comprehensive description of low-cost quantum protocols in terms of NISZ operations. These conclusions provide a possible explanation for a significant puzzle. Many companies use a standard framework that measures "average treatment effect" (ATE), but there's a significant challenge to increase its detection power while maintaining "false discovery rate" (FDR) within a predetermined threshold. Popular algorithms like the BH method struggle to control FDR, particularly when encountering positive dependence, which requires null observations to have a lower value to produce a valid discovery. In this paper, we propose new statistical techniques based on "hidden-summation" that effectively showcase their ability to effectively manage "controlled FDR" under positive dependence with successively stronger assumptions. We also present an algorithm based on "belief propagation" that can efficiently calculate the new HSR method, which offers powerful statistical properties including FDR control, dependence robustness, and positive dependence invariance. In addition, we also show an algorithm based on "thresholding" that can efficiently calculate the new HSBR method, which offers even tighter bounds under positive dependence. We evaluate our proposed algorithms using real-world data from Google Ads and Microsoft Azure, and the experimental results show that we can effectively detect ATE up to 5 to 7 times more strongly than the standard methods. The FNAL muon magnetic moment measurement also displays a $4.2\sigma$ discrepancy. In an effort to resolve the anomalies in both the W boson and muon (g-2), we have investigated the type-X two Higgs doublet model. Our analysis focused on the type-X 2HDM's parameter space for $m_A$ and $\tan\beta$, ensuring compatibility with the muon (g-2), lepton universality test, and CDF II's latest W boson mass findings. We determined that measuring the $h\to AA$ branching ratio and the mass of the extra Higgs $A$ would be essential for validating the effectiveness of this model in resolving the observed anomalies. Our study revealed that for a $35\%$ contribution of the type-X 2HDM to the muon (g-2) measurement, we require $m_A$ to be within $200\mathrm{GeV}<m_A<300\mathrm{GeV}$. Additionally, we found that for $m_A = 250\mathrm{GeV}$ and $\tan\beta = 20$, the type-X 2HDM can potentially resolve both the W boson and muon (g-2) anomalies at the High-Luminosity LHC with the construction of a Higgs factory. Our analysis provides a framework and guidelines for reconciling the recently measured values of the W boson and muon (g-2) within the type-X 2HDM framework. Adaptive synchronization in interactions, or entrainment, involves the participants in a conversation adapting or matching each other's distinctive vocal traits. To better grasp how people adapt to each other's communication style during conversations, it's necessary to analyze various acoustic characteristics and compare them through multiple measurement techniques. This work introduces a novel turn-level metric, referred to as the Neural Entrainment Distance (NED), developed using an unsupervised deep learning approach. NED establishes a method for identifying patterns within a dataset and uses them to create a common representation, or embedding, from population-wide entrainment characteristics. By testing the measure with a selection of acoustic features, we experimentally validate its effectiveness in distinguishing real conversations from artificially constructed, randomly reordered conversations. Additionally, we demonstrate the practical relevance of the proposed metric through evidence gathered from real-world interactions, revealing a significant correlation between NED scores and the emotional connection reported during suicide assessment interviews. This association aligns with previous studies. By leveraging deep learning technology, we have designed a groundbreaking, unsupervised entrainment metric with far-reaching potential for conversational analysis in multiple fields. Similar metrics could likely be developed for other domains as well. The proposed approach provides a framework for measuring and comparing entrainment among different groups, utilizing a variety of acoustic features, and might be applied to data sets beyond speech-based interactions. Furthermore, we have incorporated NED into a decision tree ensemble, allowing for population-wide unsupervised clustering based on entrainment characteristics. The accompanying AICHAO repository offers detailed step-by-step guidelines for replicating the proposed approach. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the outside-in generalizability of the model by successfully applying it to nonEnglish conversations. The proposed NED metric, along with its many potential real-world applications, could be further expanded to accommodate multimodal as well as semantic features. Moreover, we have introduced a simple yet effective technique for modeling variable-length sequences within a decision tree, followed by transfer learning, allowing for its adaptation to data sets with different numbers of observations. The models we have developed can be used to analyze a wide array of practical entrainment problems. NED can be used not only in conjunction with other relevant metrics but also in combination with visual cues and semantic properties. Furthermore, we have provided guidance on incorporating pop-independent norms into NED. The models we have designed with large amounts of data can also be utilized for multiclass entrainment classification by incorporating multiple related classes as a single collective. Domain adaptation has been applied extensively to handle distribution shifts across various fields like vision, language, and multimedia. Most existing domain adaptation techniques leverage domain-invariant features by utilizing both source and target domain data. However, when source data is inaccessible due to privacy concerns, this strategy becomes impractical. To address this issue, we propose a novel method for adaptive domain transfer that does not require source data. Our approach involves transferring domain-invariant language representations through a semi-supervised approach using a combination of unsupervised and supervised objectives. We demonstrate that our method can effectively adapt models across different domains without requiring any data from the source domain. Experimental results on multiple semantic parsing benchmarks reveal a significant boost in performance after applying our transfer technique from a highly diverse source domain to a target domain under a zero-shot setting. Furthermore, our method also showcases its adaptability in zero-shot settings across various target domains without requiring any modifications. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/jayeldee/SFT. This paper extends an earlier conference publication (AAAI'22) with additional experimental validation metrics and theoretical adjustments. A comprehensive analysis of nuclear power systems designed for Deep Space transport is presented, utilizing an advanced Gas Core Reactor (GCR) integrated with a magnetohydrodynamic generator. A compact GCR with low atomic number fuel (liquid Lithium) and an optimized isotopic fuel mix has been formulated to meet the specific energy requirements of the Apollo missions, exceeding the efficiency of traditional thermal nuclear systems. Furthermore, the system's capabilities to provide heat, produce electricity, and carry pressurized cargo have been optimized through an in-depth study, revealing significant advantages over conventional thermal converters. It is demonstrated that GCR systems offer substantial benefits, including reduced system mass, increased specific mission energy, extended lifetimes, and simplified cooling systems. The evaluation was based on detailed nuclear, thermodynamic, electrical, mechanical, and computational modeling, culminating in a thorough cost-benefit analysis of this innovative GCR power system. The success of this approach is exemplified by the first practical implementation of GCR technology since its initial development in the 1960s. It is anticipated that the insights gained from this research will facilitate the development of various GCR configurations for space applications, paving the way for systematic optimization and engineering development. It is expected that the lessons learned will be widely applicable to other nuclear energy conversion systems for space exploration and other fields. We have extended quantum resource theories to encompass complex scenarios that involve multiple interconnected resources. In such applications, an element is considered a resource if it serves a particular purpose, and enforcement of its associated rules makes up the underlying framework. In order to study the relationships between interconnected resources, we have developed a theoretical approach in accordance with the first law of general quantum resource theories. This principle indicates the preservation of internal relationships among resource Hilbert spaces. Our approach also allows the formulation of dual resource theories by identifying two distinct perspectives: one focusing on the resource itself and the other on the environment. By formulating general criteria for interconnected resources and first law compliance, we have shown the existence of two fundamental resource theories, which we have demonstrated in practical terms through the analysis of the interference of Lewis states. Furthermore, we have uncovered a broader range of interconnected scenarios, including the combination of erasable and abusable resources and the transformation of resources from environments to elements. Our research offers a framework for studying the intricate relationships between various types of interconnected resources. It also sheds light on the challenges of interpreting results from quantum information theory when applied to complex scenarios and provides a deeper understanding of the underlying principles. Examples of potential applications can be found in contexts such as jamming, fractality, and the principles governing the destruction and creation of quantum states. Our work delimits the scope of applications that can be justified by the first law of general quantum resource theories and aids in the formulation of dual resource theories, which can be used in a variety of scenarios including quantum cloning, entanglement manipulation, and metrics quantifying the utility of quantum states. In summary, we have developed a theoretical approach in accordance with the first law of general quantum resource theories, which can be applied to various types of interconnected resources and has practical implications for their study. This approach facilitates a deeper understanding of the relationships between interconnected resources and may be easily adapted to different resource theories in order to study the properties of quantum information. More broadly, it can be used as a unifying framework for quantum information theory, which may be helpful in advancing theoretical discussions and applications. One potential direction for future work is to uncover additional general principles that are not necessarily reflected in the behavior of multiple interconnected resources. Such principles could be highly valuable in refining the understanding of quantum information theories. Recent searches for supersymmetry at the classical level have not provided any conclusive signs of new physics within the framework of the Standard Model. In the SUSY parameter space, specifically in the region where SUSY masses exceed those of the top quark, there remains a lack of strong evidence. This presentation will discuss secondary analysis results from the CMS experiment aimed at exploring two high-priority regions in the SUSY parameter space. Firstly, we will focus on the region where light gauginos are likely, accompanied by a median mass gluino of 2 TeV. To achieve this, we are utilizing simulated data and developing novel searches for long-duration, high-luminosity particle collisions. Secondly, we will investigate the region where light Higgs bosons are likely, accompanied by a median mass wino of 3 TeV. To achieve this, we are simulating and promoting specific particle decays where the neutral Higgs boson is predominantly produced via strong forces. In these regions, the sensitivity of these new searches can be significantly improved, representing key opportunities for further investigation. Additionally, we are also promoting additional searches for light neutralinos and winos, with the goal of covering the entire SUSY parameter space through the rapid re-analysis of real experiment data. In total, the additional search sensitivity can cover approximately 22% of the entire SUSY parameter space by mass, while also reserving 78% for future investigation. Furthermore, with the remaining 1% probability, the SUSY parameter space not covered by these searches may hold particles with sufficiently low masses to remain undetectable even with the highest possible detection thresholds. Ultimately, the remaining SUSY parameter space not covered by these searches may only be revealed using detectors of even higher energy and sensitivity in the future particle accelerator. The future particle accelerator, known as the HL-LHC, is designed to improve sensitivity by a factor of three, with the future international linear collider achieving a sensitivity improvement of a thousand fold. Following the completion of these projects, it is projected that the remaining SUSY parameter space not covered by current searches may finally be fully revealed. In particular, it is expected that the remaining 1% probability of low-mass SUSY particles can only be explained by their respective masses ranging from 200 GeV to the Planck scale in order to remain undetectable even with the highest possible detection thresholds. In the region of their theoretical explanation, it is expected that the remaining SUSY parameter space not covered by these searches may finally be fully understood following the completion of these projects

Temporal sequence analysis typically involves time-series data that are either short-term and high-dimensional or long-term and low-dimensional, yet both are infrequently found together. In supervised learning, particularly in the life sciences, this issue poses significant challenges. To address this, a multi-signal extension of the heat equation is proposed, enabling the transformation of short-term, high-dimensional data into long-term, low-dimensional patterns that are more amenable to classification or regression. This transformed data often displays more distinct patterns, better separability, and reduced noise. To utilize this transformation in supervised learning, a synthetic minority oversampling technique is developed, aiming to replicate class imbalances through dimension reduction. To demonstrate its effectiveness, the proposed method is applied to two-dimensional, three-dimensional, and multi-dimensional time series data across various practical scenarios, showing improvements in accuracy, F1 scores, and receiver operating characteristic area under the curve metrics in nearly all cases. Furthermore, experiments on multi-label time series data reveal increased predictive power according to the global matrix calculation metric. Finally, through analysis of ECG signals using KNN3D, the proposed method is shown to effectively diagnose cardiovascular diseases. To facilitate adoption, an open-source, easy-to-use library called pyHEQ is provided, allowing for simple and efficient data transformation and classification. It operates within popular libraries and frameworks such as scikit-learn, TensorFlow, and PyTorch, and is compatible with Jupyter notebooks. This means that existing code using these libraries can be easily modified to utilize the proposed method with minimal disruption. To showcase its utility, modifications to the KNN classifier in scikit-learn and Keras libraries are presented, enhancing performance in these frameworks. This library and associated modifications are publicly available at https://github.com/mateusagray/pyHEQ. Experimental results show that learning models with longer horizons can be beneficial even when the forecasted horizon is shorter than what the model was trained on. To illustrate its utility in the life sciences, the proposed method is shown to effectively classify apoptosis cell death using a dataset of single-cell time-lapse microscopy images from the Apoptosis Dataset provided by the Unstructured Information Analysis Knowledge Base. This highlights how the proposed method can be utilized to improve the diagnosis of complex biological processes. To facilitate adoption, step-by-step technical instructions and sample code are provided, including advice on monitoring and parameter selection, and suggestions for future research. To ensure the reliability of the proposed method, thorough source code reviews were conducted, and all experiments were repeated multiple times to obtain consistent results.

Many successful methods use a valuation function approximation to determine near-optimal approaches. However, in partially observable systems, these valuations are dependent on an extensive sequence of past events and previous actions. Recent research demonstrates that neural networks specifically designed to approximate these valuations are found to internally calculate a probability distribution over latent state sequences, demonstrating a connection to dynamic programming. Furthermore, these networks can be modified into recurrent networks capable of retaining information about past events through the use of an hidden state. Our research involves analyzing stochastic processes that are either halted or bounce off the boundary of a given area. These processes' underlying mathematical operators comprise two components: a main, degrading portion that loses its effectiveness at the boundary, specifically in a direction perpendicular to it, along with a smaller, non-degenerate perturbation. Understanding the behavior of such stochastic processes plays a significant role in the stabilization of solutions to associated parabolic equations that incorporate a small parameter. In this context, metastability effects emerge, meaning that as the size of the perturbation approaches zero, solutions' long-term behaviors depend on the specific time frame considered. To effectively tackle this problem, we must integrate principles from analytical mathematics, such as operator theory, regular perturbations, and asymptotic analysis. Additionally, we must establish the dynamic properties of stochastic processes, including their absorption rates and exit times from designated areas, as well as track the movement of particles under various influences. Furthermore, we must analyze the mathematical properties of operator families that arise in the process of homogenizing a surface-operated generator featuring periodic characteristics. To streamline our analysis, we will utilize mathematical methods and theories such as dynamic behavior, Markov processes, and probabilistic methods associated with the Fredholm alternative. Moreover, we will establish the average characteristics of stochastic processes on small scales. Lastly, we will explore the mathematical connections between the analyzed stochastic processes and the super-solutions of related parabolic equations. In doing so, we will establish the analyzed problems' mathematical solutions and demonstrate the primarily asymptotic nature of the analyzed phenomena. Additionally, we will determine the mathematical criteria that define these asymptotic behaviors. And finally, we will acknowledge that these mathematical methods and theories are applicable to a broader range of analytical problems featuring small parameters and various metastable phenomena. These examples include the problems related to the modeling of turbulent particle movements, the modeling of cholesteric liquid crystals, the modeling of biological membrane membranes, and others. These discussed topics are based on previously published research articles by the authors. Recurrent neural networks have proven effective in handling sequential data across various domains, like speech and text. When extending recurrent neural networks into a distributed setting, known as federated learning, the challenge arises due to sensitive information that clients refuse to share due to privacy or regulation constraints. Recent developments in differential privacy have introduced innovative techniques to safeguard this sensitive data. Despite the widespread use of EMA (Exponential Moving Average) for stabilizing model updates in federated learning, little is known about the privacy implications of this technique. Our paper presents a new method, named DP-REC, which combines the advantages of differential privacy and robust model updates to securely train recurrent neural networks in a distributed setting. We introduce a novel technique, named DP-Strawman, which essentially wraps a robust pseudo-model around each true model and makes it virtually unupdatable. By integrating this technique with the EMA algorithm, we generate an improved version, named AMA, which exhibits superior performance. Our experiments with regression tasks confirm the effectiveness of our method, and our analysis provides insights on how to calibrate the parameters for optimal results. Our code is available for public access. Overall, our contribution lies in the development of a novel method, named DP-REC, which provides a reliable framework for differentially private recurrent neural networks. Our experimental findings indicate a 90% reduction in communication costs in conjunction with several existing privacy protection methods. We compared the performance of DP-REC with multiple existing techniques and observed that it surpasses them in terms of accuracy, which in some cases is as high as 49%. Additionally, our method demonstrates a 7-21 times lower error rate in conjunction with recent communication-efficient aggregation methods. We proudly noticed that DP-REC is the first method to achieve secure and accurate learning on 13 out of 14 challenging regression tasks, which was not previously achievable with existing techniques. We hope that our work and code will inspire future advancements in this area. Finally, our method has been successfully tested with text-based classification tasks using existing techniques like LSTMs and transformers. We look forward to the potential applications of our work in various domains. Structured tables in various documents effectively present complex information, making research in scientific papers easily accessible to scholars by compiling experimental outcomes and highlighting novel discoveries. Current table analysis techniques can fall short due to recognition errors stemming from the conversion of PDFs into document images, resulting in information loss. This study develops a solution to table extraction by leveraging Graph Neural Networks and incorporates tailored representation embeddings that improve differentiation between tables, table headers, and other document components. An experimental assessment was conducted on a combined dataset from PubLayNet and PubTables-1M to evaluate the proposed approach's efficacy. The results revealed that the proposed method achieves an accuracy of 94.7%, surpassing existing state-of-the-art techniques by over 7%. The associated source code and processed dataset have been made publicly available for further development. This study aims to provide insights for the academic community to create advanced table extraction models that adapt to diverse datasets. For practical implementation, the development of a web-based application, accessed via https://tableinsight.com, was designed to facilitate table analysis. The interface allows scholars to dynamically input table pages, generate extracted tables, and assess the model's performance on newly uploaded data. This work delves into the dynamic cognitive hierarchy theory, introduced by Lin and Palfrey (2022), within the context of multi-stage incomplete information games. In such scenarios, players simultaneously uncover peers' relevant characteristics and problem-solving abilities as the game unfolds. Building on this concept, our study provides a complete characterization of the dynamic CH solution for two-person dirty faces games. Notably, our findings indicate that lower-level players determine their characteristics in subsequent stages more slowly than their higher-level counterparts. Furthermore, our re-examination of the experimental data collected by Bayer and Chan (2007) shows that the dynamic CH solution more effectively explains the observed outcomes than its static counterpart. Lastly, our dynamic analysis yields more substantial revenue increases for Nash equilibria than the static approach, particularly in situations where an agent encounters an infinite cognitive hierarchy. Nonetheless, our dynamic reasoning still fails to surpass the revenue optimization achieved by the universal translator solution described in Lin and Palfrey (2022). Yet, the dynamic CH solution remains more computationally feasible than the universal translator solution. Finally, our theoretical framework is extended to investigate $2N$-stage dirty faces games, with the results showing that the dynamic CH solution remains consistent in smaller cognitive hierarchies while demonstrating greater sensitivity to changes in high-level characteristics. A live online experiment involving $2N$-stage games revealed qualitative evidence in support of our theoretical predictions, aligning with the dynamic CH solution's properties. An informal discussion on various generalizations of the dynamic CH theory is also presented. The code and data for our experiments can be accessed at https://github.com/leandrogomes/dynamic_cognitive_hierarchies. Precise and continuous population estimates are crucial for policy decisions surrounding vaccination initiatives and infrastructure development planning. As censuses fall short of providing the necessary spatiotemporal detail, researchers have been turning to independent approaches incorporating remote sensing data and microcensus statistics. We conducted an experiment in Mozambique, specifically estimating the population count in two districts due to a lack of recent censuses. We adapted the Estimation Spatial Populace model from that study, incorporating additional features, including urban areas' expansion and urban/rural ratio adjustments. We validated our estimates at both district and municipal levels. Although we encountered challenges, our model achieved accurate population estimates for most municipalities, especially those with established urban areas. We also addressed the underlying data quality issues in those areas. Yet, our model performed less well in districts with limited urbanization, particularly in estimating rural population figures. We observed significant correlations between estimated and actual populations, but the estimated distribution of population density across districts did not accurately reflect the actual distribution. Ultimately, we highlighted potential avenues for enhancing the model's performance. The estimated population data and accompanying code are publicly available at https://github.com/AAIhub/POPULATION_ESTIMATES. These developments led to the creation of novel systems capable of handling queries with minimal false positives, such as cuckoo and Bloom filters. Experimental findings indicate that combining two types of error-checking filters with a basic hash table results in a significant decrease of false positive results in many real-world applications. Building upon existing approximate filters, we suggest a new approach that eliminates false positives altogether, utilizing two types of on-disk error-checking filters and a cache-based hash table for query processing. Our proposed technique combines the efficiency of cubic storage and query complexity, thereby enabling faster and smaller implementation compared to traditional methods. Moreover, experimental results obtained from various real-world data sets reveal that our method yields to 2 times lower false positive rates in comparison to the most advanced cubic methods. Moreover, our technique yields speedup of up to 2 times and space reduction of up to 50% in comparison to two other contemporary overapped filters, thereby outperforming them in query processing speed while significantly decreasing storage requirements. These substantial gains in query processing speed and storage cost improvement validate the use of error-checking filters in implementing the proposed technique. Our technique can be seamlessly integrated with existing and development environments such as databases, file systems and caching, and remains versatile enough to incorporate additional optimizations like prefetching and parallel processing to further boost its performance capabilities. We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions with unpaired spin, we found that only one type of superposition of even and odd wave functions is possible, avoiding superfluid instability. In another scenario with superpositions of spin states as a result of three-body recombination, we identified a dark state that enables stable superpositions of atom and molecule states. Furthermore, we explored the interaction between two spin units and one spinless atom, using which we created stable superpositions of one atom and two molecules as well as two atoms and one molecule. Our research also involved the spontaneous emergence of molecule-molecular correlations through interactions of two spin units with one spinless atom. In a final section, we specifically considered one-dimensional systems and identified dark states in superpositions of even and odd states as a solution to the Mermin's condition for superfluidity. We demonstrated the stability of these dark states against spin-flip collisions and also showed that they can be utilized for coherent atom-molecule coupling via a laser in a particular regime. Our model is particularly useful for creating robust coherent atom-molecule interactions that can be implemented using lasers without requiring initial preparation. Moreover, in systems with binary superfluids, we showed that coherent atom-molecule interactions can be achieved through a laser that interacts with a specific superfluid component, but only if the superfluids have sufficient molecular coupling with the laser. In summary, our model is a versatile tool for creating robust atom-molecule interactions that can be efficiently implemented via laser manipulation. Furthermore, we have specifically considered the possibility of creating stable superpositions of multi-fermion states as a solution to the issue of fermionization, enabling stable atom-molecule conversion via a three-body recombination process. Our research has specifically analyzed the suitable conditions for superfluidity in a system with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Carefully designed Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics algorithms can successfully model complex fluid and fluid-structure interactions, but existing algorithms face significant computational costs due to the high resolution required for accurate results. To overcome this limitation, a new Spectral SPH - MPI approach has been developed to combine the strengths of classical SPH and material point methods. This novel framework utilizes two different particle resolutions: a high-resolution model for complex interactions and a lower-resolution model for the overall fluid dynamics. The results show that the proposed method significantly reduces computational costs while maintaining high accuracy, demonstrating its capability to model precise multi-phase fluid-structure interactions. The approach also allows for simplified boundary handling between disparate resolutions and adapts existing SPH formulations to address mixing and kinematic constraints. Furthermore, collision and penetration detection are achieved through the Multiple Step Collision Avoidance method. To validate the SPH - MPI approach, it was applied to the dynamic interaction of a non-linear pendulum with inviscid water, showcasing its ability to accurately capture key interactions, such as the creation of a vortex, the loss of equilibrium, and eventual collision with the water surface. Additionally, the method successfully modeled diverse multi-phase fluid dynamics scenarios, including the interaction of a moving sphere with a stationary box in multiple orientations, highlighting the efficiency and effectiveness of the SPH - MPI technique for complex, multi-phase fluid-structure interactions. These innovative findings indicate that the SPH - MPI approach has the potential to greatly reduce computational costs for similar fluid and fluid-structure interactions, thereby minimizing the resolution required for accurate results. Moreover, the method could also be adapted to address spatial multi-scale interactions where high and low resolutions need to coexist. Ultimately, the SPH - MPI approach represents a groundbreaking development in the SPH community, pushing the boundaries of computationally efficient modeling for complex applications. The pendulum and moving sphere demo files are available on the Git repository at https://git.io/SPH-MRI. For further information on the SPH-MRI project, please visit the website at https://materialpoint.org. The SPH-MRI Project aims to promote the use of SPH to achieve a meaningful advancement in the field, similar to what has been achieved in the multi-phase microflow and turbulent flows areas. The envisioned framework of the SPH-MRI is to extend the capabilities of the SPH-MRI project in the following key areas: solid modeling, turbulent flows, microflows, liquid and gas rheology, as well as fluid-structure and fluid-liquid interactions in the near and far

Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established. However, training traditional machine learning models can be time-consuming and may not be feasible for large datasets. In contrast, quantum machines offer a potential solution by providing a speed advantage, especially for patterns that they learn from themselves. In this study, we applied both unsupervised and supervised learning methods to real-world datasets on superconducting processors. Our results show that quantum machines can be outperformed by classical systems, but we also identify areas for further improvement in both the quantum and classical models to boost their accuracy. The source code for our project is publicly available at github.com/quantummachine/QL2_Dataset. The quantum computing protocol can be found at quantum.mpi-sieffolf.de/ql2-dataset/. The execution results of the quantum information processor can be accessed via quantum.mpi-sieffolf.de/ql2-dataset/data/ - in the future, new data will be added and a confirmation link will be provided. In the context of quantum machines, our project may contribute to the acceleration of the transition of quantum computing from concept to application. The feasibility of quantum computing has already garnered significant interest from major companies, research institutions, and a dedicated community. This work is part of a collaborative effort to establish a bridge between quantum and classical learning models, driven by the Quantum Machine Learning group at the MPI for Astronomy. The crucial element in this endeavor is the selection of suitable datasets. In our case, two real-world datasets were chosen due to their relevance to the field of astronomical research and potential to be optimized using both unsupervised and supervised learning methods. The selection of these datasets helped facilitate the development of both classical and quantum models. A primary consideration in our approach was to ensure that the quantum models, which were based on supported quantum information processors, could accurately process the dataset. The complexity of the quantum models was therefore constrained by the number of qubits and operations supported by the existing superconducting processors. In our study, two real-world datasets were used: the SDSS-DR13 view1 table dataset for unsupervised learning and the NASA Keepler dataset for supervised learning. A detailed description of these datasets can be found in our work. The primary goal of our study was to develop efficient learning models that could accurately process these datasets. In our study, two accurate classical models were applied: the K-Means and Random Forest algorithms. A detailed description of these models can also be found in our work

First, we came up with a pitch-shifting technique that doesn't change a speaker's unique voice, which helps make new speech samples sound more natural.  We also developed a training technique where FastPitch is taught how to change pitch based on speech samples with large pitch changes that were made using a natural-sounding pitch-shifting technique.  Our new algorithms are able to make FastPitch much more accurate when controlling pitch.  We only needed a small amount of speech data with large pitch changes for these models, which takes only a few hours.  Our experiments also show that these models can also make speech synthesis a bit more accurate.  We compared our models to a similar system and our results show that they outperform it.
