This research focuses on solving spatiotemporal object-based reasoning challenges in videos by employing object persistence principles. A crucial element of our approach is recognizing how to track objects throughout a video, even when they are obscured, covered or carried by other objects. Currently prevalent deep learning based methods exhibit spatiotemporal biases when applied to video-based reasoning problems. We introduce a model named Hopper that employs a multi-hop transformer to deduce object persistence in videos by iteratively skipping key frames to accurately predict the final location of the target object, given both video content and localization information. Furthermore, our proposed model benefits from using a contrastive loss to counter spatiotemporal biases. Experimental evaluations on benchmark datasets demonstrate that Hopper consistently outperforms other models by a significant margin across various benchmark datasets in all types of challenges (single-hop to multi-hop and cross-video shots). Hopper's source code can be found at https://github.com/amanmanek/hopper. Hopper won the IBM Challenge 2022 and obtained the first place in S3VGG at ECCV 2022 by J. Yan et al. and the second place in VINC at ICCV 2022 by S. Li et al. where the source code is available at https://github.com/yujie0314/VINC and https://github.com/Snailslime/VincEtc.

Our study investigates lepton-pair production coupled with bottom quarks at the Large Hadron Collider using theoretical predictions from next-to-leading order QCD. The investigation encompasses various factors, including a detailed analysis of predicted outcomes and an estimation of the associated uncertainties based on the dependence on perturbative QCD parameters. Additionally, it involves comparing these predictions to actual data and examining the impact of the predictions on the determination of the W boson mass. Using an optimized fit procedure for the W boson mass, we find that the predicted cross-section corrections contribute a small but non-negligible amount, around 0.04, and reveal that accurate simulations of the process require incorporating further corrections beyond next-to-leading order QCD. Furthermore, we demonstrate that incorporating predictions from parton distribution functions with next-to-next-to-leading order accuracy can significantly reduce the uncertainty stemming from the variation of the renormalization and factorization scales, and examine the potential for detecting lepton-pair production coupled with bottom quarks at the High-Luminosity LHC through exclusive channels. Assuming the validity of the soft-drop algorithm, the experiment would be capable of accurately measuring this process with around 20% accuracy in various kinematic regions. Ultimately, we outline a strategy for the precise determination of the W boson mass at the Large Hadron Collider. By combining predictions from next-to-next-to-leading order QCD and accurately constructed data sets, the experiment could achieve an accuracy of 100 MeV or higher in determining the W boson mass in two different scenarios: the combined measurement of the W boson mass and its branching ratio in the decay into leptons and hadrons, and the measurement of the W boson mass in the decay into muons and comparison with cross-section predictions across various kinematic regions. Remote-controlled vehicles called Telepresence robots have gained attention in various fields, thanks to advancements in technology and reduced costs. A crucial factor for these robots' acceptance is the remote control experience, as it directly impacts users' overall quality of experience. In this research, we outline three key quality of experience factors for telepresence robots: control, visibility, and interaction. To measure the control quality, we designed an experimental setup where participants remotely controlled a robot in a room, trying to catch virtual flying objects as quickly as possible. By using a random motion technique to either guide the robot or hinder the control, we induced different levels of control quality and recorded participants' interaction times. Through a large-scale user study, we evaluated the perceptual ease and discomfort of the remote control experience, as well as its practical impact on users' interaction times, discovering that control quality is crucial for an efficient remote control experience. Building on these findings, we propose a method to assess the quality of experience for remote control of telepresence robots by combining users' ratings and measurement data. The proposed approach enables remote evaluators to measure the control quality in three standardized steps, providing valuable and relevant results. Our solution offers practical benefits for both users and evaluators, as it enhances the evaluation process, aiding evaluation comparison and context transfer. Finally, we discuss the implications of our research, highlighting opportunities for future study, such as adapting the measurement model for the evaluation of other telepresence robot qualities like visibility and interaction. In this study, we revisit the core features of two Bayesian hierarchical regression models, thoroughly analyzing their full probabilistic frameworks, including the conditional distributions for each parameter. We extend these models to incorporate a linear relationship between the second-stage mean and a set of relevant predictor variables. The implementation details of the employed Gibbs sampling algorithms are thoroughly described, which are essential for estimating model parameters. Furthermore, a real-world example demonstrates the applications of these enhanced models in evaluating the effects of environmental variables on bird species density. It's worth noting that similar advanced Bayesian regression models are often absent from academic publications and educational content, but are increasingly prevalent in the field due to their growing research popularity and attention. As a result, this paper aims to contribute knowledge by documenting established yet under-reported techniques. Relevant software and data resources are provided, including a custom R package and the annotated Jupyter Notebook files, complemented by a video lecture covering the same material. This comprehensive approach seeks to document these techniques in a transparent and accessible manner, making these resources publicly available for the benefit of the research community. Each phase in the game, consisting of day and night segments, allows for various actions to be taken, with lynching occurring during the day phase. Mafia members possess special abilities that distinguish them from the citizens, who are the dominant group due to having a higher number. Researchers have developed a mathematical model that represents the game's progression as a discrete-time pure death process. They have found precise equations describing the mafia's chances of winning and the number of mafia members remaining. Additionally, the model enables the calculation of optimal strategies for both the citizens and mafia groups by using the principles from optimal control theory. Each group can adjust their respective win probabilities through modification of their actions over time, resulting in an optimal strategy when the derivative of the win probability equation is set to a specific constant. We present an algorithm for finding the optimal control that yields the best results, which has the capability to be applied to various numerical scenarios. Finally, the findings from the mathematical model align closely with the actual outcomes from actual games between citizens and mafia, showing that both groups can adjust their actions to achieve their goals. the possibility that planet interactions could be a key factor in shaping the
characteristics of gas-giant planets. To investigate this, the laboratory-like

depends on intricate electronic transport mechanisms involving the constituent
nanoscale entities. Heat units known as phonons exhibit a dual influence on
conductivity: by scattering electrons, they can hinder it but can also enhance it
by facilitating electron propagation through a complex energy terrain. In our
study, we have observed a temperature-dependent, coherent electron-phonon
interaction responsible for interwoven nanotube filaments in an experiment. Our
results demonstrate that phonon-assisted processes can significantly contribute to
electrical conductivity at room temperature. Our observation challenges the
commonly held assumption of dominant electron scattering in complex nanoscale
materials. By extending the principles of quantum conductive properties to a
large scale, our findings can guide the development of highly conductive
materials through careful manipulation of electron-phonon interactions. Such
strategies can lead to innovative large-scale materials with exceptional
electrical properties. Our work also sheds light on the intricate electronic
structure of carbon nanotubes. Furthermore, successful large-scale growth of
carbon nanotubes through atmospheric pressure chemical vapor deposition has enabled
the production of nanoscale materials with exceptional electrical conductivity,
which has crucial implications for various nanoscale electronic devices and
applications. Our results illustrate the need to examine the intricate role of
electron-phonon interactions in achieving highly conductive large-scale materials. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become crucial components of various neural networks and ensemble learning systems. Nevertheless, traditional algorithms designed for learning MoE mixtures often struggle to converge due to getting stuck in local optima, a challenge that persists despite extensive research over two decades. This paper presents a groundbreaking solution to this long-standing problem by introducing an innovative algorithm capable of consistently learning MoE mixtures. This new algorithm seamlessly integrates Ransprop, a proven method for optimizing expert parameters, with an original clustering approach that effectively merges distinct expert assignments. By merging these components, we develop an end-to-end algorithm that consistently learns MoE mixtures characterized by Gaussian experts and Gaussian noise. Moreover, we derive a more advanced version of this algorithm for applications involving Laplace noise, a scenario prevalent in tasks like denoising. The introduced methods significantly outperform existing approaches in various numerical experiments and real-world tasks, such as image denoising. We further adapt these algorithms for use in neural networks with non-Gaussian mixtures of experts. The source code and associated data can be accessed at https://motayyeb.github.io/SmartMoE. Our results demonstrate that the presented algorithms represent a major improvement over existing solutions, enabling consistent and efficient learning in a wide range of MoE models and associated applications. At the core of this progress is the development of two innovative clustering algorithms: Smart Clustering and its advanced extension, DC-Clustering. DC-Clustering, in particular, is a data-driven approach that efficiently merges distinct expert assignments by utilizing precise statistics, thereby overcoming the primary limitation of most traditional clustering methods. This set of notes offers a standalone overview of the theory of chip-firing games on metric graphs along with the theory of Jacobians and Prym varieties, stemming from the 2022 Cambridge summer school on combinatorial methods in algebraic geometry. The course covers the theory of bi-colored graphs, initial results in the theory of chip-firing games on general graphs, and the theory of chip-firing games on tri-valued graphs. Additionally, the course explores the connection to Jacobians and Prym varieties through tri-valued graph homomorphisms and applies this connection to examine degenerate cases of metric graphs. Finally, the course examines the role of bi-colored graphs in understanding the Bass connectedness of the Jacobian of a genus two curve. The course concludes by briefly discussing extended chip-firing games on metric graphs with colors. While quantum gravitational effects generally break global symmetries, their presence may hold significant value in understanding both particle physics and cosmology. Discovering well-maintained global symmetries could provide a valuable insight into the properties of gravity. A statistically significant detection of cosmic birefringence in the Cosmic Microwave Background may signify a previously undiscovered, though spontaneously broken, global symmetry in nature. A potential explanation for this phenomenon could be a very light, electromagnetically interacting pseudoscalar field, which must be protected from the effects of gravity. We demonstrate that a certain upper limit on the gravitational disruption of global symmetries would be required for this scenario to be feasible. Such a bound would have far-reaching implications, influencing the development of theories of quantum gravity as well as numerous models in particle physics. Furthermore, this would also impose significant limitations on the possible field theories of extra dimensions. We examine the potential of the Bell Test and forthcoming observations of the Cosmic Microwave Background, namely the Main Array and Simons Observatory, in order to ascertain whether they have the capability to directly measure this gravitational symmetry-breaking. Additionally, within the framework of models based on the Higgs boson, the Kaehler Sigma Model, and Little-Higgs models, we evaluate how the symmetry-breaking and associated global bounds correlate with the mass scales present in these models. We discover that in models based on the Little-Higgs models, the symmetry-breaking and global bounds can be reconciled with each other. We also discover that in models based on the Kaehler Sigma Model and certain types of Higgs boson models, the symmetry-breaking and global bounds can be accommodated, whereas in other Higgs boson models including the high-scale and mirror models as well as certain types of extra dimensional models, these symmetry-bounds pose significant constraints. We develop an understanding of why these symmetry-bounds pose considerable constraints on these models. We also recognize that our upper bounds on symmetry-breaking could be lowered if certain non-perturbative gravitational effects such as the time-dependent shift of the fixed-point, and the jump associated with these effects, were incorporated into the analysis. We leave a comprehensive investigation of these non-perturbative gravitational effects for a future thesis. Ultimately, our research indicates that direct characterization of symmetry-breaking in nature through cosmic birefringation is a highly unlikely scenario, and thus experiments seeking direct detection of gravitational effects may ultimately prove to be unsuccessful. Our research presents far-UV and near-UV data for NGC 4147, along with new far-UV images that allow us to assess X-ray variability and detect new hot stars within the cluster. We derived colour-magnitude diagrams from this data, which we combined with previous studies, and determined the UV-fainter stars that contribute to the X-ray emission in NGC 4147. Furthermore, we identified 22 new hot stars in the cluster by analyzing our UV images, and we investigated the spectral types of these stars based on their optical magnitudes and colours. Our analysis also explored the different types of variable stars in NGC 4147, particularly their distributions in the cluster and their frequency ratios. We compared these findings to those for other clusters and focused specifically on the type of variable stars known as RR Lyrae stars, assessing their zettijans and their 5.5-g magnetic field hypothesis. Lastly, we looked at the distribution of bright, hot stars in NGC 4147 and its connection to the issue of stellar evolution. Our investigation of 39 known X-ray- emitting stars in the cluster revealed a variety of spectral types, suggesting that these stars' X-ray emission could be the result of flares or magnetic activity on cooler stars or the effects of chromospheric emission on hotter stars. Our most prominent findings, however, were the discovery of new UV-bright stars in the cluster, which could play a significant role in the study of stellar and planetary evolution. Our final findings provide insight into the various astrophysical phenomena that could be occurring within NGC 4147. The goal of deep transfer learning (DTL) is to empower deep neural networks (DNNs) with the ability to draw from past experiences like humans. This capability is referred to as knowledge transferability. Although research into DTL has yielded promising results across various fields like natural language processing and computer vision, it is surprising to note that two widely accepted conclusions among experts are inaccurate. Firstly, it is commonly believed that data similarity enhances transferability, but our studies indicate the opposite is true. Secondly, it was assumed that the overlap in classes between source and target datasets hinders transferability, yet our research reveals this assumption to be unfounded as it actually facilitates transferability. This oddity suggestsexpands the scope of DTMs but also underscores the necessity of developing more accurate theories underpinning DTL. Based on these findings, we propose a new theory, to create a framework for DTM. This framework can be used to develop a practical approach to boosting transferability that can be applied in real-world scenarios. Experimental results indicate that our method surpasses baseline models in terms of accuracy and transferability. and is based on signal power, can be assessed through its accuracy in areas
such as cross-talk protection, field measurements and interference assessment.
This model's accuracy is compared with that of a continuous time model in the
form of an EPANET simulation. A direct relationship exists between the discrete
time model's accuracy and the ratio of sampling periods to signal periods.
Therefore, guidelines for choosing sampling periods in practical situations are
proposed, based on criteria like protection and field measurements. This
research also presents a new method for calculating noise levels in discrete
time models and verifies that the discrete time model provides consistent
interference assessments as sampling periods approach zero. Additionally, the
practical application of the discrete time model is demonstrated through its
use in the development of an EPANALYZER component for interference assessment.

advanced tools to support decision-making in the water industry. Specifically,
this work builds upon TOM's development of time-domain models for unamplified

for real-world applications. The results show that the discrete time model is
more suitable for links with long sampling periods or those involving complex
measurements, while the continuous time model is a better choice for situations

The widespread adoption of Android as the global leading operating system makes it an appealing target for malware. To defend against malicious code, researchers have proposed several countermeasures including advanced detection systems. These defensive systems have been found to be vulnerable to sophisticated attackers who have access to extensive research resources and use reverse engineering to bypass them. This persistent threat from advanced evasion attacks motivates the need for a comprehensive overview of these strategies in Android. This work commences by defining evasion attacks and assessing their impact on Android users. Subsequently, a critical overview of notable evasion techniques utilized by skilled attackers on Android platforms will be documented. The final section presents a summary of common evasion tactics and proposes potential countermeasures to prevent them, drawing from the wealth of available research studies. A thorough analysis of this research enables the identification of avenues for further investigation and highlights the need for a more integrated approach to counter evasion tactics, which are currently addressed in distinct frameworks. The doc can serve as a valuable resource for researchers, practitioners, and security professionals seeking an in-depth analysis of various evasion attacks and possible countermeasures across different frameworks in the field of Android security. The document is part of a larger project that aims to explore effective countermeasures to problem-space evasion attacks in Android OS. The associated project can be accessed at https://bitbucket.org/diegoarrazada/evasionattackscountermeasures/. The document is currently available in Spanish, with plans to translate it into English upon reader request. Service-oriented computing utilizes services as building blocks for constructing distributed systems. Traditionally, orchestrating cloud-based services centered around business process execution, particularly with BPEL's focus on services as processes. However, recent shifts towards alternative service motivations such as XaaS and RMAD indicate a need for an improved approach. Given these varied service types, a revised method for orchestration is required. We initially identify the essential capabilities for such a revised approach and develop a new orchestration model, named Ozy, designed to handle both process and non-process services. Our work, though, does pose limitations in its current application, and further research is needed to fully integrate Ozy's features. Additionally, a prototype implementation of Ozy based on Apache Oozie is presented. Our analysis, conducted through a user survey and case study, demonstrates Ozy's superiority in comparison to traditional orchestration models. Ultimately, our findings highlight potential enhancements to be incorporated into Ozy in future investigations. The applied research method is proposed for others to adapt in their own work on orchestrating non-process services. The Ozy prototype and related results are made accessible via a public website at ozy.io. Recent experimental observations supporting the particle-hole symmetric Pfaffian topological order are challenged by a reoccurring phase of unusual quantized nature, which is gapped in the thermodynamic limit.  Unlike other known phases such as Pfaffian, anti-Pfaffian, and PH-Pf phases, this new phase emerges at an intermediate mixing of Landau levels.  We have numerically examined the entanglement spectrum and ground-state energy density using the chiral conformal spectrum to establish the phase's anomalous characteristics.  Our findings support topological order with non-Abelian excitations through a comparison of the ground-state entanglement spectrum and the conformal spectrum, which also enables us to determine the holonomy of the system $U$. We discovered that the non-Abian phase exhibits a unique $Z_2$ symmetry in its holonomy, which is distinct from the known PH-Pf phase. Furthermore, we identified two key conditions that need to be satisfied in order to observe the unique phase: (i) The Landau-level mixing must not be excessively high, not more than 30$\%$, and (ii) The underlying material should have a fine energy variation in electron mass. We hypothesize that the unique phase could be observed in experiments using GaAs/Al$_x$Ga$_{1-x}$As systems with varying electron mass. Our study suggests that an ultra-thin undoped quantum well made of GaAs can act as an electron source with distinct mass characteristics. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the unique phase's dependence on ferromagnetic gate placement exhibits distinct patterns. We concluded our study by offering several suggested experimental approaches based on material parameters and gate placement arrangements. Our study could provide valuable insights to researchers working with topological phases in Abelian and non-Abian systems. Moreover, our study could offer relevant information to researchers working with various quantum devices in the quantum computing and quantum information science fields. Following the publication of our work, our findings have been verified through numerical torque correlation analysis by N. P. A. Allen et al. We have further established the ground-state energy density's dependence on system size using their results. Our study enables characterization of gapped phases in the quantum Hall effect, which could lead to important devices in the fields of quantum computing and quantum information science. Moreover, our work may inspire future experimental studies in the laboratory to identify various topological phases in the quantum Hall effect and related systems. Our analysis reveals that the conditions generating the Thakurta metric, previously investigated in a study by Böhm et al., involve physically implausible radiation of primordial black hole mass greater than the radiation-generated black holes themselves. This realization necessitates a recalculation of constraints derived from LIGO-Virgo observations, aiming to limit models producing such black holes. In reality, these constraints remain intact, no longer being able to bound models associated with the Thakurta metric. Instead, they can now exclude all models associated with impossible radiation leading to overtones of fundamental cosmological black holes. Furthermore, our findings indicate that even a refined model incorporating radiation, developed by Böhm et al., fails to adequately account for black hole formation. Consequently, we confirm the model's inability to generate black holes, as evidence from cosmic microwave background analysis is consistent with our conclusion. In a separate investigation, our search for primordial black hole signatures in the NANOGrav data found no significant evidence supporting these black holes as potential sources for current gravitational period changes observed in the parameter $\sin^2\theta_{\mathrm{DJ}}$. In conclusion, our analysis reveals the Thakurta model is ineffective in describing cosmological black holes; therefore, we advise against incorporating its amendments to the primordial black hole model. Instead, we suggest further research into modified primordial black hole formation theories and associated governing dynamics. Moreover, our analysis indicates that current gravitational and cosmic microwave background data confirm that there is no substantial role played by primordial black holes in the observed gravitational anomalies. This information could be useful for guiding particle physics theories and accompanying models describing the origins of these black holes. Finally, our analysis reveals that any future high-volume gravitational detection may reveal the existence of these black holes. As such, we recommend that future detection should incorporate both null and cosmological hypotheses into their analyses. Although our analysis dismisses the Thakurta model, this study does not preclude the validity of recent related studies. Furthermore, the bound on primordial black hole abundance resulting from LIGO-Virgo observations remains intact; therefore, any deviation may imply multidimensional or fractured extra dimensions as proposed by the Chandrasekhar-bound model. In a separate investigation, our analysis indicates an abundance upper-limit variation of merely one order of magnitude in confirming the existence of these black holes. Consequently, the most plausible model describing the primordial black hole formation remains the traditional standard model, incorporating the dynamically forming black holes theory. The complexity of gaseous disk structures and their impact on planet formation are still under investigation. This study focuses on how local fluctuations in gas density and velocity affect the formation of planets through pebble accretion. We analyzed the effects of turbulent disturbances with three different characteristics: extremely high Reynolds numbers, viscous forces, and non-linear phenomena. We discovered that the initial perturbations in the gas disk expansion have no effect on the growth of planetesimals but influence the formation location and pace of planets, including gas giants, satellites of Jupiter, and other planets. For instance, increased velocity perturbations lead to a shorter formation period for planets in the Jupiter belt, whereas elevated density perturbations result in gas giant locations in the outer planetary zone. This study suggests that local gaseous disk evolution could be a primary factor in the final planetary system arrangements. Extremely large, overparameterized models have achieved impressive success. In this research, we investigate whether the requirement for massive models might be partly attributed to computational limitations. We examine how the speed and price of computer chips, which dictate the size and complexity of models that can be effectively utilized, influence the development of new algorithms for training and inference. We also assess how advancements in network architecture, such as greater depth, width, and dimensionality, impact algorithms like gradient descent and its variants, enabling us to interpret overparameterization as a combination of computational capabilities and statistical attributes. We demonstrate that, despite the potential overfitting introduced by computational constraints, overparameterized models possess a well-supported theoretical advantage over efficiency-conscious models, which may only attain similar performance with significantly more data. We also identify specific scenarios where overparameterized models can deliver significantly superior results. The research suggests that computational limitations should be considered when designing algorithms for supervised learning tasks. We examine these concepts in the context of linear regression, neural networks, kernel regression, and Fourier features. We also conduct experiments to validate our findings and prove a related theoretical result. A related video is readily accessible at https://youtu.be/dc8tO_2JrRw. Three results concerning the presence of large Bohr sets in the sum of two sets within countable abelian groups have been established. Initially, the proof showed that for any set $A$ of size at least $5$, there exists a $B$ with $1\mu(B)=1$, where $\mu$ denotes the Haar measure, and $A+B$ contains a Bohr set with volume at least $1/5$. We propose a Branch-and-Cut algorithm to tackle this challenge, leveraging insights from established route paths to identify and exclude non-viable solutions, thus enhancing lower-bound estimates for arrival times. Additionally, this technique allows us to introduce new valid inequalities that accelerate the optimization process. We also observed that, as problem sizes scale up, our algorithm remains efficient due to its capacity to tackle much larger problems than those used in our computational study. Finally, our analysis reveals that, as vehicle quantities increase, the expected minimum arrival time converges towards a finite limit. We demonstrate the practical applicability of our findings by estimating that, under plausible assumptions, the dial-a-ride problem can be solved in real-time for up to 500 users. Natural Language Processing employs a crucial task called text classification, which sequential models efficiently handle, though their connection to linguistic semantics in output predictions often falls short. This study presents a novel score called I-score, offering a straightforward tool to evaluate linguistic semantics in text classification models. The S-score and I-score can be used to assess the level of interpretability in these models, while the I-score specifically aims to identify meaningful patterns in linguistic data. An experimental setup was designed with recurrent neural networks and tuning of hyperparameters to highlight the disparity between pure predictive models and those that interpret linguistic semantics effectively. The results show that incorporating linguistic semantics in model design enhances their performance and aligns their goals with the entire model. In this study, we examine how electronic interactions affect spin-orbit effects in metals. Through microscopic calculations based on Symmetry and a Sliding Mode approach, we derive an effective spin-orbit coupling Hamiltonian, which incorporates damping and oscillatory influences. By analyzing this operator, we find that in metals exhibiting ferromagnetic, semiconducting, and heavy fermion properties, the effective spin-orbit coupling strengthens due to electron interactions. This enhanced interaction is facilitated by processes such as orbital alignment, and in the case of heavy fermion compounds, by the attraction between electrons and holes. By examining the effect of interactions on spin precession speeds, we identify a new structure-related influence that is absent in materials without strong correlations. Our study's primary findings are two-fold, as they shed light on distinct mechanisms governing spin-orbit effects in metals and semiconductors. By distinguishing between these two material types, we reveal fresh insights that might be indispensable for developing strategies to strong spin-orbit materials in the future. Additionally, we observe that in heavy fermion systems, the proportion of spin-orbit effects resulting from electron interactions to total spin-orbit effects can be substantial, ranging from tenfold to several hundredfold, which could be crucial for understanding magnetic properties and related phenomena in these systems. Furthermore, we propose that in certain materials, the effective spin-orbit coupling can be modified not just by interactions but also by adopting complex topological structures with multiple band crossings, which might pave the way for the precise design of novel materials. The combination of these two principles provides considerable freedom for developing materials of interest, topological or otherwise. Lastly, we begin exploring potential experimental implications of our theoretical discoveries and anticipate that these outcomes could inspire fresh avenues in the pursuit of material science research. To facilitate future research, we have made all of our code and data openly available. Furthermore, we anticipate that these theoretical findings might also contribute to the expansion of theoretical physics as a whole. The use of data-driven approaches to analyze code and data can be particularly valuable in this regard. The major objective of our work is therefore to stimulate a deeper comprehension of the intricate relationships between structure, interactions, spin-orbit effects, and various physical phenomena at play. To this end, we have endeavored to provide accessible explanations of the underlying concepts, emphasizing and encouraging further research into the development of innovative materials. Given the regulatory restrictions on medical software and the scarcity of comprehensive labeled medical datasets, our approach revolves around predicting a model's performance in an unfamiliar setting using its predicted responses alone, without requiring any modifications to its training process. By integrating predictive models at two stages - during training and after deployment - we are able to effectively evaluate the effectiveness of our approach through application on various medical and non-medical tasks. Our empirical results demonstrate that this technique is capable of effectively estimating AI models' performance in diverse scenarios. Furthermore, we have made our source code available to the public, thus enabling seamless access to these findings. Our goal is that these methods can be utilized by regulatory bodies to assess the performance of AI models in various settings, thereby facilitating safe deployment of AI-powered medical devices to the public. The Asymmetric Numeral System, proposed in 2014, was designed to efficiently replace Huffman codes for data compression. Despite being optimized for optimal compression ratios, experiments revealed significant discrepancies between theoretical and practical entropy values. To address these disparities, a method was developed to assess optimal codeword asymmetry. Utilizing this approach, it was discovered that the most efficient codeword distribution is not necessarily one with the highest asymmetry. In comparative studies with Huffman codes, Asymmetric Numeral System encoding demonstrated comparable or greater efficiency on real-world datasets, with the potential to compress large datasets more effectively by up to 10%. Furthermore, ANS encoding outperformed Huffman codes when the underlying data distribution is unknown, as it produces more symmetrical codewords, reducing their potential inefficiencies. In contrast to Huffman codes, which require computational overhead when building the codeword tree, ANS encoding eliminates this expense, making it well-suited for applications requiring rapid compression. Overall, the Asymmetric Numeral System proves to be a valuable method for data compression. Its versatility in compressing datasets efficiently, whether the underlying distribution is known or unknown, often at near-optimal rates. When performing cosmological inferences based on the Lyman-$\alpha$ correlation functions, standard analyses usually only consider a specific feature related to baryon acoustic oscillations. In this research, we investigate whether these standard analyses adequately capture the relevant cosmological information. To address this, we directly fitted synthetic Ly$\alpha$ correlation functions, including cross-correlations with quasars, without compressing the data, and then compared the results to the conventional method. Our approach provided significantly more precise measurements, constraining the matter density to 3.5% and outperforming the conventional BAO method. Our study showed that the additional information, except for the spectral index constraint, came primarily from two distinct effects: the Alcock-Paczy\'nski effect and redshift space distortion. Utilizing the full information without compression may offer more efficiency in exploring Ly$\alpha$ correlations in future surveys. Based on these findings, we propose a new cosmological analysis procedure that uses direct fittings to securely and efficiently extract cosmological data, including non-Gaussian constraints, from Ly$\alpha$ correlation functions without compromising accuracy. Our proposed method is scheduled to be implemented for future observational projects in the forthcoming MOOC "Cosmology with Lyman-$\alpha$ Forests''. The code used in this research is now available under the MIT License at https://github.com/lymanalphauni/dci. The code for generating synthetic correlation functions is also included. To our knowledge, the code used in this research represents one of the first publicly accessible implementations of a Ly$\alpha$ forest correlation function generator that's compatible with the PoliPol algorithm. A fundamental component of various technologies, including surveillance, autonomous driving, and robotics, is multi-agent tracking. Numerous studies have analyzed the behaviors of multiple entities within these systems over extended periods. Conversely, the natural human pattern of interacting with multiple entities is characterised by periodic intervals of engagement and disengagement from others. Current prediction methods fail to account for this natural pattern, instead focusing on short-term forecasting with little consideration for the influences of other agents. Therefore, it is essential to develop an innovative approach that incorporates a socially aware model Capable of Learning Patterns Over Time. By acknowledging the natural periodic interactions between multiple entities, we have proposed a new method - the Sliding Sequential Continuous Vector Autoencoding Model with a Receptive Field. Our model is capable of modeling relationships not only between adjacent entities but also between entities that are farther apart over time. We have also introduced a time variant socially-aware model Rethinking Module which captures the inherent socially aware pattern of periodic interactions between multiple entities. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art forecasting models. Furthermore, we have introduced a new benchmark dataset called Trajectron2Plus, which extends the existing dataset, incorporating periodic socially aware pattern, thereby allowing for rigorous evaluation of our proposed model. This research aims to compare and contrast these measures objectively by exploring their core principles, as well as their implications and limitations. To this end, we conduct a thorough examination of their mathematical underpinnings, focusing on their applicability to Boltzmann machines, a subset of neural networks. Furthermore, we discuss recent advancements in this field and highlight areas for further investigation. Our aim is to provide an in-depth, detailed review that facilitates meaningful discussions and comparisons of these measures in practical applications. As such, this paper is written in an accessible, non-technical tone suitable for readers with varied levels of mathematical expertise. Despite this, some sections requiring advanced mathematical concepts are clearly labelled and set apart from the main text. As of January 2023, this paper remains one of the most up-to-date comprehensive reviews on the subject, incorporating insights gained from participating in a Related States of the Art Semantics in Motion workshop, where researchers discussed their respective approaches. Nonetheless, further efforts are warranted to distill key ideas into concise modules, much like chapters in a traditional book, and to foster more targeted discussions focusing on practical applications or theoretical contributions. As for practical applications, we have attempted to make our analysis more relevant by incorporating concrete numerical examples related to training Boltmann machines, a subset of neural networks, using measures of complexity. This has helped us evaluate the practical implications of these measures in a real-world context, much like computer simulations. Following these examples, we have briefly discussed potential avenues for further theoretical developments. Much like the existing literature, our analysis is divided into two parts, one focusing on foundational work and another exploring practical applications. Due to space constraints, our numerical examples are provided in the appendix, and the practical contributions are concluded in the final chapter. However, determining this potential requires the full Hamiltonian, posing a significant challenge for complex many-body systems. A recent approach, proposed by P. W. Claeys et al., utilizes an approximated, variational gauge potential. In the case of a two-component fermionic Hubbard model, this potential can be expressed in terms of Green's functions or spin currents. Using an exact diagrammatic expansion, it is possible to achieve precise control over the driving process, yielding results indistinguishable from those obtained with exact gauge potentials. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that variational gauge potentials can efficiently facilitate the creation of states with desired properties even in the presence of interactions. Notably, in the case of a Hubbard dimer, it is possible to perfectly preserve the total spin and its projection onto a specific direction. Moreover, it is feasible to drive a $t$-$J$ model into a $t$-$J_z$ model by adjusting the coupling between gauge potential and spin-inversion degree of freedom. These findings highlight the potential of variational gauge potentials as a driving strategy for complex many-body systems. Color-neutral images with tailored tone Reproduction Operator characteristics are generated by a novel, fast-decolorization approach, employing an aberration-corrected pseudo-color temperature transformation. Utility of the proposed technique is demonstrated in the domain of tone mapping, leveraging the perceptually uniform HSL color space and its resulting H-S plane. Key transformations within this domain are identified and analyzed, particularly with respect to the color wheel, enabling an optimized solution to the problem of high dynamic range (HDR) to standard dynamic range (SDR) tone mapping via pseudo-color temperature conversion. Therefore, various pseudo-color temperature algorithms have been adapted and refined, and their results compared using metrics such as multi-scale structural similarity, mean square error, and computing time. A survey of existing tone mapping techniques serves to illustrate that most methods alter color properties without considering the H-S to RGB-Cb-Cr transformation, resulting in distortions that are compensated by the proposed approach. Furthermore, the proposed technique transforms color properties through an exponential warming process, transforming the HDR to standard dynamic range (SDR) color temperature from warm to cool. To apply this transformation to video, a blurring algorithm based on Gaussian distribution has been implemented. The method effectively removes video noise, preserving key image details in the presence of noise. The proposed technique achieves high scores on SSIM, MSE, and CFA metrics, and its performance is further evaluated in the domain of multi-exposure HDR to SDR tone mapping, resulting in optimized tone reproduction operator characteristics. The proposed high-speed decolorization algorithm is fast, efficient, and suitable for real-time video applications such as video tone mapping. Videos demonstrating the proposed technique can be found at https://youtu.be/2O6yj3Ksklo and is part of an ongoing patent application, EP3410338A.

This research develops an expression to decompose infinitely differentiable complex-valued functions into a sum of exponentials along with a corresponding set of polynomial functions. A specific form of the exponential expression serves as the basis for the new decomposition, which is derived by reinterpreting the expression in a different functional context. Several key properties associated with this new decomposition are identified, including a proof that it is consistent everywhere and that the two sets of functions are unique with respect to specific function configurations. As applications, it is demonstrated how this new decomposition can be used to establish certain identities involving exponentials, generate series expansions for exponentials, and develop a decomposition method for complex-valued functions. Furthermore, an alternative proof of the original expression is developed using the theory of distribution theory. The research concludes by identifying areas for further extension and exploration. 

In the companion paper \cite{ieeetcs2022}, the existing and new decompositions are used to variously formulate the Maucher-Spitz approximation method. Moreover, an extensive collection of approximations are developed using the new decomposition, which is compiled in an upcoming textbook \cite{textbook}.

We examine the RDF data exchange process based on relational data, constrained by Shape Expression schema. Our research involves addressing two critical issues: first, determining the feasibility of solutions for source data instances; and second, developing a single comprehensive solution that represents all possible outcomes. To achieve this, we incorporate typed IRI constructors to form RDF IRIs from relational values and translate Shape Expression constraints into target dependencies. Additionally, we have identified certain data exchange settings as 'core', meaning their solvability is unaffected by the (in)finiteness of the input data. We found the rational complete core to have an understandable solution syntax and relatively lower complexity, compared to other types of data exchange settings. Moreover, we have found the solution quality of the rational complete core to be satisfactory, especially for certain data exchange settings with restricted structures. Finally, we demonstrated the feasibility of using the CaRet algebra to produce RDF solutions from different data exchange settings and highlight the user's difficulty in interacting with the rational complete core solutions, resulting from their non-uniqueness nature. To summarize, our research focuses on data exchange constraints, as distinct from other approaches, such as universal rule sets or logical programs. Additionally, we have contributed to the existing data exchange literature by introducing a new type of core with superior solution quality and a more manageable solution syntax compared to other existing data exchange settings. We have also established a new algebra, rational CaR-rXID, to be applied independently of the recent RDF data exchange progress made by Guerreschi et al. in 2018. However, further research is needed to address various data exchange problems related to CaR-rXID, such as unique and universal inclusion dependencies. A new field of shape-constrained nonparametric regression is rapidly growing across various disciplines including economics, statistics, operations research and artificial intelligence. Recent advancements in the analysis of productivity and efficiency now bridge a significant knowledge gap in this field. The application of these techniques has been hindered due to significant computational requirements and lack of accessible, user-friendly software. To address this challenge, we create an open-source library called pyStoNED to implement advanced techniques such as multivariate convex regression and the determination of efficiency metrics with enhanced capabilities for handling noisy data. Additionally, this tool allows for the estimation of a Pareto efficient frontier in various contexts including productivity and efficient use of resources. We demonstrate the effectiveness of pyStoNED using real-world data sets from economics and operations research. This library is made available under the BSD-3 open-source license, allowing for easy integration into a variety of environments including MATLAB, Python and R. Furthermore, accessing the package pyStoNED through GitHub underlines its status as a dynamic and constantly evolving project aimed at adding new techniques and improving computational performance. As a result, pyStoNED plays a central role in promoting shape-constrained nonparametric regression analysis to a broader range of users and researchers. The accuracy of speech-based applications heavily relies on high-quality Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR). Despite having access to advanced ASR tools, the lack of sufficient training data for languages other than English severely hampers progress in these fields. To fill this void, we utilize Kaldi to develop German acoustic models utilizing datasets under a Creative Commons license. This has the added benefit of making these models redistributable and significantly lowering the barriers for researchers and developers in German ASR. With a combined total of 412 hours of audio data, which includes the valuable resource of the Spoken Wikipedia Corpus, we are able to achieve notable improvements. Specifically, the word error rate is lowered by 26%, with the top performing model reaching a word error rate of 4. An exhaustive evaluation is conducted on the Interspeech 2008 De speech test data, thoroughly examining the effects of data combination, language models, and data normalization techniques. Additionally, we highlight the significance of pre-representation feature creation through a thorough error analysis. As a result, our study not only yields state-of-the-art results on the Interspeech 2008 De speech test data but more importantly, contributes to the advancement of German ASR by promoting open source, open data, and open results, ultimately facilitating future research in this field. The origin of Be-type stars is still unclear with many theories proposed,  However, a recent study of the 30 Doradne region has given us a glimpse into how these stars are formed as it has revealed several Be-type stars in the early stages of the cluster. Deep neural networks, known for their robust performance across various tasks, work well when trained with large datasets.  However, their interpretation capabilities are largely unutilized.  Several recent studies have focused on increasing neural model transparency.  One such study introduced "Neural Tangent Learning", a method that turns any neural network into a trainable Gaussian Process.  We build upon this concept and introduce "Non-Fungible Tangent Kernels" to address the challenge of fitting a Gaussian Process directly to a large image dataset like ImageNet.  Unlike the earlier work, NFT-K enables the generation of image-like outputs using latent function representations, thereby allowing the generation of new image data using the generated process.  We develop a new algorithmic method for NFT-K and present results indicating its efficiency in fitting a Gaussian Process on the entire ImageNet dataset while maintaining computational efficiency.  We compare NFT-K to NT-Net and Outlier Exposure, revealing that NFT-K outperforms them in fit quality at typical training scales.  Moreover, we show that NFT-K exhibits a unique trade-off between the benefits of neural networks and Gaussian Processes, thereby making it useful for both properties and GP-like behavior.  We study the properties of NFT-K at infinite depth and derive an upper limit on the number of training samples that can be effectively utilized, which we find to be in line with the current computational limits.  Given the current state of NFT-K implementation, we are able to fit the entire ImageNet dataset; however, we could only effectively utilize around two-thirds of the dataset due to the current limitations of NFT-K and ImageNet dataset prep.  The source code for NFT-K is available at https://github.com/krishnan-krishna/non-fungible-tangent-kernels.  Our study is the first attempt to fit a Gaussian Process to image data, thereby marking an important contribution to both the extrinsic and intrinsic transparency of deep neural networks.  Additionally, NFT-K provides valuable insights into the nature of deep neural networks and Gaussian Processes, thereby paving the way for future research in these areas.  Importantly, NFT-K opens up novel avenues for the interpretation of deep neural networks, thereby making it an important study.  Lastly, NFT-K validates the GP property of neural networks as initially demonstrated in 2105's "GpFlow", thereby making it an important empirical study. In this work, the impact of electron-electron interactions on one-dimensional non-Hermitian systems is investigated with the use of exact diagonalization and the extended Hubbard model. The results show that correlations cause a correlated transition from an open gap to a gapless non-Hermitian phase for systems with fermions, whereas in the bosonic case, interactions lead to the closure of the one-dimensional non-Hermitian chiral model's gap. The analysis, however, reveals that the bulk topology remains intact in both scenarios. Furthermore, correlations are found to weaken the strength of the edge resonance, although the edge state's position remains largely unaffected. The observed phenomena are predominantly attributed to the electron-electron repulsion rather than band formation caused by truncation. The understanding gained from these findings may facilitate the identification of correlated non-Hermitian topology in real-world systems. The associated data can be accessed via the link https://gitlab.com/sn0wman/correlations_in_chiral. The code is also made available on this link for others to reproduce the results. The approach employed in this study can be adapted to investigate chiral symmetry breaking in one-dimensional systems with low energy variability. It is however essential to utilize different numerical methods to analyze the model in the latter case. It is anticipated that the results of this study can inspire future experimental and theoretical investigations. It is also worth noting that future works should focus on characterizing and identifying topological features through parameters other than the gap and edge resonance position alone. The approach of combining different measures to characterize topological features is similar to that used in identifying symmetry-enforced symmetry-protected topological phases. When plotting the matter density parameter Ωm against the radiation density parameter Ωr in phase space, a closed trajectory is observed that would allow the Universe to repeat the cycle indefinitely. This idea brings concepts from areas like chaos theory and dynamical systems into the study of quantum foundations. Despite this potential, developing a clear hidden-variable model for it has been a challenge, making it hard to properly evaluate. In this piece, a hidden-variable model for the theory is developed and several aspects of the theory are analyzed with it. Our results indicate that many arguments supporting the theory fail when examined closely. The model itself displays superdeterministic and nonlocal properties in line with the original theory. The paper's main goal is to introduce this new model to facilitate further analysis and discussion of the theory, with the ultimate goal of incorporating it into the list of theories being regularly tested by quantum foundational experiments. Moreover, by developing this hidden-variable model, we are able to formally assess claims about the theory using formal methods and mathematical tools, making quantum foundations more rigorous. In the end, some potential connections between the new theory and other concepts like Bell's concept of "the world" are explored. While this paper does not aim to fully resolve these connections, it does contribute to the ongoing discussion on quantum foundations. The main paper's conclusions are independently verified using formal proofs within the Coq toolset. All of the main paper's code is hosted at bitbucket, along with other related projects. The paper ends by asking the community to consider incorporating the hidden-variable model and the new theory into ongoing experiments to test their validity. We examine Neural Networks (NNs) for keyword spotting on devices such as smart speakers and wearables. Our focus is on NN execution within devices with limited resources; thus, we suggest a Compact Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture. This CNN features (i) reduced computation requirements via limited multiplications. (ii) an economical use of model parameters to minimize memory usage. (iii) an efficient L1-based loss function allowing training and inference on devices such as microcontrollers without a host CPU. (iv) fast processing via sampling techniques including data augmentation and input subsampling. (v) enhanced robustness through noise-resistant input preprocessing. The evaluated CNN models achieve a high SiSPl (speech-ingredient similarity proportion) of 65 percent when processing pre-trained models, outperforming existing IoT-friendly architectures such as VGG-like and Tiny YOLO. Additionally, we extend LDA-based input preprocessing in combination with a L1-loss NN. Our proposed processor, RAVN, is a hardware module optimized for evaluating NN models, and is capable of processing both NNs mentioned above. RAVN is highly efficient, requiring just 24k gates and achieving a 155mW power consumption at 1GHz clock speed. When processing these models, our test of RAVN on IoT devices yields extremely low latency of 7ms along with low error rates for out-of-vocabulary words at around 10 percent. Using Audio-Word models, we successfully identify the individual words within a spoken keyword at rates of greater than 90 percent accuracy. Audio experimental testing has been conducted using Raspberry Pi 4, Nucleo Board NUVOTON M482, and Nucleo Board STM32L476. The described processor may also easily integrate with recently-published 15kG gate RISC-V processor with IP block. In recent years, the needs of embedded systems have grown more complex.  These systems not only require reliable, predictable, real-time operating systems but also support various system services such as virtualization, security, and debugging tools.  To meet these demands, we have developed a custom hypervisor, named T-Visor, which integrates with embedded CPUs to provide a higher-level virtualization platform beyond what is offered by operating systems.  In this study, we explore the advantages of using hypervisor virtualization in embedded systems by comparing it to traditional kernel-based virtualization.  Our evaluation shows that T-Visor outperforms the kernel approach in both execution speed and memory usage, confirming the benefits of using hypervisor virtualization in embedded systems.  Furthermore, we have incorporated the Coq proof of the T-Visor's safety features into its source code, thus ensuring the stability of the hypervisor and protecting the security of its scheduled tasks.  Our experiments validate the effectiveness of this measure, demonstrating that T-Visor's inclusion of proof-based verification, safety checks, and testing exerts no negative influence on its performance, which meets or exceeds the expectations set by the Linux kernel in embedded systems.  To showcase the practical application of this concept, we have successfully integrated T-Visor with the FreecOS.  Our final analysis compares the performance of T-Visor and the FreecOS under both hypervisor and kernel configurations, revealing that T-Visor's integration results in a significant, 2.71 times improvement in execution speed over the FreecOS's kernel-based virtualization.  This substantial gain underscores the importance of using hypervisor virtualization in embedded systems.  In a subsequent work, we could build upon this discovery by developing a custom FreecOS with T-Visor virtualization, which we refer to as FreecOSv.  Our investigation reveals that FreecOSv outperforms the FreecOS's kernel-based virtualization, thus providing substantial, provably-improved performance gains.  To confirm the authenticity of this concept, our experimental results show that FreecOSv's performance is comparable to what is achieved using the Linux kernel in embedded systems. In metric geometry and general relativity, specifically Einstein's vacuum equations, generalized differential forms play a significant role. They involve applying Cartan's structure equations and generalizing them to explore new concepts. By associating flat generalized connections with a metric, researchers gain new insights into Einstein's vacuum equations and their solutions in four-dimensional Lorentzian geometry. This work showcases how particular generalized connections and geometries can effectively encode Ricci flat metrics in unique and novel ways. The findings also correlate with previous work using differential operators by Gualtieri and Herzlich. However, in this context, the focus is on discovering distinct generalized structures within a fixed metric, rather than constructing new metrics or geometries. The resulting applications not only contribute to understanding Einstein's vacuum equations but also the topology of a fixed Riemannian 4-manifold. By linking certain topological questions to Einstein's equations, researchers can potentially use generalized geometry to approach open problems in topology. The work primarily relies on the work of N. Poncharov, A. Beltrami, and V. Gromov, specifically their independent discoveries in generalized geometry, to reveal the deeper relationships between Einstein's equations, Lorentzian geometry, and the topology of four-dimensional manifolds. The ideas presented can be extended to more recent developments in higher dimensional theories in string theory and M-theory. However, in this paper, the focus remains on the simplest classical generalizations of Riemannian geometry that are essential and fundamental. The results described have various implications in the quantum field theories mentioned, and some of the concepts involved have been published in a series of papers by the author and his collaborators. However, in this paper, the content is new and has not been published before. The connections between Einstein's equations, generalized geometry, and the topology of four-dimensional manifolds provide novel and classical insights into the fundamental structures underlying general relativity and quantum field theories. The work is a compilation of the author's understanding in this field, and similar topics have been discussed in a course on string theory and M-theory by Emil Martinec at UCLA. The result is an integration of quantum field theories, relativity, and string theory, and the related mathematics of differential forms, metrics, and connections, as well as the topology of four-dimensional manifolds and their connections to string theory and M-theory. The result is an integrated understanding of relativity and string theory, and the provided references demonstrate the connections between quantum field theories, relativity, and string theories.

Utilizing the multivariate method and resultant elimination techniques, we establish novel categories of sparse permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube orders, with various degrees of completeness, for any $q=p^{k}$ where the prime $p$ equals $2$ or $3$. What's more, we devise a direct method for creating elements of the general linear group that can be represented by sparse matrices with specific row and column ranks for any $q=p^{k}$ where the prime $p$ equals $2$ or $3$. As a result, we obtain a large number of APN and almost perfect nonlinear functions in multiple variables across finite fields with square and cube orders. Furthermore, we show that the derived polynomial families can be used to construct complete permutation polynomials with various degrees of completeness and demonstrate their utility in creating cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generators. This work introduces a novel approximation technique for a broad category of zero-sum-free stochastic differential investment and reinsurance models. It incorporates both proportional reinsurance and loss-overlimit reinsurance models. A straightforward, reduction approach is used to convert such non-zero-sum games into a set of one-dimensional non-zero-sum forward-looking mean-variance models. For these forward-looking models, different methods including dynamic programming, deep neural networks, and quasi-monotone operator technique are applied to obtain approximation solutions. Furthermore, the approximation technique is shown to converge asymptotically in a weighted L1 sense. Numerical examples are presented to demonstrate the advantages and efficiency of the approximation technique. In particular, the approximation technique is used to determine optimal reinsurance strategies for certain situations. It reveals that the characteristics of reinsurance contracts significantly impact investment outcomes and that the approximation technique is capable of capturing this impact. Due to its efficiency, the approximation technique can quickly determine optimal reinsurance strategies even in situations with a high number of regime transitions. At the same time, the technique is capable of producing highly accurate outcomes for such situations. Finally, the approximation technique is used to show that in certain circumstances, the limit value can be expressed in terms of a parabolic partial differential equation solution. Key words: non-zero-sum games, regime-switching jump-diffusion models, mean-variance representation, deep neural networks, convergence technique. ## Introduction

This research presents a novel Proportional-Integral-Derivative-Accelerated (PIDA) control strategy, integrating a derivative filter, to enhance quadcopter stability in chaotic and unpredictable flight conditions. The PIDA algorithm, built using the genetic algorithm's Direct Search method, is designed to minimize oscillations. The parameter estimation process is supported by five decision-making filters, helping to prevent the system from becoming stuck in local optima. The effectiveness of the proposed PIDA control is demonstrated through simulation tests, showcasing its capacity to improve tracking accuracy and maintain a smooth, stable flight trajectory. The results show that quadcopter dynamics using the PIDA control yield higher Positivity Ratio values and lower Navigability and Robustness Factor values compared to the traditional Proportional-Integral-Derivative-Accelerated (PIDA) control. Additionally, the proposed method successfully prevents parameter sensitivities, enabling stable flight in chaotic conditions. The proposed method has been successfully tested on real quadcopter prototypes, showcasing its practical applicability. The research aims to contribute practical and theoretical insights into control strategies for unstable systems. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded forward pixel detector prototype featuring a novel readout system and third disk was introduced, integrating eight pilot blades built using advanced digital readout chips. Through pilot module testing, researchers obtained practical experience in operating the upgraded detector. This study reports the results of analyzing data captured with these pilot modules, including a detailed explanation of the reconstruction process and associated software implementation. Furthermore, it includes statistical assessments of hit finding, track finding, and track fitting, as well as a description of the physical characteristics of the track parameters derived from the pixel data. The findings showed that all three pilot modules operated within expected parameters, generating minimal false hits and accurately computing physical track parameters with a dispersion consistent with noise levels. Moreover, the hit efficiency was found to be nearly 100%, and the hit residual signed absolute mean was within the predicted range. These positive outcomes indicate that the upgraded pixel detector prototype functioned as intended, paving the way for integration into the CMS system. The code developed for this initialization has been made publicly available through the CMS software framework, known as CMSSW. It can be accessed via the link https://github.com/CMSAnalyzer/CMSSW/tree/CMSSW_9_1_0_XXX.xdigipix pilot. For those interested in the underlying physics of the silicon pixel detector, the associated physics analysis can be found at https://github.com/CMSAnalyzer/CMSSW/tree/CMSSW_9_1_0_XPHIPIL. The root directory for the prototype data and associated files can be accessed at https://hep.cms.gov/pxdproto. We have developed a machine learning-based system to accurately identify the types of Active Galactic Nucleus (AGN) host galaxies within the first billion years of the universe's existence. To do this, we employed two AI algorithms. Firstly, one algorithm was trained on observed images, with the aim of categorizing early host galaxies based on their visual appearance. Secondly, another algorithm was trained on digital simulations, with the objective of both reducing biases and increasing the accuracy of their initial training. To minimize errors, our team also developed a system to recognize and filter out distorted galaxy images. To ensure the reliability of our classification model, we trained it using the SEDmatch galaxy simulation program and obtained satisfactory results. We utilized this model to analyze the Drift survey dataset and identified or classified 123,591 AGN host galaxies. Our findings will be utilized to investigate the evolution of these galaxies. We also created a database containing detailed information about the host galaxies, which is available online. This host galaxy catalog contains over 123,000 entries and can be accessed through the following website: https://github.com/HostGalaxyEclipse/hostgalaxy_eclipse. To maximize the potential of this host galaxy catalog, our team plans to integrate it with the rest of the Drift survey dataset. We intend to achieve this by conducting further machine learning training using the Drift survey dataset and the galaxy classification AI algorithm. Once complete, the combined dataset will be accessible through the European Southern Observatory's Exabyte Science program. We plan to utilize the host galaxy information to calculate key host galaxy properties such as their merit, morphological types, and mass. To take the project to the next level, we are also training an AI algorithm to predict the evolution of dwarf galaxies based on the CONCERTO Legacy Survey. To do this, our team is utilizing a machine learning framework to develop a mathematical model that simulates how normal and star-forming galaxies transform into elliptical galaxies. This model is based on a series of established rules that are supported by scientific evidence, including both physical principles and observations. We are also applying this model to simulate the evolution of AGN host galaxies. By combining our model with the Drift survey dataset, our team is able to generate a series of predictions about the future of these galaxies. We plan to utilize these predictions to test a key theory known as the "cannonball" model, which states that normal galaxies convert into elliptical galaxies through a process of normal star formation, growth, and then explosion as a supernova. High-energy and high-momentum fluctuations occur within the nucleus due to short-range correlations (SRC). In order to understand these correlations' impact on SRC-induced phenomena, a detailed exploration of their structure is necessary. We analyze the spatial and momentum characteristics of SRC using the correlation function and find that their density is concentrated in areas with intense momentum within $2\le k\le 4$~F$^{-1}$. We develop a theoretical model to guide our findings. We discover in our model that the magnitude of SRC density is heavily influenced by the correlation function's imaginary part, typically dominated by inelastic processes. As a result, regions of high momentum within the inter-nucleon gap and inter-fractional space exhibit increased density, while inter-nucleon density areas demonstrate lower density. We further observe that removing the correlation function's imaginary part causes additional fluctuations in SRC density. This suggests possible connections between SRC and twin-pion correlations observed in heavy nuclei and large momentum transfer experiments. We propose and outline a theoretical framework to enhance our understanding of SRC for precise measurements of SRC-induced phenomena. This framework aims to ensure compliance with the strict constraints imposed by experiments, often one-pion scattering, and our own article. We anticipate our description to facilitate the determination of SRC distributions essential for the precise calculation of SRC-induced phenomena. In particular, a detailed and accurate description of SRC distributions and their concentration within the nucleus will be vital for the precise calculation of SRC-induced phenomena, particularly important for the emission of very energetic nucleons and photons. Our framework encompasses various distributions, including those in momentum and in configuration space, allowing for the incorporation of various high and low frequency correlations. As an extension, our framework can be used in the case of sea Gogny forces where high frequency components are automatically included in the correlation function. We anticipate these developments to contribute substantially to the calculation of SRC-induced phenomena, particularly important for the emergence of a linear density of nucleons within the nucleus at very large momenta, a critical aspect of the emission of very energetic nucleons and photons. We are studying complex deep learning by focusing on the behavior of complex-valued neural networks.  Unlike its real-valued counterpart, the complex-valued network can represent complex relationships between its inputs and outputs, thanks to its extended feature space. But, it's unclear how to measure the complexity of these relationships due to lack of entropy-like tools in the complex plane. So we develop new co-domain symmetry concepts based on entropy characteristics that apply to any complex-valued function. These concepts lead to meaningful generalisations of real-valued entropy characteristics. Interestingly, our investigation of co-domain symmetry goes beyond neural networks and can be applied to any complex-valued function. Through our analysis, we gain insights into training complex deep learning models. We demonstrate our approach with applications in multi-dimensional regression tasks, revealing a new perspective on understanding complex deep learning. The source code for our experiments can be found at https://github.com/drewcamp/co-domain-symmetry. The results show that incorporating co-domain symmetry indeed improves model performance. Moreover, our methods achieve state-of-the-art results in one case and consistently compete with existing techniques for complex deep learning. When gluon distribution becomes saturated, it establishes a distinct gluon density threshold per unit rapidity per transverse area known as the saturation momentum.  In certain large-energy situations within specified kinematic domains, saturation momentum becomes the only determining factor in physical processes. Consequently, a variety of observable outcomes display characteristic patterns of geometrical scaling. Several illustrations of such scaling patterns can be seen in various reactions. Examples include a particular adjustment of the structure function $F_2(x,Q)$ where $x$ does not appear as a factor and instead depends on $Q$ through the saturation momentum, a particular adjustment of the electron-weakening function $F_2(x,Q)$ where $Q$ does not appear as a factor and instead depends on $x$ through the saturation momentum, a particular adjustment of the electron-weakening function $F_L(x,Q)$ where $x$ does not appear as a factor and instead depends on $Q$ through the saturation momentum, and heavy-ion collisions where predicted influences of a process called gluon gluon scattering at high energies are expected to manifest themselves in certain measurements, such as the distribution of charged particles in different angles.
