The PALEOCCENE concept has the potential to develop and utilize a large-scale, sensitive and efficient low-energy detector to investigate astrophysical processes using colored atomic ions in free space or within a host material. This simplicity is a significant advantage over current techniques involving color centers in insulators, which are prone to destructive surface radiation damage.  With multiple ionization mechanisms including electron scattering and multiple nuclear excitations, PALEOCCENE can also serve as a collaborative project to advance the understanding of ab-initio calculations of collective nuclear states.  Furthermore, because scientists can manipulate and observe individual ions, PALEOCCENE allows scientists to perform both wave-like and particle-like nuclear recoil measurements in various recoil energies and kinematic configurations.  Finally, because individual ions can be manipulated with lasers, it breaks the limitations of counting events within a defined time frame, which enables PALEOCCENE to offer a range of analysis tools above standard kinematic analysis methods.  This talk will examine the theoretical basis for PALEOCCENE, its potential applications and the necessary conditions for developing the technology required to bring this project to life.  Some innovative spin-offs including new types of magnetometry, simulations of stellar processes, high-speed rotation spectrum measurements, and rare particle detection are also within the reach of this idea.  Initially developed within the "Luis de Galarza" research group at the Universidad Industrial de Santander as a requirement for her PhD, it has since been evolved through a collaboration with established scientists.  The primary objective is to secure the necessary funding and collaboration to test the PALEOCCENE technology at leading research institutions such as SLAC, Los Alamos, or CERN.  The initial prototype, currently being developed, incorporates PALEOCCENE's core technology and will serve as a key tool in testing its capabilities prior to scaling up to larger sizes.  Ultimately, PALEOCCENE aims to contribute significantly to low-energy astrophysical research and earn a spot among the top priority projects within the research community at an international level.  This work offers a detailed understanding of the various components required for building PALEOCCENE and similar technology concepts.  Some potential drawbacks and challenges, together with suggestions for how to overcome them and implement effective solutions, are also included.  Finally, because PALEOCCENE relies on the development of cutting-edge new technologies rather than simply applying existing ones, it is primarily suited towards research within new, independent research groups or as part of cutting-edge research projects.

We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient in 2D space. One particle is driven actively in a specific direction by a constant force, while the direction-of-travel of the second particle is randomly fluctuating. Within a scenario where both particles respond to the activity gradient in a nonlinear fashion, we investigate their behavior across a wide range of activity disparities. The impact of varying activity levels is explored through the lens of different system phases, comprising two distinct regions: one comprising high-activity clusters in 3D space, and another with curved, ring-shaped coexistence patterns in 2D space. By employing 3D simulations and resolving temporal dynamics, we demonstrate how these unique structures influence the directional persistence of active colloidal dimer pairs, ultimately revealing that persistence is significantly enhanced in response to unique nonlinearities and varied activity disparities. Our comprehensive analysis provides an in-depth understanding of active colloidal behavior in complex, nonlinear response scenarios. Furthermore, our findings are supplemented by 2D simulations and rigorous analysis informing our calculation of the effective potential governing active dimer pairs, as well as the phase diagram of the dimer system in different dimensional contexts. A theoretical model, rooted in nonlinear nonequilibrium response, is developed to qualitatively explain the observed behavior. Notably, our results may be readily applied to observe nonequilibrium structural phase transitions in various systems featuring directional self-propelled entities. Moreover, our comprehensive investigation offers a wealth of insights and practical knowledge for 2D and 3D contexts, potentially be realized in upcoming experimental and colloidal particle studies. Ultimately, our primary contribution lies in the systematic exploration of the intricate and multifaceted effects observed in the context of active colloidal systems and nonlinear response systems. Moreover, our collection of simulation data is accessible through a GitHub repository, while selected results from this study have been visually presented in supplementary materials, aiming to enhance reader understanding and clarity. We investigate numerically the spectral properties of fractionally charged quasiparticle excitations and multiple magnetoroton modes within the SU(2) gauge-invariant picture of the nu=1/2 quantum Hall wavefunction system. Our findings include the nu=1/2 system adhering to sum rules of conformal field theory and the emergence of two distinct magnetorotons, possessing g factor values of 1 and 2, which display robustness against varying Coulomb coupling. We propose that the SU(2) picture may effectively capture the spectral characteristics of su(2) gauge fields in the true ground state of the system. Furthermore, SU(2) picture provides an accurate description of the SU(2) gauge field in the nu=1/3 system, possessing two magnetorotons with g factor values of 1/2 and 1. The g factor of 1/2, in this case, arises from charged quasiparticle pairs that, in the case of nu=1/2, yield a g factor of 2. Our study also indicates the distinct emergence of the third magnetoroton mode in both the nu=1/2 and nu=1/3 systems, as the Coulomb coupling increases. We support our main conclusions with two independent calculations: one, based on the exact wavefunction, and another, born of density-matrix renormalization group methods. The findings of our studies align with the results of ongoing or recently completed numerical works on nu=1/2, nu=1/3, and other quantum Hall systems with various nu values. We plan to extend our research to other numbered fractions like nu=2/3, nu=3/4, and nu=3/8. Epidemics on massive contact networks with millions of individuals pose significant challenges for analysis and containment due to their immense scale. However, for networks that can be segmented into groups, describing the spread of an outbreak between these segments is significantly more manageable. Typically, studies have relied on dividing individuals into equitable subgroups; however, this is often impractical for networks lacking nearly equal populations within each subgroup. In this paper, we offer a new approach to categorizing networks into practical clusters by defining a divide that minimizes the spread of an outbreak along edges between clusters. This partition is identified through a specialized variant of the k-means algorithm tailored to handle the unique nature of epidemic networks. Our approach is validated by applying it to various real-world networks and comparing the outcomes with the SIR model's predictions. By leveraging this algorithm and SIR model simulations, we provide actionable strategies for containing an outbreak. Furthermore, we develop mathematical frameworks that enable us to precisely determine the optimal division of a network and the most effective containment policies and also enable us to derive a closed-form solution that minimizes a weighted edge spread for large clusters. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our algorithm produces satisfactory results, yielding a maximum error of less than 0.05% for networks with up to 10 million vertices and a maximum error of less than 0.18% for networks with up to 100 million edges. This methodology holds potential for expanding to even more complex models and networks. It also has the potential to further advance into other domains such as data clustering problems. The developed algorithms are available in an open-source library called ClusterPy. ClusterPy can handle networks up to 10 million vertices and a large number of requested clusters within a few minutes, demonstrating its scalability. In addition, we have included a detailed guide on installing and using ClusterPy along with its default settings as part of the supplementary materials. Lastly, the figures in this paper have been generated using Matplotlib, an open-source plotting library. The maximum likelihood estimator used in CMB map-making provides optimal, unbiased results as long as the underlying data model is accurate, but inaccuracies often arise due to sub-pixel structures, instrumentation flaws such as time-varying gain and pointing errors or sampling patterns like striations and ring effects. To mitigate these inaccuracies and prevent CMB maps from being distorted, various techniques like de-weighting, de-trending, de-pixelisation and de-sampling are employed. Some of these methods have been integrated into the CMB Map Making Library which is open-source, allowing for an intercomparison of their effects and advantages. In this study, the impacts on CMB maps of varying types of errors and the effects of ring disease are evaluated with the goal of choosing the most effective methods and minimizing artifacts caused by sampling patterns, while also exploring possibilities for preserving sky correlations by de-weighting instead of de-pixelising. Furthermore, a new method is suggested for handling instrumental errors by demodulating and subtracting a time-dependent trend instead of a single value. The possibilities of simultaneously demodulating and de-pixelising are also considered and scheduled in a future research project. The current limitations and potential improvements of this method will be the subject of future investigations. In addition to CMB data sets, the maximum likelihood estimator and the associated map making tools are versatile and can also be applied to CMB foreground maps, cosmological surveys, solar neutrino measurements and other fields that benefit from maximum likelihood estimation. In fact, some of the underlying principles of MAP making were initially developed in a 2002 conference on maximum likelihood estimation in astronomy and astrophysics, with the current research as its most recent contribution. In summary, the goal of this research is to explore ways to prevent X-es in a variety of data sets and the associated demonstrations of their effects and the different techniques for avoiding them will be presented at the TAC NAFAA19 conference. The current research has significant implications for upcoming and future experiments such as the LiteBIRD and the main BOOMERANG. The X'es in CMB maps have also previously been attributed to non-Gaussianity, although this interpretation is not universally accepted. In CMB map making, the current standard practice is to prevent Gaussian errors, but not non-Gaussian ones, which are the focus of this research. The CMB map making field and the accompanying scientific community of CMB map makers is international and the CMB map making library has previously contributed to various international projects such as the POLARBEAR

Interpreting teaching instructions with natural language can be compromised by word ambiguity. When mentors use indistinct vocabulary to specify rewards or constraints, their instructions may hold multiple reasonable interpretations. We introduce a teaching method that considers the contextual implications of the mentor's words during the learning process. We also develop a series of practical tasks inspired by everyday situations that showcase the effectiveness of our approach in overcoming reference ambiguities. Compared to a previous landmark study, our results reveal a substantial boost in performance achieved through the proposed method. We demonstrate the feasibility of our approach using a new dataset we created to assess relational task acquisition in a simulated setting. This dataset, called Grounded Phase-Neutral Reinforcement Learning (G-PNRL), presents a range of real-world challenges, including varying object counts, environmental complexities, and differences in syllable count. By utilizing a computer-ran primer, we automatically generate training objectives for agents to acquire skills in a controlled environment. Following our experimental evaluation, we plan to further develop our model through a study involving human teachers. The dataset and associated materials can be found at https://sites.google.com/view/our-work-at-icml. Data and resource links are also included below.

Quantum process tomography, crucial for developing quantum devices and understanding quantum dynamics, lacks efficient protocols due to excessive experimental requirements. New approaches, such as reduced parameters and machine learning, have improved this efficiency, but further enhancements are needed. particularly in the channel domain. We introduce shadow process tomography (SPT), an updated protocol for quantum channel characterization, combining the efficacy of unitary process tomography and the efficiency of congruence between channels and circuits. Given a fixed number of experiments, SPT outperforms the traditional method by constructing a larger virtual space containing more distinct channel matrices than the actual number of free parameters. Consequently, the free parameters can be determined more robustly. We implement the SPT protocol on a IBM quantum computer, successfully reconstructing the Amplitude Damping channel with fewer experiments than traditional process tomography. These results make SPT a promising tool for characterizing quantum channels. To further solidify this concept, we provide a practical guide for SPT implementation. Our study showcases the advantages of SPT, offering a new hope for quantum channel characterization. The primary human-readable code for this work can be found at the repository provided. Additionally, the code for generating figures and the executable code for demonstrating SPT with an FRQ circuit are also available at the repository. A more technical description of our methodology and fence posting is documented within the repository.

The conformation of surface molecules greatly affects their functions. For Sc2TbN@C80, the conformation directly relates to the presence of an electric and a magnetic dipole moment. As a result, the adsorption of this molecule on a substrate changes the work function, thereby qualifying the system as magnetoelectric. Research conducted on a monolayer of Sc2TbN@C80 on h-BN/Ni(111) revealed a range of interesting physical and magnetic properties. However, the impact of temperature on these properties was not addressed. The current study explores how temperature influences the conformation, work function, and magnetic properties of the Sc2TbN@C80 monolayer through first-principles simulations. The results indicate that the conformation of Sc2TbN@C80 undergoes a significant transformation from an armchair to a zigzag configuration when sitting on a hexagon. The temperature dependence of the work function shows a decrease for the armchair and an increase for the zigzag configurations. The calculated work functions for both configurations align with experimental findings. The study also determines that the magnetic properties of the Sc2TbN@C80 monolayer are sensitive to temperature and can be modified through a transition from the armchair to the zigzag configuration. The current research may pave the way for the development of magnetoelectric materials. The study's data could be applied directly in experimental design and the development of related theoretical models. The work contributes valuable knowledge to the quantum spin dynamics, magnetic properties, and electronic structure fields. The work influences the development of materials with unique magnetoelectric properties and expands the scope of relevant scientific investigations. The Ramsey sequence serves as a prime illustration of quantum phase measurement for a spin qubit, and its efficiency in measurements can be enhanced by strategically choosing the duration of phase accumulation, $\tau$. A well-designed experiment can reach the limits set by quantum principles, resulting in optimal performance. We introduce a cutting-edge experimental technique that actively adjusts parameters based on real-time data collection. Our adaptive experiment design is grounded in Bayesian theory, continuously updating the qubit's state estimate and related uncertainty as new measurements are taken. A Bayesian method is used to determine the most favorable $\tau$ setting to achieve minimum variance in measurements within a predetermined timeframe. Utilizing a heuristic approach, known as the multi-armed bandit problem, our design efficiently simulates a vast array of potential measurement scenarios and determines the optimal $\tau$ setting. Our results indicate that this approach yields significant improvements, reducing variance by 90%, as well as demonstrating the inherent connections between uncertainty reduction and time, showcasing the efficiency of our adaptive design in optimizing Ramsey sequence measurements. Furthermore, our method exhibits robustness in the face of various qubit dynamics, including both linear and non-linear degradation. Additional advantages of our approach include diminished energy usage and reduced occurrences of detrimental late switching events in measurements. Our ground-breaking adaptive experiment reduces the necessary exploration time by approximately two orders of magnitude. In summary, our research provides an efficient framework for optimizing Ramsey sequence measurements through innovative and autonomous quantum protocol management, thereby paving the way for rapid and precise qubit ensembles reconstructing methods. It is noteworthy that Bayesian-based experimental design has extensive potential in various frontiers of quantum information processing. Our method may facilitate the creation of intelligent, autonomous quantum information systems, capable of independently planning and executing complex operations within quantum information frameworks. It is conceivable that techniques like the multi-armed bandit problem and noise filtering could be applied in other cutting-edge quantum algorithms such as quantum Bayes nets and QAOA. Network centrality metrics quantify node importance using various geometric and diffusive characteristics, focusing on distinct scales. From a multi-scale perspective, a network can be viewed as comprising multiple levels of analysis. The small-scale perspective examines local connections between nearby nodes, whereas the large-scale view involves analyzing nodes across the entire network. Gromov centrality, a new metric, assesses importance based on the severity of the excess triangle inequality violations surrounding a node. Due to its multi-scale properties, it examines the structural characteristics of a network closely. From our empirical analysis using over 50 real-world networks, Gromov centrality correlates strongly with existing metrics like Degree centrality and PageRank. A comprehensive evaluation is presented, including an analysis of a geometrically structured random graph model, to further understand Gromov centrality's properties. The proposed approach offers a scalable analysis of network centrality with computational complexity nearly linear in size. Gromov centrality has numerous applications, including data analysis, biology, and graph analytics. From a purely non-relativistic perspective, we derive the Poisson equation solution for empty space in a scenario with a rotating gravitational system, analogous to the Sun, and consider the implications of this solution for the behavior of test objects within its gravitational field. The general solution to the Poisson equation, expressed in terms of the distance r and angle θ, is shown to exhibit properties consistent with Newton's inverse square law of gravitation to the lowest order. This analysis yields two significant outcomes when considered to various speeds of the gravitational source: a speed of zero (classical Gravitational Frame), and the speed of light (Lorentz Gravitational Frame). This Lorentz Gravitational Frame leads to a modified gravitation theory, commonly known as General Relativity, when applied to spherically symmetric spaces, and this modified theory reveals a discrepancy at the orbital level of Mercury in the Solar system, as evidenced by the precession angle. However, the proposed Azimuthally Symmetric Gravitation Theory appears to be in agreement with the observed precession angle. Furthermore, this theory is expected to generate a range of phenomena not accounted for in General Relativity, including previously unexplained behaviors in the Solar system, and phenomena associated with white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes. A companion paper will explore the fundamental aspects and general implications of this gravitational theory. Future research aims to verify this theory through experimental testing in the Solar system, asteroid belt, and other locations. If successful, the ASG Traction Initiative could be a pivotal discovery in our understanding of gravitation and space-time. Given a subindex, a specific type of set containing the subindices is defined and explored in detail. We demonstrate that the set of these indices, along with the monic bundle ${\mathcal M}_i$, forms a group under the operation of combining indices. The operation results in a new index and a bundle ${\mathcal M}_{i \circ j}$ obtained by multiplying the original bundles. Additionally, the effect of the operation on the units of the set ${\mathcal M}_i$ is examined and we prove that ${\mathcal M}_{i \circ j}$ can be represented as a tensor product of the original bundles. Furthermore, the set of these indices, along with the monic bundle ${\mathcal M}_i$, satisfies the defining properties of a module over a ring and forms a commutative semigroup under the operation of combining indices. Using these results, the set and the bundle of matrix pencils under the operation of combination can be represented and mapped in a manner similar to T.W. Samsel's work on the operation of addition. Samsel's set and the unitary bundle of commutative matrix pencils under the operation of combination. Lastly, the results provide a connection between different operations, namely, the operation of combination and the operation of addition. Notably, both operations yield relatively similar, though not identical, sets and units. Consequently, the operation of combination can be viewed as a generalized version of the operation of addition. For C1-smooth discrete-time systems exhibiting strong monotonicity, the prevailing long-term behavior of linearly stable cycles is established in a probabilistic framework. This research then extends to periodic parabolic equations and reveals new findings regarding the ubiquity of periodic solution convergence. Notably, in Neumann-bound equations defined on convex domains, the set of initial conditions corresponding to homogeneous periodic solutions is shown to be prevalent, while in radially symmetric domains, the set of radially symmetric periodic solution trajectories exhibits prevalence among initial values. Moreover, in planar discrete-time systems featuring strong monotonicity, the prevailing long-term behavior of quadratic-like functions is also elucidated. Ultimately, these probabilistic results are utilized to establish prevalence among cone-invariant sets comprising limiting sets and full invariant sets in the context of discrete-time dynamical systems supporting a global attractor. The method employed and its implications are discussed, involving characterization of invariant sets via maximally invariant subsets or their half-space closures. This approach is found to be versatile, applying not only to discrete-time systems but also to continuous-time dynamical systems, including ordinary differential equations (ODEs). However, in the continuous-time setting, the notion of prevalence requires modification due to its dependence on path-length considerations, leading to a definition that differs from the discrete case. Despite these distinctions, the prevailing long-term behaviors exhibited in the mentioned examples remain intact. Furthermore, in Neumann-bound ODE systems, the set of initial values corresponding to homogeneous limiting sets is demonstrated to be prevalent, while in radially symmetric cases, the set of radially symmetric solution trajectories exhibits prevalence among initial values. The presented findings contribute to the body of work regarding prevalence in the context of dynamical systems through its creation of novel open conditions. In particular, in the spirit of the Half-Space Conjecture regarding the prevalence of periodic solution convergence, a new conjecture is proposed in the context of discrete-time systems featuring strong monotonicity. This conjecture postulates prevalence among initial values with negative or nonnegative entries in the basins of attraction corresponding to different periodic orbits, with a notable example in the present paper involving quadratic-like unimodal maps, where such prevalence is shown and serves as evidence for the proposed conjecture. A prevalence-based result for the convergence set of quadratic-like unimodal maps is independently established for the case of odd unimodal maps without the necessity of strong monotonicity assumptions. Consequently, further research is needed to ascertain the general applicability of the proposed conjecture regarding the prevalence of periodic solution convergence

The potential of using noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers with the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) lies in molecular simulations, where accurately constructing an ansatz using a shallow quantum circuit is key to successful implementation. Instead of employing fermionic-excitation evolutions to create ans\"atze, our approach utilizes qubit-excitation evolutions, which adhere to qubit commutation relations. By doing so, qubit excitation evolutions can accurately construct ans\"atze, even with a few gates, and is less susceptible to noise due to lower SU(2) matrix dimension. We present an adaptive QVE (AQVE) method where qubit-excitation evolutions are used to update VQE parameters, and demonstrate its effectiveness in molecular hydrogen and water simulations using IBMQ processors. Notably, our AQVE outperformed fermionic evolutions in terms of fidelity and required fewer SU(2) matrix inversions, and successfully ran on IBMQ processors with reduced Pauli transfer requirements. The proposed AQVE presents a promising method for noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers in molecular chemistry applications. We propose an unsupervised speech synthesis approach that builds on recent research in automatic speech recognition and existing neural-based speech generation methods. Employing only raw, unlabeled audio and text data, as well as a dictionary, our technique enables high-quality speech synthesis without requiring a prelabeled dataset. Human evaluation confirms the synthesized speech produced by the unsupervised system is comparable to that of a traditionally trained model in terms of its naturalness and ease of understanding. We make our data and implementation publicly available at https://github.com/muhenai/unsupervised_speech_synthesis. We also discuss potential applications for this research, including its implications for voice conversion and the development of low-resource speech synthesis systems. Furthermore, we highlight the potential of the observed transfer learning effect to simplify the development of speech synthesis systems in limited resource environments. Lastly, we reflect on the potential of the unsupervised speech synthesis approach to unlock more efficient and effective neural language models. The unsolved challenges of the problem are outlined in the Conclusions section below. Moreover, the research presents a new method for the generation of neural speech synthesis: a two-stage neural speech generation approach, where a neural component with a focused loss generates a proxy label, and a secondary neural component transposes the proxy label into speech. We prove that the synthesized proxy label is highly correlated with the true proxy label, and through adversarial training, we achieve a situation in which the distance between the proxy label and the true proxy label is small. We empirically verify the effectiveness of this method by conducting both the zero-shot and weak-supervised speech synthesis tasks. We demonstrate that the neural speech generation approach leads to a significant improvement in the quality of the synthesized speech in the weak-supervised task. We also show through the human evaluation that the neural speech generation approach produces speech that is superior to that of the widely used Sequence2Sequence model in the zero-shot task. We make the implementation of this model publicly available at https://github.com/jay-kim123/zero_shoted_speech_synthesis. These data, gathered by the thermal plasma experiment, cover a distance range from 29 to 44 solar radii, spanning the time period from June 2018 to December 2018.  The measured energy flux exhibits significant variability and significantly correlates with the solar wind speed over the recorded interval.  An analysis of the speed and energy flux relationships reveals that for solar wind speeds less than 380 km/s, the energy flux displays a consistent dependence on velocity, but for higher speeds, the relationship becomes nonlinear. A new method inspired by finite volume schemes leverages a cell-average based neural network to solve partial differential equations. By utilizing the weak formulation of these equations, the method trains a feed-forward network to accurately predict solution evolution between time steps, circumventing traditional numerical limitations. After offline training, the neural network model exhibits flexibility in accommodating a range of spatial and temporal discretizations, including adaptive techniques such as local refinement. Furthermore, the method avoids dependency on specific numerical schemes, while maintaining mass balance and preserving key properties of conservation laws. We demonstrate the method's capabilities by achieving high-order accuracy in both space and time for a variety of equations, including nonlinear conservation laws and parabolic equations at increasingly high orders. Additional details on the method's implementation are provided in the supporting code, which includes a user-friendly research framework known as RegressorPDE. RegressorPDE facilitates offline and online operations, as well as modeling and simulation configuration passing, with a modular structure similar to torchscript. We also showcase the method's practical applications in multiscale and weak solution scenarios and discuss its inherent strengths such as decreased computational memory demands over traditional methods. The Unruh effect can emerge not only through the entanglement of left and right Rindler modes, but also between forward and backward light cone modes in high-speed accelerating observer frames. We show that this time-like entanglement can be detected by observing correlations between the zeroth and fourth Wigner components of a measured quantum field's quasi-classical state across future and past light cones in these observer frames. The threshold for observing this time-like Unruh effect is the acceleration-dependent Planck frequency $\hbar \sqrt{\frac{a}{3\pi}}$, below which it will be masked by thermal noise. Furthermore, the amount of time-like entanglement present is quantified by the von Neumann entropy of the two future and backward light cone regions in question. The relation between this time-like Unruh effect and the geometric phase, or Berry phase, is examined and we find that as the acceleration planck scale is approached, the influence of geometric phase on time-like Unruh effect previously considered to be the most pressing experimental challenge in quantum field theory may ultimately not present an overwhelming technical difficulty after all. Conclusions are drawn about the time-like Unruh effect in de Sitter space and three-dimensional Schwarzschild black holes. We end with a discussion on the future-like Unruh effect in four-dimensional Minkwitz space. The formation of magnetically-driven jets from a spinning black hole following a compact binary merger is a potentially significant event, capable of launching relativistic outflows that explain the phenomenon of short gamma ray bursts and kilonovae. By utilizing the detection of gravitational waves by LIGO and Virgo and subsequently modeling the associated gravitational signals, we have developed a method to evaluate parameter dependencies in an advanced magnetohydrodynamic simulation of accretion disks. Specifically, we have optimized parameters within a simulation of a disk with an initial marginally stable spin of 0.5 (in units of the dimensionless spin parameter J), which leads to the generation of collimated outflows. Our investigation into the behavior of these simulations reveals that various parameters influence the formation of jets from the spinning black hole. Moreover, we have identified the potential for these outflows to carry significant amounts of angular momentum, which could be key in understanding the behavior of magnetically-driven disks. Additionally, we have determined that the energy and momentum ejected in the jets from our optimized simulations align with expectations for magnetically-driven relativistic jets from spinning black holes, which could explain observed data of kilonovae and short gamma ray bursts. Furthermore, we have identified the probable influence of various parameter adjustments on jet behavior and have determined that the best matches with observational data of kilonovae and short gamma ray bursts are achieved with advanced magnetohydrodynamic simulations featuring high neutrino cooling rates and collimated outflows. A type of Gaussian process regression that accounts for the variability in data points, called heteroscedastic Gaussian process regression, is utilized to develop predictive models for the specific loads an offshore wind turbine will experience. The randomness inherent in turbulence and wave conditions makes the resulting loads more accurately described as probabilistic events rather than fixed values. The effect of these stochastic factors on the loads is also contingent on the prevailing environmental conditions, with variations occurring more noticeably under higher mean wind speeds than lower ones, a characteristic known as heteroscedasticity. The surrogate models developed through this method demonstrate the ability to efficiently and effectively predict the probability distribution of 10-minute mean pitch and yaw loads across a wide range of offshore environments, with minimal computational requirements, further enabling the optimization of turbine design with these probabilistic models. By comparing the predicted distributions of pitch and yaw loads with the actual loads experienced by the turbine NREL-5.0-M130 within the Database of Ocean Turbine-Generated Waves, it was found that the model offers high accuracy in general but overestimates the degree to which standard surrogate models fail to account for variability in the data. A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce infinitely many oriented asymptotically non-intersecting non-closed loops in G. We will demonstrate that virtually solvable groups and nilpotent quotients of generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups possess the $R_\infty$ property. This achievement addresses an unresolved query introduced by Scherker in 1977. Our approach involves the resolution of Scherker's query for a distinct subset of these groups, namely solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups, utilizing a combination of the Lind-Rodriguez Palma Gap Theorem and Dubins Loop Pipeline Method. For the remainder of these groups, the result is established through the application of Kechin's Method for constructing oriented non-closed geodesic paths, a technique which itself represents significant independent contribution. Furthermore, it has been found that certain solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups possess the $R_\infty$ property in a manner determined by a fixed finite set of values. To accommodate this, the notion of property $R_{\infty, n}$ has been defined and the presented findings fall under a broader generalised Lind-Rodriguez Palma Gap Theorem framework. A comprehensive overview of groups exhibiting property $R_{\infty, n}$ will be provided. Lastly, it is speculated that the work presented could be extended to a broader subset of groups including metabelian groups and groups with presentations comprising two generators and two relations, a exploration which is themselves worthy of significant scientific inquiry. The associated thesis produced as a result of this research has been made accessible at the UoE repository via the URL provided at the bottom of this response. Our analysis reveals that the average of the squared difference between theta and its average, multiplied by the average rate of change of exponential theta, is less than or equal to 2ht, where h is Planck's constant, t is time, and the inequality is associated with Jarzynski's fluctuation relation for non-projective measurements. Moreover, we derive a stronger form of this inequality that doesn't rely on the non-markovian character of the measurement process and find that it is connected to the impossibility of lowering the entropy of a closed system when subjected to a series of measurements. Furthermore, we discuss a form of the gholtzmann-Kramers equation applicable to non-markovian processes and explore its implications for the inequality. Our analysis also reveals that the thermodynamic uncertainty principle and the fluctuation inequality become identical when the average rate of change of exponential theta is constant or when the memory of the non-markovian process is infinite. Finally, we verify the validity of our analysis with the results of a non-projective measurement experiment and demonstrate the non-applicability of traditional inequalities such as the arra and braunstein inequality. Our analysis also reveals that the thermodynamic uncertainty principle exceeds the precision of a classical clock, where the precision of a clock is denoted as hbar. Furthermore, we derive a relationship between a non-projective measurement and a quantum version of knudsen's formula. We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2-structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define deformed nearly G2-structures and instantons. We further derive a necessary and sufficient condition for rigidity in G2-instantons, and utilize this condition to describe the deformation space of SU(3)-instantons on a 7-manifold with a nearly G2-structure in terms of harmonic 1-forms. Furthermore, we show that the SU(3)-instantons on a 9-manifold with a deformed, homogeneous de Sitter structure are rigid. Through the use of spinors and Dirac operators, we establish the deformation theory of SU(3)-instantons on a 9-manifold with a nearly G2-structure, and prove that the SU(3)-instantons on a 9-manifold with a homogeneous, hyperbolic de Sitter structure are rigid. As part of the effort to combat this crisis, contact tracing technology, known for its success in other outbreaks, has been widely adopted.  However, this technology poses significant concerns regarding user data security, as it entails data collection and analysis that can potentially reveal an individual's identity, location, and behavior. The implications of this are especially dire when considering large-scale public health services, which are inherently vulnerable to data breaches.  Despite this, contact tracing technology continues to be a vital tool for managing the COVID-19 outbreak, prompting the development of various national contact tracing projects. Additionally, this paper proposes recommendations to strengthen the security measures of Coronav-SUS and similar projects, which are crucial for maintaining trust and protecting users' data. Furthermore, this paper invites readers to replicate the analysis presented in this research on other contact tracing projects, in order to foster a greater understanding of these essential tools to combat the COVID-19 pandemic.

Historically, this has primarily been a focus for chemists, neuroscientists, and biologists. This study proposes that the brain's ability to acquire and utilize random patterns can be efficiently achieved through the combination of two established physical principles - thermodynamics and quantum mechanics - thereby providing a potential explanation for the brain's extraordinary capabilities. We provide theoretical frameworks, support existing, and initiate novel experimental studies, with a focus on key roles for entropy, entanglement, and non-locality in brain function. We also outline significant implications for understanding the nature of intelligence. This analysis suggests that quantum behavior could contribute to key brain functions, and therefore potentially other complex systems, more so than previously considered. We also evidence that quantum properties may offer a crucial explanation for the brain's extraordinary capabilities. This analysis provides a potential framework for integrating quantum mechanics and entropy to explain how complex systems, such as the human brain, acquire and utilize random patterns. Furthermore, key concepts in this analysis - nonlocality, entanglement, and nonlocal quantum systems - are relevant to the fundamental question of whether there are two types of random patterns: the random behavior typically attributed to thermodynamics versus the more exotic quantum entanglement. In conclusion, we speculate that the pattern of random waves in brain function - whether due to thermodynamic or quantum entanglement - may be a fundamental property that underlies the nature of intelligence. This analysis must be considered in the context of a large body of experimental and theoretical studies in neuroscience and quantum physics, and we propose that the most suitable next step would be a comprehensive review to integrate these two disciplines for understanding the nature of intelligence. Such a review could offer a potential explanation for the extraordinary capabilities of the human brain and thereby contribute to a deeper understanding of the nature of intelligence. We anticipate that the next steps in this analysis - both experimental and theoretical studies - could offer a potential explanation for the extraordinary capabilities of the human brain. Furthermore, we also evidence how the concept of entropy in thermodynamics could offer a potential explanation for the nature of randomness in brain function. Consequently, we propose that the pattern of random waves in brain function - whether due to thermodynamic or quantum entanglement - may be a fundamental property that underlies the nature of intelligence. We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^2-equivariant theory constructed in Bar22, share a key decomposition. This key decomposition facilitates reducing the T-equivariant cohomology computation to T^2-equivariant cohomology of complex spheres, whose computation is already available from Bar22. Consequently, we derive a formula for the T-equivariant cohomology of CP(V) in terms of the highest weights of V and its dual. This formula is further shown to be compatible with Chern-Weil exact sequence and the Adams-Getzler spectral sequence, and it recovers known results from Gre05 when T is a 1-dimensional group. Moreover, it leads to a new understanding of the Adams-Getzler spectral sequence in the context of equivariant elliptic cohomology, which highlights the crucial role of weight monodromy in the equivariant spectrum. Ultimately, our results provide a new perspective on the computational aspects of equivariant elliptic cohomology. The study derived the numerical expressions for total and differential cross sections, specifically $\frac{d\sigma}{d\cos\theta}=A+B\cos^2\theta$, and included newly-calculated QCD corrections. This analysis led to moderate enhancements of the $\alpha_\theta$ parameter in $J/\psi + \chi_{c0}$ and $J/\psi + \chi_{c1}$ and significant reductions in $J/\psi + \chi_{c2}$ production; the value for $J/\psi + \eta_c$ remained unchanged. Comparing our predictions with experimental data, we found enhanced agreement and determined the $\alpha_\theta$ parameter for $J/\psi + \chi_{c0}$ and $J/\psi + \chi_{c1}$ to be sensibly modified in line with the corrected QCD corrections calculation results. Furthermore, applying our angular distribution model to an unhindered $\chi_{c1} \to J/\psi + \eta_c$ decay and using the $\alpha_{\theta,\chi_{c1}}$ value from the corrected QCD corrections calculation results allowed us to obtain the $\sin^2\theta_w$ parameter in accordance with the recently measured value of 0.2309. Additionally, using the angular distribution model for $J/\psi + \chi_{c0}$ we were able to calculate the ratio of spin-triplet to spin-singlet quark combining production, yielding a value of 0.733, in reasonable agreement with the recently measured ratio of 0.52. Finally, we established that the $\alpha_{\theta,\eta_c}$ and $\alpha_{\theta, \chi_{cJ}}$ values for $J/\psi + \eta_c$ and $J/\psi + \chi_{cJ}$ (for $J=0,1$) are insensitive to the $\alpha_s$ value; in the case of $\alpha_{\theta,\chi_{c2}}$ it is Confinement-sensitive. Numerous languages attribute gender not just to living entities but also to inanimate objects. When such a gender-based distinction is present in a language, statistical models often mirror this bias in their representation, as found in experiments with Spanish and German. Although existing numerical word representation models like word2vec incorporate grammatical gender, the effect of gender on their performance and accuracy remains unclear. We investigated this phenomenon by adapting the word2vec model to work with both morphological and lexical forms of German and Spanish words, focusing on inanimate objects and evaluating their results using semantic similarity tests. Surprisingly, adding a constraint based on gender according to a thesaurus produced better outcomes in all cases we examined. Moreover, our results showed that by fixing the gender of inanimate objects, the accuracy of our model increased by up to 15% in German and 11% in Spanish, using a very small dataset, as compared to an unsupervised approach. Our discovery suggests that incorporating grammatical gender into a model's training can significantly boost its efficiency and efficiency even when the dataset is limited. We have made our modified code available for public use. Overall, our research indicated that incorporating external knowledge based on a language's characteristics can greatly boost the efficiency of pre-trained word embedding models. Such knowledge can be utilized as a soft constraint to improve these models' performance and accuracy. We plan to further develop these concepts and apply them to other areas of investigation. For instance, we could investigate the effect of various types of soft constraints on the performance of pre-trained word embedding models. Another potential area of research could be to develop and train artificial neural networks to function as a type of knowledge base, where the constraints that affect the data during training continue to influence its processing. Finally, we could explore the potential links between grammatical gender and the words it influences at the linguistic level. Such links might represent an instance of the connection often referred to or related to the concept of anthropocentrism. A detailed explanation of this can be found in our study, where we also discovered additional examples of the effect of gender on German and English words and evaluated their connection to gender overall. One of the key takeaways from our investigation was that incorporating external knowledge based on a language's characteristics can greatly boost the efficiency and accuracy of pre-trained word embedding models, even when the dataset is very small. Estimating an object's pose is a crucial aspect of most visual pipelines in robots and 3D vision as a whole. This study tackles the challenge of accurately positioning new objects with no prior knowledge. This method builds on previous work by removing the necessity for object-pose-labelled data or category-specific 3D models during both training and inference. Our contributions are threefold. Firstly, we define the concept of zero-shot, category-based pose estimation and frame it in a way that incorporates semantic information. Our approach utilizes semantic information by utilising class embeddings in both training and inference. Secondly, we introduce a novel training method that simulates zero-shot scenarios and proposes a suitable metric for evaluation. Lastly, we demonstrate that by incorporating semantic information and using a suitable training method, we can achieve superior results on the dataset 'Thingspace'. This dataset is unique as it requires objects to be rotated, and all objects are presented from a life-like viewpoint, mimicking real-life scenarios. Results show that our method achieves superior performance when compared to baseline models that incorporate category information. This code can be accessed at https://github.com/alexkamani/zero-shot-pose. Blazars with certain spectral energy distributions display a notable increase in ultraviolet and soft X-ray frequencies, which can be attributed to distinct radiation mechanisms. In an earlier study, researchers employed the Monte-Carlo program PARTESAN to investigate polarized patterns resulting from the Compton scattering of high-energy electrons on background photons via polarized external fields. The program was used to simulate various scenarios of Compton scattering on multiple unpolarized fields, producing semi-quantitative estimates of polarization degrees for extremely high energy gamma rays interacting with external fields of comparable intensities. The current research builds on the previous findings and predicted polarization degrees for all energy ranges, including a focus on UV and soft X-ray frequencies. The authors have selected four blazars with notable UV and soft X-ray excesses: 3C 279, 3C 454.1, PKS 1158-137, and PKS 1427-608. The research aims to provide a comparative analysis of observed and calculated polarization degrees for these four blazars in a bid to identify and explain the underlying radiation mechanisms of UV and soft X-ray excesses. The results of this study will be expanded upon in a companion paper, focusing on the application of MAPPIES to the observation data of PKS 1158-137. The companion paper will also compare the theoretical polarization degrees of multiple energy ranges with a large dataset of high-energy peaked blazar spectra. The expected outcome is the identification of a new non-thermal radiation mechanism in blazars. In the helioseismology of solar dipsides, the rotation speed of solar active regions is measured through Doppler shift measurements and by calculating the speed of sound along the latitude axis. An issue arose when the APO method was found to underestimate the rotation speed of these areas, with a difference of approximately -65 m/s per rotation period per degree in latitude.

It has been discovered that the discrepancy between the APO method and measurements of solar active regions correlates with periodic changes in solar equatorial rotation speed. Furthermore, research using simulated data from the GURPS program revealed that the discrepancy might be attributed to the contribution of solar flows outside of active regions as opposed to the stagnant areas within them. An attempt was made to quantify this contribution by adjusting parameters in the GURPS model to fit the discrepancy found in the APO method results. An optimal set of parameters was identified and demonstrated to accurately replicate the discrepancy found in the APO method results, thereby offering a potential explanation for this phenomenon. An assessment of this solution was, however, confined to the realm of the GURPS model due to the limitations in available data for a comprehensive analysis. An essential requirement for further studies would be the collection of longitudinal speed data for both stagnant and moving active regions, an acquisition currently hindered by the constraints of available data resources. Until then, the proposed solution shall remain provisional until verified by the results of actual measurements. An additional file, SupplementaryInformation, is also provided to aid in the understanding of this solution. An additional remedy to the active region discrepancy in the APO method could also be sought in the construction of simulated data for analysis. An illustration in Fig. 2 reveals the magnitude of this simulated discrepancy. Light field technology is currently a focal point of interest for the research community due to its various potential uses. A key aspect of utilizing this technology lies in reconstructing high-quality 3D images from the captured data, particularly for applications like free-viewing and virtual reality. However, the process is hindered by the substantial data requirement. Studies have previously approached this challenge by applying lossy compression methods, such as those based on discrete cosine transform, that enable a certain trade-off between compressed data size and the quality of the reconstructed 3D images. Nevertheless, these methods are inefficient and fail to consider the micro-disparities within the data. In contrast, this study proposes a novel compression system that employs a disparity model, effectively reducing the data's complexity and enabling more efficient compression. By integrating a practical model and structure, this method enables efficient light field compression. Our proposed system significantly surpasses the performance of the leading approaches, marked by a 62.113% decrease in data requirements to achieve the same reconstructed quality. Furthermore, it also surpasses the performance of the leading optical flow-based compression methods in terms of encoded data requirements to achieve the same reconstructed quality. Moreover, our proposed system is capable of generating micro-disparity maps, whereas the leading approaches are limited to coarse-scale disparity information. In cross-lingual information retrieval, the challenge lies in retrieving documents relevant to a query text written in a different language. Despite significant advancements in modern architecture, such as the Cross-Attention mechanism, achieving low gap rates for uncommon languages remains a hurdle. This research explores how to overcome this limitation by leveraging the strengths of interactive and non-interactive models. We propose a hybrid approach, combining the unguided encoder-decoder model and the cross-attention-based retriever to tackle query gap reduction. The former is optimized using the REINFORCE algorithm to learn from user feedback. Our experiments demonstrate that this hybrid strategy significantly decreases the gap rate for rare languages and concurrently improves it for common languages, especially when integrated with data augmentation methods. Our proposed method achieves remarkable results on the GLIR dataset, yielding a 6-point improvement in gap rate compared to the cross-attention-based retriever. Furthermore, the source code for our model is publicly available at https://github.com/dulieuit/CLIR. This work converges modern architecture performance, setting a new precedent for rare language gap reduction. To the best of our knowledge, this study initiates the first attempt to integrate the principles of interactive and non-interactive models for cross-lingual information retrieval. Our proposed technique draws inspiration from the user-centered paradigm, viewed as one of the most effective information retrieval strategies. Ultimately, the proposed model enables faster convergence and superior performance in low-resource languages, holding vast potential for cross-lingual applications and information retrieval advancements. An in-depth analysis of the underlying reasoning is provided in the main paper. This supplementary material includes additional numerical results, serving to enhance the main paper's clarity. Although the main paper is primarily self-contained, this supplementary material helps ensure a complete understanding of the proposed technique. Ultimately, the proposed model has far-reaching implications for resource-constrained languages, paving the way for future advancements in cross-lingual information retrieval. The urgent need for comprehensive health and demographic reports has driven an increased focus on geographic studies, often utilizing detailed, pixel-level maps, particularly with the emergence of mobile sensing technology and the advancement of deep learning-based image analysis. Drawing from recent research on health and demographic modeling, we investigate the application of detailed built-up area models in low and middle income countries during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our analysis involves assessing relationships between disease cases, demographic characteristics, and spatial factors, with a primary objective of assessing the impact of social distancing policies. Two key estimation techniques are employed: a design approach, combining aggregated data, and a model-based statistician-designed approach, incorporating prior knowledge of demographic ratios. Both methods are adapted to address the challenges of small population sizes and multi-county compositions. Our findings suggest that the model-based approach yields more accurate results, with greater robustness, and a higher geometric mean, as well as a lower relative bias. In a real-world application, we apply these methods to recent research on COVID-19 in Kenya, using detailed pixel-level data from a satellite image. Our study indicates that the model-based approach prefers images with sharper boundaries and those aligned with urban growth patterns. Using the model-based on average, we estimate that the partial lockdown policy led to a 74% reduction in daily COVID-19 cases, with the design-based average standing at 69%. In summary, we recommend the model-based approach for detailed pixel-level maps, with the potential for incorporating further spatial, demographic, and economic factors. Furthermore, we suggest incorporating prior demographic data and using model-based approaches for more accurate assessments of the effectiveness of social distancing policies. Finally, future research is suggested in several areas: a deeper investigation of the sources of uncertainty in estimated models, an integration of survey and aggregate data, and the inclusion of additional spatial factors in modeling. Additionally, there is scope for methodologically enhanced image processing techniques, with potential increases in image accuracy observed. As images with deeper meanings, they can yield insights beyond the tangible world. Lastly, our study provides a foundation for applying these methods to a variety of applications such as demographic, health, and economic modeling. In a world where geographic data has an ever-growing role, it is imperative that researchers and practitioners contribute towards developing a robust, theory-driven estimation toolbox for researchers. Such a set of methods and models can empower a brighter, spatial future. Introducing a modified Kelly betting strategy, we show that partial quantum coherence in the betting outcome can increase expected net profits when compared to the classical Kelly Bet and Frazier's variant. A general condition for this outcome is derived and provided. Additionally, we investigate the anti-blocking property in the context of semi-relativistic kinetic theory and discuss its potential implications. To address this, we present a probabilistic interpretation of quantum state measurements, revealing that the limitations of our betting strategy are a direct consequence of the quantum memory's inherent noise. This suggests that the use of quantum processing may be necessary to eliminate this noise and increase net profits in such scenarios. The magnetic field is believed to play a crucial role in the process of prestellar core collapse, which eventually forms a protoplanetary disk. Recent studies employing 3D MHD simulations have significantly enhanced our understanding of this process. This paper details such a simulation, beginning with the core's formation in a molecular core and spanning 0.5 free-fall times, and examines the associated magnetic and angular momentum issues. Our simulation reveals that the core's collapse is slowed by the accumulation of magnetic energy, and that the core's center forms without significant polarization. Instead, the magnetic energy is transferred to the periphery of the core, where reconnection occurs and angular momentum is transferred from the periphery to the center. Our simulation, which employs a conventional equation of state for the core, suggests that the core's collapse is complete within 2 free-fall times, drawing parallels with observations of prestellar cores. During the core's collapse, our simulation identifies a transitional phase, lasting roughly one-third of the free-fall time, within which disk formation takes place. At the outset of this phase, the core's rotation velocity and magnetic field strength are comparable, and a substantial fraction of the core's mass and angular momentum reside at radii exceeding 30% of the core's extent. Over the course of this phase, 60% of the core's mass and 55% of its angular momentum are transferred to the core's outer regions, resulting in the formation of a rotating disk accompanied by two magnetically levitated poles. However, during the final stage of the core's collapse, these magnetically levitated regions lose their constraints and collapse due to magnetic reconnection, ultimately contributing to the formation of the disk. Our simulation suggests that the disk formation takes place some time after the core's collapse has initiated, requiring around one-third of the free-fall time, and involves mass and angular momentum transferred from the core's outer regions, accompanied by magnetic levitation and a substantial magnetic energy buildup at the periphery of the core. At the outset of this phase, the disk extends to radii beyond 200 AU, but over the course of this phase, the disk expands to cover a substantial extent, reaching up to 800 AU. A significant amount of mass, estimated to be around 0.2 M_sun, and angular momentum are transferred during this process, potentially resulting in a substantial disk extent and a significant mass accumulation. Our simulation suggests that the extent of the disk should be a function of time, potentially explaining observed variations in disk

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors are based on atmospheric models which have yet to be verified through on-site measurements. We've carried out a detailed analysis of these models over the 315-665nm wavelength range using cross-dispersion spectrographs, which have an accuracy of 18 milliarcseconds. By comparing various models in detail, we're now in a better position to make informed decisions for upcoming telescopes, allowing us to set precise tolerances for their construction. We're also developing a novel aperture-weighted method for modeling dispersion, which yields satisfactory results in atmospheric model characterization. Moreover, we're proposing a technique to determine atmospheric dispersion on-site directly from the surface, which would become the new reference standard. This new approach would facilitate the optimization of ADC designs without requiring a visit to the site. Finally, we're now equipped to take our measurements to the milliarcssecond level, which presents a significant opportunity for improvement. To take these results to the next level, we plan to apply them to the GRIS, a gravitational redshift instrument, which relies heavily on the accuracy of atmospheric dispersion modeling. This paper employs a refined hierarchical latent variable model to capture patterns in multi-period time series data, which exhibit dynamics governed by various time-sensitive factors. Traditional stacked RNN and DBN models lack the capability to incorporate tendencies spanning multiple periods and often overlook redundant input variables, which contribute nothing or negatively affect predictive power. By integrating the hierarchical latent variable model and the Bayesian posteroptive mean and predictive, our proposed method achieves the capacity to model complex, multi-period patterns with the capability of selectively input exclusion. Furthermore, this proposed method has been evaluated through experiments with synthetic and real-world datasets of multiple courses, which demonstrate substantial improvements in predicting accuracy compared to commonly employed time series models such as LSTMs and GRUs. For instance, our method has outperformed the LSTM model by nearly 60% in predicting Lymph node Lymph node metastasis based on Lymph node history. Similarly, our method has outperformed the GRU model by nearly 40% in predicting Amazon purchase history. Furthermore, our method has successfully predicted air quality in Denver by accurately modeling the temporal relationships between the many environmental factors influencing air quality. In a setting that combines continuous logic, we establish a connection between Stone duality and Pontryagin duality by treating Pontryagin duality as a particular instance of Stone duality. This is achieved in the context of a topological abelian group $A$, and its associated group $\mathcal F$ of continuous homomorphisms from $A$ to the circle group $\mathbb T$, where $(A,+)$ along with $\mathcal F$ form a continuous logic structure $M. Consequently, the local type space $S_\mathcal F(M)$ directly corresponds to the Pontryagin dual of the group $\mathcal F$ if it is viewed as a discrete group. Furthermore, employing the correspondence established between compact and discrete abelian groups through Pontryagin duality, it follows that the local type space $S_\mathcal F(M)$ represents the Bohr compactification of the given topological group $A$. As an example, it is demonstrated that when $A$ is the real line $\mathbb R$ then the Bohr compactification of $\mathbb R$ is the compact monadically complete type space consisting of the set $S_\mathcal F(M)$, where $M$ is the structure formed by taking continuous automorphisms of $\mathbb R$ along with their associated operations. By applying this construction to other groups, it is shown that their Pontryagin duals are the Bohr compactification of the given group. The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods known as federated learning, or differential privacy. A pioneering approach, this study creates a unified ethical federated learning framework, seamlessly integrating all three techniques in harmony. Experimental results based on the Adult, Bank and Dutch datasets showcase the "interplay" between precision, equity, and confidentiality that occurs empirically between federated learning, fairness, and differential privacy. Additionally, the findings highlight the ethical dilemmas that arise from trade-offs between precision and confidentiality, precision and fairness, and fairness and confidentiality. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the proposed framework can be optimized using each technique as a baseline to achieve superior outcomes. Consequently, the proposed framework offers innovative avenues for enhancing deep model fairness and protecting subject confidentiality. Related, open-source code is available on GitHub at this address: https://github.com/tae898/fedgp2d. Moreover, the proposed framework is capable of handling challenging problems by protecting user confidentiality using differential privacy in both fairness and loss regression processes. Following this, the concept of EFLP is further developed with the addition of two optimization techniques: gradient projection and trust region, which can be employed as secondary optimization methods. Interestingly, the use of differential privacy as a baseline is a key factor in enabling the user to effectively model data security concerns. We explore a smart reflecting surface-aided wireless-powered communication network where a multi-antenna energy transmitter broadcasts an exclusive energy signal to a powered transmitter that initially absorbs the energy, then sends an information message to the destination despite potential external interference. To optimize this setup, we've formulated an analytical problem but due to its computational complexity, we've also devised a machine learning-assisted solution that can operate in real-time with minimal training. Using a dataset of trained samples, we've created a look-up table for optimal parameter values. Experimental results show that this approach can effectively maximize throughput and is competitive with optimal solutions. Furthermore, the throughput performance can significantly improve with increased use of the reflecting surface, provided proper adjustment of the information message power is made. A comparative analysis also demonstrates the efficiency of our approach in scenarios involving multiple energy harvesting periods. We believe this study contributes to the development of efficient solutions for smart surfaces in wireless-powered communication networks. Moreover, the concept can be easily extended to more intricate problems involving more components. A companion software is available online.

We explore the intersection of dark matter and leptogenesis within a unified theoretical framework, which includes three right-handed neutrinos, a fermionic dark matter particle, and two additional scalar fields beyond the Standard Model. The interaction between these scalar fields influences both the dark matter relic density and the connection between right-handed neutrinos and dark matter. Our analysis centers around a resonant leptogenesis mechanism that produces baryon asymmetry through TeV-level right-handed neutrino masses. A viable parameter space is established to satisfy relic density constraints, which is particularly flexible when the scalar fields' mixing is substantial. Our findings demonstrate that dark matter can constitute either a majority or a minority of relic particles, while the latter case is primarily driven by warm dark matter when the dark matter particle is within the reach of direct detection experiments' sensitivity. Moreover, we show that in some cases, dark matter can indirectly contribute to baryon asymmetry through radiative decay processes. Finally, we outline specific scenarios in which dark matter annihilation patterns may leave observable signatures at the Gammapolice and CMBR experiments. A primary objective of this research is to investigate theoretical possibilities rather than ruling out particular models. Our analysis does not aim to comprehensively scan the entire parameter space; instead, our goal is to illustrate the complex relationships between baryon asymmetry, relic density, dark matter properties, and associated observable signatures within this conceptual framework. To facilitate further research, we have publicly released the code used in our study, making it accessible upon publication. All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and exhibit a comparable relationship with quantum Liouville theory. A new, powerful tool has been created in conformal field theory by constructing a vertex operator algebra from the Euler-Poincar\'e polynomials and identifying a corresponding extensive set of Ward identities within the Toda CFT framework. Focusing initially on the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda CFT, researchers have been able to establish a connection between the newly developed identities and known results, as well as derive new, crucial evidence for the spectral parameter in relation to correlation functions. This breakthrough is instrumental in further understanding Toda CFT. For the optimal utilization of these identities, a novel, partitioned approach to the Euler-Poincar\'e polynomials and a corresponding, partitioned methodology for the construction of Ward identities have been formulated. This innovative method provides a comprehensive, useful strategy to investigate the properties and applications of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda CFT. As such, it holds significant potential for the construction of an advanced, systematic framework to analyze and simulate $\mathfrak{sl}_N$ Toda CFTs for any chosen value of N. Although comprehensive within this research, the theoretical scope of these constructions is seemingly unbounded, thus enabling an extension into broader theoretical areas. A related mathematical framework for the construction of Ward identities in the context of the classical integrable systems, such as the Sato's Toda Conformal Field Theory, holds a well-established presence in the literature, as outlined in the provided references. Consequently, it would be more precise to describe these constructions as instruments extending and expanding previously established ideas rather than innovative breakthroughs. Please note that a related publication is currently in preparation by the author for publication in The Journal of Mathematical Physics. Furthermore, our findings in this research were presented at a meeting of the Seminar on Modern Mathematical Physics held at the University of Milan in 2019. In this study, we investigate the Toeplitz algebras of particular classes of Toeplitz operators on the Fock space with a weight function that holds a non-negative constant in every ball where it's defined, as well as on the Bergman space with a weight function that has a non-negative constant at the origin. We establish the equivalency of several, previously proposed sufficient conditions for the Toeplitz algebras' completeness in both settings. Additionally, we tackle the algebra's dense ideal question on the Fock space with a weight function that subharmonically grows and applies the same concept to the Bergman space, analyzing its application's limitations. We also demonstrate a corollary regarding the boundedness of Toeplitz operators on the Fock and Bergman spaces in relation to their corresponding symbols' boundedness. This work's methods of proof offer an alternative to existing ones found in the field. As a result, we arrive at a new characterisation of completely non-classical Toeplitz operators on the Fock and Bergman spaces, which we show to be equivalent to several, distinct sufficient conditions. Furthermore, in the context of the Bergman space, we are able to precisely define the boundary between classical and non-classical operators by identifying a necessary condition for operator adjointity via its symbol's real part. In the Fock setting, such a necessary condition remains undefined due to the non-positive definiteness of the Fourier transform of the weight function's second derivative. In the Bergman context, we explore via example, the interplay between sufficient conditions for bounded, Toeplitz algebras and its subharmonic weight function's growth, which doesn't hold for its counterpart in the Fock space. Ultimately, in the context of the Bergman setting, we observe that sufficient conditions for bounded, Toeplitz algebras are met with relative ease, while those of its counterpart in the Fock space, pose significant challenges. As a result, in the context of the Bergman setting, we are able to precisely define the boundary between classical and non-classical Toeplitz operators with a positive harmonic symbol, while in the Fock setting, such a necessary condition remains undefined. The methods of proof employed in this work provide an alternative to existing ones found in the field. Recent open-vocabulary object detection methods have been developed to address this issue by training on a set of base categories, enabling detection of unseen object types. To mitigate this limitation, we present a technique to automatically produce pseudo annotations of diverse objects using image-caption pairs and pre-trained vision-language models. Experiments on the COCO-Novellation and ImageNet-V2 benchmarks confirm the effectiveness of our approach, demonstrating improved detection accuracy compared to base-category-only training. Furthermore, our proposed method outperforms recent state-of-the-art open-vocabulary object detection methods, with results verified on multiple benchmark datasets. A young B star in the Rho Ophiuchus cloud produces a significant HII region and a photodissociation cavity, forming in an egg-like shape. This cavity is primarily restricted on the west and southwest by a dense molecular cloud ridge and is expanding into a lower density area on the north and east. Analyzing a variety of recent and archival data from SOFIA, GMRT, APEX, and other telescopes provides a comprehensive study of photo-irradiated ionized and neutral gas properties. Emissions from [C II], [O I], HCO+, and HCN are detected at the western edge of the cavity and exhibit high extinction ratios. Ionic components such as [O I] and HCO+ appear predominantly on the western side, while the ratio of HCN to [C II] suggests that the gas is primarily composed of atomic hydrogen. The significant column densities are expected to persist for a long time, and the cloud is likely to retain these properties even when it reaches its final stages of expansion.
