Mortality forecasting models built on the classical factor framework, such as the Lee-Carter model and its variants, often oversimplify real-world conditions. The models assume factor loadings remain static over time despite the significant influence of variables such as advancements in medical treatment and environmental shifts. We expand the classical model to create a factor model that accounts for the evolution of factor loadings over time. We introduce two methods for forecasting factor loadings and apply them to a model that effectively captures the changing relationships in mortality datasets and improves forecasting accuracy for various timeframes and regions. Moreover, a new technique based on analyzing critical points is developed to identify optimal forecasting intervals for long-term and short-term predictions, and simulated studies verify the performance of the model in multiple scenarios. The analysis includes mortality data from Canada, covering nearly eight decades and spanning across 8 regions and 8 provinces with diverse demographic and geographic characteristics. We also explore the model's capabilities in forecasting for independent cases, such as the US state of Connecticut and the Spanish region of Aragon. Ultimately, the models' parameter estimates can be interpreted and used to assess mortality risk. Notably, the mortality transition theory does not apply in forecasting approaches, and therefore, we do not rely on unrealistic assumptions inherent in some models. Instead, we suggest modifying the model formulation by avoiding negative factor loadings and reparameterizing the model accordingly. Additionally, we propose an alternative method for estimating the pioneer parameter and defining time periods for analysis. The models' uniqueness and effectiveness have been confirmed through numerous Mortality Forecasting Model Comparisons, an initiative promoting reproducible research and code on mortality modeling. The related code and data can be found at the provided GitHub links. Specifically, the repository contains code for generating figures and tables in Chapter 5 and Appendix D, while data can be accessed at the data repository. Fortunately, our models' applications extend beyond actuarial purposes, and therefore, we do not encounter any practical obstacles in our research. Nevertheless, future studies can explore the models' implications for actuaries. One potential area of work could involve adapting the models for insurance pricing, an area where professional certifications, such as the Fellow of the Casualty Actuarial Society, may come into play. Similarly, the Chartered Fellow of the Institute of Professionals Assisting with Tax Issues could find relevance in tax-related aspects of the models' applications. Ultimately, the models' utility and adoption would depend on the results of any resulting calculations and policy implementations. The existing code and data provide a clear starting point for future research directions.

Reducing the cost of neural architecture search (NAS) by sharing weights among different child models is a popular strategy. However, due to interference from other models, there is often a poor correlation between predicted accuracy and actual performance of the child models. This study investigates the cause of interference by comparing how similar the effects are when child models are trained with shared weights and reveals that the level of interference depends on data diversity and model complexity. Based on these findings, a method is proposed to reduce the impact of interference through weighted averaging of child models' predictions. Experimental results using NASBench and other benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method can significantly improve the accuracy of predicted top-performing architectures. Specifically, the difference between predicted and actual top-performing models decreased from a median of 29 to 5, demonstrating the potential of this approach to support effective NAS. The proposed technique is available for public use at https://github.com/hughesjrob/AI-press//tree/main/interference_nas. Our team also runs an online NAS platform at https://nas.quick.ai. This platform, which provides access to 1000 curated datasets and supports searching for scikit-learn machine learning models, has been viewed by over 70,000 users. Time series data in various scientific disciplines are analyzed and measured. One common technique for evaluating the characteristics of these data sets involves computing multiple statistical measures or features, which can then be represented as a feature vector for further analysis in the context of supervised learning and data mining applications. Applying this approach enables researchers to tackle real-world classification and regression problems. The resulting feature space generated by this approach offers numerous advantages, such as decreased dimensionality and the ability to perform unsupervised exploration, while also facilitating supervised classification and regression operations. The use of this technique has gained significant traction across various fields. The purpose of this study is to introduce a unified framework for feature-based time series analysis that is accessible through the R programming language and incorporated into the theft package. This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine the extremal gain resulting from optimal power control in contrast to binary (on/off) power control in large-scale interference networks. By exploring extremal cases in 2-user and K-user scenarios, we reveal that binary power control falls short in K>2 scenarios, leading to a GDoF gain gap of $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ when K is large. To establish this finding, we first establish the extremal network characteristics under which binary power control performs poorly, followed by determining the extremal network conditions that demonstrate the efficacy of optimal power control. Despite its simplicity, binary power control is widely employed due to its computational ease, which we now mathematically justify as a limit of large K. To support our theoretical findings, we also conduct Monte-Carlo simulations to empirically verify the order of the gain gap. Additionally, we extend the analysis to a multi-hop interference network to further illustrate the significance of our analysis. Interestingly, in large K scenarios, the gain gap diminishes as the number of intermediate transmitters increases in a multi-hop scenario, suggesting that intermediate transmitters can help reduce the gain gap. To further analyze the impact of channel knowledge, we also investigate the gain gap when channel knowledge is limited to average instead of perfect knowledge. Finally, we also show that the gain gap is unaffected by the topology of the interference network, leading to similar analysis and results for random, tree, and mesh network topologies. Consequently, our analysis and results offer network designers valuable insights on the computational trade-offs involved in choosing between binary and optimal power control in large-scale interference networks. Moreover, the extremal networks identified in this work can be utilized as benchmark examples to evaluate the efficiency of existing and future network control algorithms. To the best of our knowledge, this work provides the first comprehensive analysis and analysis tools to compare binary and optimal power control in terms of GDoF gain gap in large-scale interference networks. In the rapidly evolving landscape of Internet of Things (IoT) networks, periodic firmware updates are vital for maintaining optimal security and reliability. Given the trend towards implementing security measures via codified policy decisions and exchangeable code (software), it's now possible to deploy and manage IoT systems similarly to conventional software-based systems. However, conventional approaches to network management are often inadequate for IoT firmware updates, and still, very few IoT devices have been successfully updated en masse. This paper delves into the performance of current IoT networks, specifically those using 802.15.4 (zigbee) and 802.11 (Wi-Fi) protocols, to understand how they measure up to the requirements of reliable firmware updates. Our investigation reveals that, even with a large number of IoT devices, the time needed to perform an update via either mesh networks or ligther-weight Wi-Fi networks is remarkably short, and could easily be completed within the time frame of a typical video sequence's framerate (1/30th of a second). That is to say, even when numerous IoT devices are in use, the time of a typical update is merely equivalent to a brief video snippet. For instance, in a network of 256 devices using the 'Wi-Fi' protocol, the total update time is a minuscule fraction of a second - equivalent to a mere 8 milliseconds. This breakthrough discovery has a multitude of implications for a wide array of potential applications, and we propose one particular use case in the paper - the creation of a highly secure and highly dynamic audio/video surveillance 'blackbox'. In a future work, we intend to design and create the preliminary work for the creation of a highly secure and highly dynamic audio/video surveillance 'blackbox' prototype. Furthermore, in a future research endeavor, we intend to design and create the foundational work for the implementation of a highly dynamic and intelligent surveillance system. And finally, in a future research endeavor, we intend to design and create the initial work towards applying IoT firmware updates to a wide array of domain-specific use cases. Our results show that the local self-energy's imaginary component, which governs the decay rate of initially localized states, can serve as a probabilistic phase transition order parameter, facilitating the characterization of critical behavior and multifractal nature in many-body localized states across various disorder intensities. Moreover, we establish that the fractal dimension associated with the local self-energy's singular component is non-universal and exhibits self-averagement, whereas other fractal dimensions, such as those characterizing initially excited states, display a distinct disorder-amplitude dependence that varies according to the disorder strength. At the phase transition point, these fractal dimensions diverge non-trivially with system size at any given disorder strength. Critical behavior of the local local self-energy's singular component is found to be characteristic of a universal universal singular point, however it can be eliminated through a simple averaging procedure involving the local self-energy's component across different sublattices. Furthermore, we construct and study a renormalization group fixed point in a disorder-free model, incorporating a term of variable strength that mimics the disorder's effect on single-site transmission probabilities. Our findings suggest that the disorder-free model can serve as an effective renormalization group scheme that yields consistent results with those obtained from the original disorder-QTM. Lastly, we outline the implications and potential applications of our findings, highlighting their relevance to experimental systems, such as ultracold atoms and the study of localization phenomena. We expect that our results may inspire the development of novel renormalization group schemes and related physical applications and phenomena. Furthermore, a proposed technique can handle partial process instances in three formats: based on the order of processes, the order of process results, or the order of process inputs. This is done using a model-to-instance approach, based on the process type definitions. A test system and a real-world business are used to evaluate and validate the proposed method. Accurate prediction and simulation of radio wave transmission are essential for optimizing modern mobile networks. Existing propagation models are broadly classified into two types - empirical and deterministic. While empirical models are straightforward, they often compromise on precision. In contrast, deterministic models based on physical principles guarantee transmission accuracy but are often impractical due to the complexity of terrain and human-made obstacles affecting signal patterns. This study proposes a novel, data-driven approach to determine propagation maps using layers within deep neural networks, leveraging previously unexploited information. The method is demonstrated with real-world data on a case study site and is compared with conventional Suvee's two-ground model. The outcomes reveal significant advantages of the neural network method in terms of precision, yet with enhanced usability. Building upon this work, we can develop a comprehensive map of radio wave transmission using a large, freely available data stream. The resulting model can potentially replace existing methods and broaden the scope of radio wave simulation software. The research data and associated Python code are accessible via GitHub for immediate reference. The convolutional neural network has been implemented using the TensorFlow framework. Power system expansion planning models, used to integrate renewable resources, rely on complex optimization problems involving various economic and technical factors. These factors carry significant uncertainties, yet their impact on model accuracy is poorly understood. This study introduces a new approach to assess the sensitivity of power system models to specific parameters by measuring the increased costs resulting from inefficiently allocating generation capacities. Through case studies involving capital costs, varied weather conditions, and differing spatial and temporal resolutions, we demonstrate the method's value and reveal that model sensitivity significantly exceeds theoretical thresholds. Additionally, we identify critical parameters whose refinement offers substantial improvements. Our findings shed light on the optimal trade-off between model complexity and resource investigation. The proposed method is expected to enhance the efficacy of parameter estimation and model evaluation in power systems. The model code and data are available at https://github.com/caubel/sensitivity_power_models. The model's performance can also be evaluated using https://data.energiabarilla.it. To guarantee matching among all agents, the Deferred Acceptance algorithm traditionally demands complete and ranked preference lists from each party. However, studies show that using only the agents' top choices isn't enough; it lacks the necessary stability to ensure a match and requires at least two ranking positions from each party. In this paper, we explore what happens when agents are asked for a variable number of ranking positions - or partial profiles. We discover that using more ranking positions doesn't guarantee a match, and there's always a crucial amount beyond which one must exist. In an effort to optimize this point, we introduce a concept, called concept of query-stability, that reflects the effectiveness of different information requests. We show that using two ranking positions is generally the best choice and that using more than three positions isn't necessary. We establish that using ranking positions up to the size of the largest component in a graph where agents are connected, especially 3 in non-empty graphs, is necessary and sufficient to guarantee a match. We conduct experiments to see how the size of the ranking positions and the structure of the relationship between the agents affect their ability to match. We also study how different information requests influence the final matches, especially in the context of the college admissions problem in the US. We find that using more ranking positions leads to fewer applications from less suitable agents, but more ranking positions aren't always necessary to guarantee a match. In addition, we find that using ranking positions rather than complete preference lists leads to different preferences, especially for agents with multiple relationships. We thank Nathanael Collier for pointing this out and showing its significance. We conduct a case study to investigate whether using ranking positions from school documents is a realistic way to obtain these partial profiles, as required in the college admissions process in the US. A new method for extracting a sparse signal from cross-related data is presented. This approach differs from conventional methods by utilizing a quadratic formulation to recover the signal. Initially, we establish a mathematical proof that signals with a specific sparsity and structural consistency can be recovered through quadratic programming. Next, we develop a mechanism for determining the measurement matrix's sensitivity to noise. Building on this analysis, we create an efficient algorithm for signal recovery that adapts to the characteristics of the data. This algorithm not only reduces computation but also decreases the impact of noisy data. Furthermore, we experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method using numerical experiments with matrices of varying sizes. The findings confirm that our approach outperforms existing linear programming methods, especially in large-scale data sets. Additionally, the method for estimating noise sensitivity is validated using real-world data from MRI technology to scan the internal structures of the brain and the peripheral nervous system. Using noise sensitivity estimation, we develop a procedure for identifying the minimum number of cross-related data required for reliable signal recovery. Overall, the proposed method offers a scalable signal recovery solution capable of handling complex data sets. This paper presents a novel evaluation engine for big stream and data processing pipelines called H-STREAM. By integrating the capabilities of stream processing and database querying, H-STREAM enables the development of versatile and scalable analytics pipelines that can be leveraged across various use cases. The engine's modular design, based on pipelined relational algebra, facilitates querying and leveraging both real-time and historical data across different data sources. H-STREAM's features include automatic data materialization, stream processing, and query optimization to provide streamlined performance. Through a comprehensive case study, we demonstrate H-STREAM's capabilities in building complex analytics pipelines with real-world data sources, showcasing its potential for big data applications. Additionally, our experimental evaluations confirm the effectiveness of H-STREAM in efficiently processing data and yielding meaningful query results in both stream and historical scenarios. Lastly, we outline opportunities for further optimization and research based on H-STREAM's design. The proposed H-STREAM architecture is currently available as an open-source software framework.

The hunt for Top and Bottom companions is a key area of study for both the ATLAS and CMS experiments, as their single production offers considerable detection possibilities. Though past research mainly focused on the resonant production mode of these hypothetical particles, new findings indicate that a different type of diagrams, known as non-resonant t-channel contributions, significantly impact results and might even surpass their resonant counterparts in certain cases. In this paper, a comprehensive analysis is presented by combining the full standard model with two different models proposing the existence of Top and Bottom companions. The results obtained demonstrate that accounting for the non-resonant t-channel effects is crucial for both the standard model and the double effective top quark coupling model. Furthermore, different scenarios for the parameters of these models are explored and the corresponding bounds on the parameters are established. In particular, it is found that in the standard model, the limits on the parameter at its origin can be increased by a factor of 3 when considering the non-resonant contributions. Finally, a comparison between the standard model and the double effective top quark coupling model is performed and the consequences of their respective parameter ranges on the latter are determined. The findings obtained in this paper are expected to have a significant impact on future studies of Top and Bottom companions. A recent breakthrough in translating English to SPARQL using neural machine translation (NMT) models has shown potential, but translating English to SPARQL proves more difficult than the reverse process. Building upon the successes of previous models, we introduce a novel architecture, the copy mechanism for NMT, to improve translating English to SPARQL by handling knowledge base elements (KBElements) more effectively. We enhance existing models with this copy mechanism and, as a result, achieve significant improvements in terms of accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach leads to increased accuracy, with improvements ranging from 5.46% to 18.52% and 3.21% to 12.28% for two respective baseline models, when evaluated using the KBElementAccuracy metric. Furthermore, our approach yields modest gains in terms of BLEU scores, with improvements ranging from 0.97 to 3.14. The implementation of this architecture can be accessed at https://github.com/alexkежdc/sparql-nmt. We also release a new dataset, the extended QBAMT dataset, at https://github.com/alexkежdc/sparql-e2e-dataset. Extending this dataset allows us to conduct additional experiments that demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in handling KBElements more accurately. We observe that incorporating KBElements leads to decreased translation quality in both translation directions, which underscores the significance of our approach in improving translations that incorporate KBElements. Furthermore, our approach has the added benefit of increasing translations that are semantically accurate. We hope that our architecture and the QBAMT dataset will facilitate future research in this area. We provide detailed explanations of these contributions in the paper's introduction. In particular, the copy mechanism's performance is most effective when used in models that have a baseline accuracy of at least 60, as this allows KBElements to account for at least 30% of the total translations. Consequently, we derive the hypothesis that improving this baseline accuracy through additional data may ultimately allow the copy mechanism to produce more KBElements from a richer knowledge base. Such a development could pave the way for more extensive KBs and more accurate NMT models. In light of these contributions, we propose a second hypothesis that increasing the size of KBElements from 30 to 100 can improve accuracy by as much as 5 times that of a baseline model. Ultimately, we aim to improve translations that are both accurate and semantically rich by harnessing the power of KBElements. The accompanying video can be accessed at https://youtu.be

In a recent study, researchers employed direct numerical simulations within a triply periodic box, artificially suppressing geostrophic vortices to investigate the properties of turbulent flows. These experiments revealed an inertial wave turbulence that conforms to a specific spectrum first described analytically by Galtier in 2003. Interestingly, it was found that the same underlying mechanisms could give rise to the spectra of both rotational and inertial waves. Furthermore, it was observed that the energy contained within large-scale geostrophic vortices is directed downwards, counteracting the instability of the inertial wave turbulence. Consequently, the net effect is a reduced rate of decay of the kinetic energy when compared with scenarios lacking external influences. Recent advances in artificial neural networks (ANNs) claim to simulate aspects of primates' and humans' neural performance. However, these ANNs primarily rely on basic visual characteristics when performing object recognition tasks, unlike humans. Additionally, ANNs are hindered by unusual or misleading input, such as distorted images or irrelevant visual information. We investigated how both humans and the most advanced machine learning models handle complex visual data by testing their performance with heavily manipulated images. We found that humans' ability to identify objects despite severe image distortions is significantly greater than the capability of the current state-of-the-art models. We observed humans and machines reacting differently to these transformations and discovered that changes affecting high-level visual features are particularly challenging for ANNs. This finding suggests that despite their cognitive similarities with humans, these ANNs are not effectively modeling the complex visual processes in primates and humans. We propose that developing more intricate models, similar to those employed in board games, could help bridge this gap and enable the creation of more precise simulations of biological neural systems. Our study provides valuable insights into the limitations of the current generation of machine models and outlines novel strategies for developing more effective models. We have made our dataset and accompanying tools available to the public through our repository at https://github.com/islaiola/eit. We also aim to encourage future research to investigate the other key finding of our study, namely that small adjustments to ANNs' hyperparameters can sometimes lead to corresponding changes in their performance on these challenging image classifications, thereby potentially facilitating the development of more biologically accurate models. We have made all the code for our experiments and hyperparameter search accessible on the repository mentioned above. We hope that this research will inspire other researchers to build upon our work and advance our understanding of biological and artificial neural systems. We have also actively contributed to two existing open-source platforms, namely ImageNet-C and BigAN, by submitting improved versions of our code, which can be found at https://github.com/image-net/C and https://github.com/bigrat/bigan. Our analysis revealed significant, aligned radial gradients in the star's magnetic fields, which ranged from -0.2 to -0.8 kilogauss per thousand kilometers per second. We observed these gradients in the star's spectral lines in both emission and absorption, which vary due to the dependence on the star's atmospheric state. Our results demonstrate that the star's magnetic fields decrease as velocity increases, indicating that the upper atmospheric regions with higher velocities have weaker magnetic fields than lower regions. We observed a strong correlation between velocity and magnetic field strength, which suggests the star's magnetic fields decrease with increasing velocity. This relationship may be influenced by magnetic field dissipation due to electron-ion interactions at the upper atmospheric layers of the star. Designing effective state observers for nonlinear epidemic models presents significant challenges. This difficulty stems from the inherent nonlinearity of these systems, which often follows the law of mass action and results in large, locally-dependent Lipschitz constants, making conventional design criteria unsuitable. This paper introduces a new state observer that improves estimation capabilities for nonlinear systems, including epidemic models, by mitigating the influence of nonlinearity in the error dynamics. To establish the observer's performance, sufficient conditions for convergence are formulated in the form of algebraic Riccati inequalities and linear matrix inequalities. These conditions provide a framework for evaluating and optimizing the observer's design for accurate state estimation. The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models, and consequently, in applications that rely on these embeddings. Despite this opportunity, previous research has given it little attention, and models developed to account for time frames often show only slight improvements over their static counterparts. Rather than adapting static models, many current studies have created new models designed specifically for temporal knowledge graphs. We propose an alternative approach, SpliMe, that takes advantage of the effectiveness of existing static models by modifying the input data. Our method is informed by the techniques of signal processing and past work in graph embeddings. Our experiments validate the effectiveness of our approach, demonstrating that the modified static models' performances surpass those of existing temporal KG embeddings in a real-world evaluation of link prediction. Additionally, SpliMe's resilience in the face of challenging scenarios was confirmed, and its ability to be adapted for other tasks was briefly discussed. Ultimately, SpliMe offers an efficient and simple solution for generating high-quality temporal KG embeddings. We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer arbitrarily small local spectral expansion.

Our research involves presenting a probabilistic algorithm that takes an input high dimensional expander X and generates a sub-complex Y, also a high dimensional expander with infinite covers of bounded-degree simplicial complexes. The generated Y preserves X's graph structure, reducing link complexity and inherits a sparsified form of X's links when the link size of X is O(log |X|). The application of graph embedding for predicting links in various real-world applications has been highly successful and widely recognized. Graphs used in real-world settings often have a sparse connection structure. Despite their practical relevance, existing methods for graph embedding have been shown to yield unfavourable results when dealing with such networks, primarily due to the emphasis placed on preserving high-order neighbourhood relationships. To address this challenge, we present SSNE, an innovative node representation approach tailored to predicting links in sparse networks. SSNE accurately capture a sparse network's underlying structure through a novel, two-stage clustering process for nodes. It effectively captures high-order neighbourhoods while also preserving local and distant network properties. Experimental evaluations conducted across multiple sparse networks demonstrate that SSNE outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in predicting links. Additionally, SSNE proves to be robust against potential inaccuracies in its network clustering. SSNE's source code is publicly available at https://github.com/fangxu1995/SSNE. Results reveal that SSNE's node representations are interpretable and capture a combination of local and distant network properties. Importantly, SSNE's performance is shown to be largely insensitive to Clustering Error. Ultimately, SSNE's benefits for sparse networks are discussed, and areas for further improvement identified. Analysis suggests that SSNE's performance in capturing low Clustering Distance for nodes contributes significantly to its success. In contrast, existing methods struggle when dealing with nodes having high Clustering Distance. As a result, SSNE's performance in sparse networks cannot be replicated through modifications to existing state-of-the-art node representation methods. Instead, SSNE's design is specifically tailored to accurately capture a sparse graph's underlying structure. Analysis of SSNE's properties and performance properties yields valuable insights for guiding future research in sparse graphs. In summary, SSNE's key differentiators include its unique, node-clustering-based design tailored to sparse graphs, its unique ability to effectively predict links in such networks, and its unique ability to interpret and understand the characteristics of its generated node representations. Although deep silicon vapor cells offer benefits of increased atom density, conventional manufacturing methods are costly and time consuming. The newly designed cell has a 6mm depth and 5mm inner diameter, allowing for 2mm thick silicon spacers and a stainless steel outer housing. Its thermal stability is tested through its effect on rubidium atom density across an 80K temperature range and the measurement confirms  90% efficiency. The predicted enhancement in vapor cell performance with doubled atom density is observed, demonstrating good performance from this manufactured cell. The integration of this cell in an experimental setup demonstrates stable and long-lasting operation of laser-cooled rubidium. The developed manufacturing technique facilitates mass production of such cells at low cost, offering a promising solution for novel atomic physics experiments. The cells have potential in precision measurement and quantum information applications due to their high sensitivity. The technique has also been applied to the creation of a 4mm thick magnesium oxide film, enabling the construction of anti-resonant fiber Bragg grating devices. The developed method is also capable of producing other thin-film materials in a similar manner. The study concludes by outlining a range of potential future applications for these cells, including novel atomic and quantum optics experiments and sensitive detection devices. The development of a magnetic field meter with potential to reach levels of noise below that of the standard quantum limit remains a possibility with further research. Wildfires pose a significant threat to biodiversity and cause substantial economic damage worldwide.
Satellite technology plays a crucial role in identifying and tracking wildfires across the globe.
Researchers propose a novel framework, known as FIRe-GAN, for using deep learning to combine visible and infrared satellite imagery of wildfires.
By leveraging visible and thermal infrared images, FIRe-GAN creates synthetic thermal images that mirror the visible spectrum, thereby enhancing wildfire detection and tracking accuracy.
Using the Wildfire Dataset for Image-based Remote Sensing, the results show that FIRe-GAN surpasses baseline models and state-of-the-art fusion techniques, demonstrating improved performance through FIRe-GAN. Furthermore, FIRe-GAN is tested for its generalization capabilities across various thermal sensors, and the results indicate robust generalization. Lastly, using the Wildfire Dataset for Image-based Remote Sensing, the results show that FIRe-GAN detects known wildfires, outperforming other models. The proposed framework is extensively analyzed for its fairness, and the results indicate that FIRe-GAN is a fair approach. Overall, FIRe-GAN's results show that using FIRe-GAN in practice yields notable advantages. The most significant practical implication of FIRe-GAN is its potential deployment in alerting systems that require real-time imagery, such as satellite operators, environmental agencies, and emergency responders. Early detection and treatment of depression is essential to prevent severe repercussions, making the utilization of multiple detection methods necessary, particularly when they do not rely on physical examinations.  Observing social media expression patterns is highly advantageous for identifying mental health, since individuals tend to convey their emotions less frequently through explicit language and more frequently through implicit language when posting about their personal lives as opposed to their public interactions.  Implicit knowledge about current life events can be deduced from explicit text even if it may not directly pertain to mental health, making the analysis of social media data a valuable tool for identifying depression through machine learning.  Although prior studies have explored social media analysis for mental health, they have failed to make accompanying datasets available to the public, hindering the advancement of this field.  Consequently, this study establishes a new dataset to facilitate research on depression detection through social media in both English and German languages and examines multiple detector types, such as logistic regression, decision tree, support vector machine, k-nearest neighbor, random forest, naive Bayes-likelihood ratio, and deep learning, to compare their effectiveness.  Our research primarily focuses on differences in deployment of explicit and implicit language in describing depression symptoms among social media users, revealing that implicit data is more relevant for understanding depression.  Our analysis also reveals that related concepts like loneliness, fear, or database connection have the potential to uncover depression, while visitors from foreign countries may be identified as having a higher depression risk.  Furthermore, our study highlights the significance of large social media dataset availability for advanced research.  Our empirical findings suggest that certain machine learning methods deliver better results than others, while considering user-specific features can improve depression detection.  Our empirical findings lead to several contributions including the establishment of a new dataset, the analysis of deployment of explicit and implicit language in describing depression symptoms and the comparison of different depression detection methods. The corresponding stochastic model takes into account these distinctive features, characterized by two key variables: the first governs the total number of infected cases, including both active and recovered individuals, while the second represents active cases. This work combines elements of mathematical modeling, policy analysis, and computer science to address the unprecedented global challenges posed by COVID-19. In total, the research comprises four primary components: a mathematical model, a computational approach, policy recommendations, and theoretical generalizations. Each component represents a critical aspect of the overall project, showcasing the utility of integrated model-based analysis and policy simulation in informing data-driven decisions during the pandemic. As the study concludes with thoughts on future directions for COVID-19 model development and policy extension, it paves the way for a range of potential extensions, including extending the model to capture other essential pandemic features such as vaccination, plasmid transmission, and mental health disparities. In today's commercial recommender systems, sequential models play a crucial role. These models predict the items users are most likely to engage with by analyzing their previous platform interactions. Despite their importance, many of these models struggle to grasp the underlying motivations driving users' actions online, making intent modeling vital for user understanding and optimal long-term engagement. We've developed a novel approach to probabilistically model user intent using variational autoencoders and inferred latent variables from user behavior signals. Our approach then adjusts the recommendation policy accordingly, based on inferred user intent. We've validated the efficacy of our approach through offline and live testing on a massive industrial platform. We've demonstrated substantial user experience enhancements via joint modeling of user intent and recommendation. Moreover, our approach outperforms benchmark methods in overall user satisfaction and predicted performance. The underlying user intents discovered through our approach reveal new, actionable insights for platform optimization. Powered by collaborative learning, our approach maximizes long-term user happiness and helps the platform achieve better user experiences. We've also established a benchmark for future research and comparison. The code for our approach is now publicly available on GitHub, contributing to the advancement of recommender systems. For more details on our research, please see the accompanying paper on arXiv.

The reducible double confluent Heun equation stands out due to its unique unfolding into a Fuchsian equation through a general symmetric process. Utilizing the monodromy matrix, we demonstrate that the Fuchsian equation corresponds to a specific special case of the monodromy-free hypergeometric differential equation. Building upon Fuchsian equations, we derive a corresponding special case of the Schrödinger operator associated with the Lichnerowicz Laplacian on Riemann surfaces, displaying a specific meromorphic singular behavior. Additionally, we show that the distance between essential and regular singular points tends towards zero as the unfolding parameter vanishes. Our findings provide a foundation for a general symmetric unfolding of the origin in polynomial systems. Specifically, we consider a particular dissipative Lotka-Volterra system and demonstrate that its singular limit points can be represented as the zero set of a discriminant function, whose geometry offers insightful visual illustrations. Moreover, we showcase that the resonant spectrum of a certain tritrophic Lotka-Volterra system, when unfolding from a hyperbolic equilibrium, admits specific limit points, organized within a Julia set corresponding to the complex multiplication system, which is distinct from the original folded system. Lastly, we expand upon a concept of monodromy-free integrability and extend it to include a class of finite singularities. Although the notion of monodromy-free-ness lacks a clear physical interpretation, it does provide a useful framework for the classification of systems. The text is supplemented by six figures and three appendices. \medskip

Low-rank matrix recovery issues with complex high-dimensional data are ubiquitous in statistical and machine learning domains. This research investigates the theoretical recovery boundaries for a wide range of such problems. We specifically address the problem of estimating a matrix of rank one from observations with differing Gaussian noise levels across various matrix components. We derive exact formulas for the mean squared error in matrix and factor estimation in an ideal scenario with an infinite number of observations. We demonstrate that these formulas can be utilized to determine sample sizes required for matrix recovery in contexts involving finite noise levels and randomly distributed matrices. Experimental results confirming our theoretical findings are also presented. We further illustrate the applicability of our results to real-world data with an example using single-cell RNA sequencing. Our approach provides theoretical grounds for the success of many matrix estimation methods, including those based on maximum likelihood and maximum likelihood with variance adjustment. This study may serve as a foundation for assessing the effectiveness of any matrix estimation technique, thereby facilitating the design of highly accurate methods. It also opens up avenues for further research on finite sample-size recovery bounds. Calculation methods and code for computing empirical recovery thresholds are provided online. Additionally, a related theorem for the bounded inverse multiway tensor decomposition problem is also introduced. We demonstrate that many matrix estimation problems are equivalent to tensor decomposition problems, thereby allowing our findings to be applied broadly. In this research, we examine the vibrational spectrum of a constrained ring, taking note of its distinct properties that defy symmetry expectations inherent to topological models. A unique characteristic arises due to 2nd-order exceptional points, where an otherwise trivial band structure becomes topologically complex. The emergence of fractional boundary states and fractional periodic boundary states is observed. The fractional boundary states, facilitated by the constraint, endow the system with an inherent topological property, and one that is impermissible in typical symmetric topological models. Moreover, fractional periodic boundary states appear along imaginary frequency axes. The notion of fractional properties in the absence of symmetry symmetry underscores the significance of constraints in uncovering novel topological phenomena. The predicted phenomena are experimentally verifiable via the spectroscopy of a freely rotating ring, encompassing systems like the nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond. Our research offers an innovative framework for uncovering hidden topological properties in everyday materials. The theoretical model proposed here has far-reaching implications for the analysis of periodic systems in the absence of symmetry, and may be adapted for the study of systems under electromagnetic waves and superconducting quantum circuits. Importantly, our approach can maintain stability even in the face of dynamic changes to network connectivity, by leveraging principles from convex optimization and the master-slave approach. The study of eco-evolutionary dynamics is being limited by an exclusive focus on fast-changing ecology and evolution, typically occurring over short periods, as evidenced by the rapid changes observed in Trinidadian guppies and other laboratory and natural populations. We argue this perspective is overly narrow and neglects potential interplay with slower evolutionary processes that can be just as significant. For instance, at a larger spatial scale, local populations are susceptible to sudden changes in larger ecological contexts, altering competition and facilitating adaptation. Furthermore, subtle modifications to environmental pressures can unexpectedly provoke intense evolutionary responses. We propose the incorporation of timescales and rate modulators into eco-evolutionary models to better grasp the complexity of ecological systems and to bridge the gap between deep-time and short-time eco-evolutionary dynamics. By doing so, we aim to broaden the scope of eco-evolutionary theory to encompass a broader range of temporal and spatial relationships between organisms and their environment. A more comprehensive theory, recognizing varied interaction timescales and settings, is shown here to offer valuable insights into contemporary eco-evolutionary processes. The theoretical framework presented provides examples of profound adaptation pressures that can arise from modifications to environmental conditions, even in scenarios like habitat fragmentation and changes to complex network systems. The effect of rate modulators on facilitating adaptation in diverse ecological systems is also illustrated through spatially structured populations subject to sudden changes in large ecological networks. We show that intense adaptation can be expected when conditions that modulate evolutionary processes vary significantly across different settings, as is the case with geographic fragmentation. However, our models also suggest that high population flow can reduce and even minimize adaptation, and that high migration rates can have a similar effect by creating unstable conditions for selection to operate. The outcomes presented in this work highlight the necessity to integrate rate modulators and various timescales into eco-evolutionary theory, which in turn has significant implications for the prediction and assessment of eco-evolutionary processes. Furthermore, our theoretical framework provides an opportunity for deeper understanding and improvement through interdisciplinary research. The examples shown in this paper indicate that deep-time eco-evolutionary processes can have significant consequences for contemporary dynamics, suggesting potential for future research into the interplay between slower and faster evolutionary processes. Finally, our models also indicate that modifications in large network systems can have significant impacts on adaptation, providing avenues for future investigation. The theories and frameworks proposed in this paper can serve as a foundation for future interdisciplinary research; however, the primary conclusion is that deep-time evolutionary processes may have unexpected and varied impacts on dynamics occurring over a small fraction of that time frame.

A recently established benchmark called SUPERB drives research into learning speech representations by comparing supervised and self-supervised performance on low-resource and semantic tasks.  Despite achieving similar performance as supervised models, the self-supervised models exhibit severe vulnerabilities to adversarial attacks on speech inputs. This study presents a novel framework named AD SUPERB that integrates the SUPERB benchmark with adversarial training to enhance speech self-supervised learning robustness.  By adapting the adversarial training approach from text models to the speech domain, AD SUPERB achieves superior performance on a variety of robustness metrics across multiple self-supervised frameworks.  Our results show significant improvement over the original SUPERB benchmark, accumulating to 6% relative reduction in word error rate after adversarial training, as well as 87% reduction in disturbance strength required to impair model performance similarly to weakly-perturbed metrics.  Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/jay-krishnan/AD_SUPERB.  This research is an initial step in understanding and addressing the adversarial vulnerability of speech self-supervised models and demonstrating the Adversarial SUPERB paradigm's efficacy in producing robust and precise speech representations.  Additionally, our study extends the boundaries of adversarial training in speech to include semantic tasks such as named entity recognition, and our experiments indicate promising results with significant performance improvement, albeit near-optimal performance according to the original SUPERB benchmark.  However, our results show increased error resilience and more robustness to adversarial manipulation on a variety of speech recognition tasks after adversarial training.  Ultimately, this research aims to bridge the gap between recent text adversarial training advancements and the improved robustness of speech self-supervised models.  The outcomes of our study provide valuable insights for future research in adversarial training for speech self-supervised learning and robustness enhancement.  As such, this work presents a novel theoretical framework for enhancing speech self-supervised learning through adversarial training and robustness metrics in the context of semantic speech tasks.  Additionally, our code is publicly available for replication purposes by referencing https://doi.org/10.5330/MMS.2022.2022-0001.

A new analytical framework, referred to as Sensitivity Analysis, evaluates how conclusions based on incomplete data can be affected by uncertainties in underlying assumptions. We build upon an existing metric known as the E-value, which measures the reliability of causal inferences, and apply it to scenarios with missing outcome data. Through case studies on Facebook's partially-observed conversion events, we develop an approach to conduct large-scale sensitivity analysis by contributing three key improvements. Firstly, we develop a Bayesian estimation technique for sensitivity parameters using unreliable benchmarks; this approach offers superior scalability and precision over its traditional frequentist counterpart. Secondly, we devise a strategy to efficiently compare benchmarks in practical scenarios. Thirdly, we address challenges including correlative missing data and confounding variables within causal inference frameworks. We implement the proposed methods in a Python library, which is made publicly available on GitHub. Analytical findings and simulation results confirm our Bayesian approach outperforms its frequentist counterpart. We apply the proposed methods to Facebook's conversion events, and the results reveal that they greatly expedite sensitivity analysis without compromising accuracy or reliability. We believe this work contributes innovative solutions to conducting sensitive analysis and anticipate that such approaches will become essential for research practices involving partially-observed events in the future. The new Bayesian estimation technique developed here can also be widely utilized in diverse fields within machine learning and statistics. The open-source Python library provided can be easily used for a broad range of statistics and machine learning applications. The conversion to frequentist estimation is straightforward and simply requires replacing the Bayesian techniques with their frequentist counterparts. The proposed methods remain effective even in complex scenarios involving event time-series data. However, such cases may not allow for reliable conclusions to be drawn due to limitations of binary observation data. Therefore, future research aims to extend this framework to more complex scenarios, including multivariate outcome data and time-series observation patterns. The resulting Bayesian estimation for sensitivity analysis can be great improved by incorporating multivariate data. Additionally, future research aims to develop more sophisticated algorithms for handling sensitive analysis in a broader range of applications. The proposed methods are not limited to Facebook's data and can be applied to a diverse range of statistics and machine learning settings. Understanding universal properties of a critical quantum spin chain model requires identifying key components of conformal field theory, notably the coefficients of operator product expansion, which describe operator fusion. Research suggests that these coefficients can be computed using wavefunction overlaps of low-energy states in the spin chain. We have demonstrated that central charge, conformal dimensions, and operator product expansion coefficients are encoded in wavefunction overlaps, accompanied by universal corrections that rely on cyclic orbifold CFT components. This approach allows for numerical computation of all conformal data without relying on lattice regularization. We have applied this method to compute the Haagerup model's conformal data and found agreement with established results. Additionally, this method enabled the determination of operator product expansion coefficients and low-conformity numbers for the Haagerup model and Ising transverse field model. Using this approach, we calculated the Regnault-Congemi operator product expansion coefficient for the first time, and our results for the Haagerup model conformal spectrum differ from prior work based on the density-matrix renormalization group method. We have obtained spectra in both the interior and exterior regions of the Dilogarithm Asymptotic Sequence and found the non-universal parts of the conformal data to be predominantly rational. We suggest applying our wavefunction overlap method for computing operator product expansion coefficients and low-conformity numbers in spin chain and other models with known exact ground states. Furthermore, this non-entanglement approach to conformal field theory may facilitate numerical studies of universal universal finite-size corrections in a wide variety of models. The observed rationality of the non-universal conformal data suggests that it could be related to a property called quantum integrability, and further research is recommended to investigate the relationship between our findings and existing understanding of conformal field theory and spin chain models. The mathematical concepts and methods used in this study are explained in detail, and accompanying Jupyter notebooks, available on GitHub, provide supplementary numerical computations and plots. These numerical support materials demonstrate the applicability of our method to universal and non-universal conformal data for the paramagnetic Ising transverse field model for any value of J/H. Moreover, these supplementary materials should enable users to compute the conformal data for any value of J/H, as well as apply our method to other exactly solvable spin chain models with unique ground states. This research focuses on developing a method to calculate a utility function from a non-differentiable but locally Lipschitz candidate of a demand function. Using this method, we derive two new criteria that a demand function candidate must meet. First, it must be symmetrical and have a negatively semi-definite Slutsky matrix, and second, it must be a unique concave solution to a specific partial differential equation globally. Additionally, we describe a method to calculate a differentiable utility function from a differentially smooth demand function candidate. Our results provide several key implications including that a locally Lipschitz demand function candidate that meets the two new criteria will have a differentially smooth representative in a certain space and the representative is the only utility function that corresponds to the candidate with the same minimum or maximum dispersion among consumers. The uniqueness of the representative is also demonstrated for certain demand function candidates such as homogenous functions and functions with specified symmetries. Theoretical predictions from Haig's law and other economic principles can also be derived from differentially smooth demand functions. In the category of sets, the best partial order approximation of the image in such a case is obtained by forming the cofibered image of the original preorder above the epimorphism. In categories satisfying regularity conditions, the existence of such a cofibered image of a partial order is well-established. However, the existence of the cofibered image of an equivalence relation in these categories is not necessarily guaranteed. This work presents a necessary and sufficient condition on a regular category $\mathbb E$ ensuring the existence of the cofibered image of any equivalence relation in $\mathbb E$. Moreover, this condition is shown to be equivalent to the absence of certain loops in the category $\mathbb E$. The authors' research is also applied to categories of topological spaces or ordered sets. The obtained conditions on these categories are connected to existing notions in the literature and are related to the Wright condition for totally ordered semilattices. Finally, an analogue of the duality between the categories of spaces and the categories of ordered sets is identified and demonstrated through the use of the Axiom of Choice. Additionally, the authors consider a simplified version of the condition that is free from topological dependencies and can be expressed solely through logical operations involving certain existing mathematical notions. This simplified condition is shown to be equivalent to the existence of a certain type of well-ordered subset in the power sets of the category's objects. Ultimately, the authors' research is shown to be connected to a well-known theorem in the literature and the conclusion drawn is that the literature's requirements are essentially equivalent to the use of the Axiom of Choice. Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationship between satellite wind speed data, wave height observations, and extreme weather patterns is examined in the North East Atlantic between 2007-2018. A template-based approach is used to compare and combine wind and wave data from satellites and historical forecasts. Analysis involves standardizing wind and wave measurements and applying an extreme value model to estimate the probability of severe storms in specific locations. Results from this investigation reveal a significant decline in extreme weather correlations among Metop satellite wind speeds, wave forecasts, and wave measurements over a range of 600 to 800 kilometers. A location-specific extreme weather model is also developed, revealing that Metop satellite wind speeds can predict 25% of severe storms at the Azores, while 65% of severe storms at the Azores are predicted by wave forecasts from the ERA5 reanalysis. Combining wind and wave data improves the prediction of severe storms at the Azores by 10%. Overall, this research demonstrates that a simple statistical method can accurately estimate the probability of extreme weather by combining wind and wave data from various sources. Its widespread applications also imply that similar techniques could be used to study the interactions between other components of the atmosphere, such as those found on ships, with land-based weather data. Additionally, this approach could potentially enhance the prediction of severe maritime conditions such as those occurring during the winter storm of 1999. The application of machine learning in image diagnostics within pathology and radiology is undergoing significant transformation.  Despite research-based models performing equally well as human experts, these models need to be integrated into standard clinical practice. For this to happen, there needs to be a universal standard interface between the machine learning and clinical communities. Currently, different proprietary systems for image annotation and model output usage are causing obstacles for their implementation in clinical settings.  To address this issue, a standardized Python library named highdicom for encoding digital pathology images and machine learning outputs has been developed. This library is compatible with the DICOM data structure.  By using the highdicom module, users can easily include images along with machine learning-based diagnostic outputs within digital pathology clinical workflows, thus enhancing interoperability between the machine learning and clinical communities.  To showcase its, utility the highdicom module was used to evaluate a breast cancer prediction model performance in a clinical setting as per the quantitative imaging biomarkers pharmacometrics and pharmacodynamics guidelines.  By making the highdicom module freely available through the public repository GitHub, it has the potential to facilitate cooperation and exchange between the machine learning and clinical communities, thus accelerating the implementation of machine learning models within clinical workflows. A new, systematic method referred to as the Clebsch canonization has been proposed to convert Lie-Poisson equations into equivalent canonical Hamiltonian systems through a momentum map connection. We detail the momentum map's constraints, explicitly derive the corresponding Hamiltonian systems, and provide two illustrative examples, including the application to Euler's equations for rigid body rotation, which are equivalent to Poisson brackets of the particle kinetic energy with respect to angular velocity. Another example involves the application to the material frame induction (MFI) equations for Euler's equations, which are equivalent to the Hamiltonian formulation of the summed kinetic and potential energy. Furthermore, we extend this approach to systems with integrals of motion and discuss its utility in solving Lie-Poisson equations. By leveraging the momentum map connection, we present a useful, canonical approach for solving a variety of Lie-Poisson equations and exploring their properties. It is shown that momentum map constraints can be represented as conservation laws for the corresponding Hamiltonian system, while integral properties can be effectively utilized to simplify the solution process; specifically, we use the Clebsch canonization to derive canonical equations for the generalized Euler equations and apply it to solve the MFI equations for the 2D Euler equations. Additionally, we derive canonical equations for the 3D Euler equations via the MFI approach and present further applications, such as the Euler-Poisson equations for a heavy rigid body, to explicitly demonstrate the Clebsch canonization's utility in understanding Lie-Poisson systems and their solutions. We conclude by distinguishing the Clebsch canonization from other approaches, such as the Legendre transformation-based method for converting Lie-Poisson equations into Hamiltonian systems, which are equivalent to canonical systems with non-constant coefficients due to the emergence of a Legendre transform 'ghost' momentum. While the Legendre transform method leverages the dual momentum map for Lie-Poisson systems and does provide a solution but with an auxiliary 'ghost' momentum, the Clebsch canonization offers a more direct and simple approach to converting Lie-Poisson equations. Ultimately, the Clebsch canonization presents a powerful, canonical solution method for a wide array of Lie-Poisson systems. The accompanying Jupyter Notebook contains detailed mathematical implementations of the derived results and serves as a practical tutorial for accessing the canonization approach. The provided reference codes enable users to generate and utilize the momentum map, Hamiltonian system, and various illustrative examples, including the application to the material frame induction equations for Euler's equations. We apply the friction concept to various systems involving the movement of charged test particles in the presence of strong magnetic fields, neutron stars, black holes, cluster environments, and the early universe. We also extend the friction study to other fields and systems, including the presence of neutral particles and the behavior of neutral media under electromagnetic forces. Our goal is to facilitate the physical sciences' recognition of friction as a unifying and vital component. We anticipate that future research will incorporate mechanical principles in the friction context. For instance, future studies could examine the effects of friction in the presence of gravito-trapping phenomena. However, such an analysis would fall outside the scope of the present work. We also recognize that our research on friction in the material medium can be supplemented by the comprehensive treatment provided in the monograph "Friction in the Gravitational Field. II.

In the context of an unevenly distributed classification problem, most popular classifiers are known to favor larger groups, and the nearest neighbor classifier is not immune to this phenomenon. This issue is addressed in a newly proposed statistical framework for the nearest neighbor classification method, which handles datasets where the majority classes outweigh minority ones. Initially developed for binary classification problems, this method is extended to accommodate multiple classes. In addition to providing asymptotic consistency and robustness characteristics, this approach is distinguished by its capacity to not only rely on majority voting but also explore other optimization methods such as probability protoning. Furthermore, the proposed method is shown to be resistant to model dependence and is instead based on a non-parametric approach. Extensive simulation studies and real-world data analysis confirm the efficacy of this method in accurately classifying classes in unevenly distributed datasets, surpassing other popular classifiers such as \( k \)-nearest neighbor, kernel nearest neighbor, logistic regression, and support vector machines. This method is made available through the nncsp R package, facilitating its implementation. The findings of this research are presented in an article that is currently available online. We have successfully observed the charge-tunneling phenomenon occurring between a quantum dot and a superconducting island using a technique that employs radio-frequency sensing. Our approach has allowed us to distinguish between different types of tunneling events, specifically those driven by individual particles as well as by pairs of particles called Cooper pairs. Furthermore, we've found that the quantum dot can be utilized to detect changes in the superconductor's electronic state without needing traditional electrical current measurements, providing us with insight into previously inaccessible subgap energy states. Our findings offer valuable insights for future research focused on detecting parity-dependent interactions between these quantum dots and superconducting islands, potentially revealing the existence of elusive Majorana modes. Ultimately, this research paves the way for exploring a range of topological quantum computing concepts. Using advanced simulation techniques, we were able to explain our experimental findings and gain a deeper understanding of the underlying charge dynamics. Our findings are expected to open up new avenues in quantum information research, specifically in the design of reliable and stable quantum memory devices. With the support of advanced quantum information tools, we plan to push the boundaries of our experimental setup even further, ultimately aiming to develop a sophisticated three-layer device combining superconductivity, semiconductivity, and quantum spin dynamics. This research promises to contribute significantly to the rapidly evolving field of quantum computing. Our approach has significant broader implications, connecting to fundamental concepts in the study of charge fluctuations in superconductivity, where it has been established that superconductors are capable of resisting certain types of external electromagnetic fields. Our work reveals a related phenomenon where the presence of external quantum dots affects the ability of superconductors to resist certain types of external electrical signals, providing a new understanding of the complex interplay between quantum dots and superconductors. This research has further demonstrated that the dynamics of Cooper pairs in superconductors can be influenced by external quantum dots, where the presence of these particles alters regular parity-changing interactions within the superconductor. At the equilibrium state, we define a shock in a system of equations as a discontinuity that has a specific entropy -reducing effect. To expand existing requirements for these shock criteria, we consider geometric markers and prove two key theorems: the first related to the behavior of these markers during the contraction, and the second confirming the existence of specific shocks in conservation law systems under certain conditions. To validate our results, we apply our theories to an example model in two-dimensional physics, specifically a system of equations that model rotating fluids in the presence of magnetic fields. Our analysis allows for the visualization of shock criteria using a specialized map, and our findings are verified by computational simulations. Our research contributes to a deeper understanding of shock behavior in systems of equations by identifying key factors that influence the behavior of these shocks, including the effect of markers on shock contraction and the role of parameters in shock formation. Our theories may also be applied to more complex systems of equations for the study of physical phenomena such as fluid dynamics, meteorology, and oceanography. We explore novel view generation -- the challenge of generating distant, unseen views by virtually navigating a given image -- through a new, promising approach. Our contribution is DiffDreamer, an unsupervised system that synthesizes novel long-distance views by simulating camera movements and training on internet-sourced nature scene images alone. Our results confirm that conditioned diffusion models excel at extending long scenes while accurately maintaining both detailed and overall consistency, surpassing prior methods based on GANs. To achieve this, we modify the standard diffusion model so that it can generate views from given images while considering the perspective of virtual cameras. Our model's performance is further enhanced by capturing and processing image details from numerous freely accessible image datasets online. According to our experiments, the integrated techniques enable the creation of high-quality, detailed and consistent novel long-distance views that humans cannot distinguish from authentic images, opening up numerous applications in generative vision. With just internet-sourced training data, our system outperformed a range of state-of-the-art methods. Many complex systems feature interconnected components that spread information and resources across networks. Due to the numerous parameters influencing system behavior, accurately modeling these dynamics from first principles can be highly challenging, if not impossible. As a result, researchers typically rely on limited, noisy data collected from observed systems for insight. This study introduces a novel method grounded in machine learning to take advantage of that data. It integrates a sequence-to-sequence model for forecasting system behavior, system optimization, and controller design at the model level. Although the approach operates independently of physical laws, it yields models useful for decision-making. We test this method using synthetic data, then apply it to the epidemiological model Susceptible-Infected-Removed to anticipate outbreaks and design control strategies in real-world air transportation systems. Due to the time constraints involved, we use synthetic data resembling time-series observations from the actual system to demonstrate the efficacy of our approach. We validate our model by leveraging historical flight data and assess its accuracy using metrics such as continuous ranked probability score and mean absolute error. Despite some shortcomings, our approach successfully generates useful models, enabling set-valued controller design and system optimization. We believe this research opens new avenues for analyzing complex systems, offering avenues for further advancement. Its application to actual air transportation systems holds significant practical value. We plan to adapt this method for time-series prediction in the US air transportation network, then design control strategies based on the generated model to prevent outbreaks during epidemic outbreaks. As the underlying processes remain unknown, we intend to integrate our prediction and control models with real-time data from the actual system to achieve closed-loop operation. This method holds the potential to be a game-changing predictive analytics tool for various networked systems, potentially shedding new light on the intricate behaviors of the systems it seeks to model. The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model that uses the axisymmetric Stokes equations to examine the effect of liquid-solid slip on a film coated on a fiber undergoing the Rayleigh-Plateau instability. The new theoretical model reveals that slip leads to a higher rate of instability and longer wavelengths than predicted by previous models. Consequently, larger drops tend to form on fibers with high slip coefficients. The accuracy of the theoretical model is supported by numerical simulations and experimental results from studies using static of fibers, liquid films, and drop formation processes. This comprehensive analysis provides quantitative models for experimentally evaluating the effect of slip on liquid films and predicting the morphology of drops on fibers. Our work sets the stage for exploring the dynamics of liquid films on fibers in a wide range of flow conditions. It's expected that these findings will contribute significantly to various fields, particularly non-newtonian fluid dynamics and liquid droplet physics. Furthermore, the effect of slip on the Rayleigh-Plateau instability and its related processes has not been delved into previous studies, and this work offers an opportunity to rectify these gaps in the knowledge base. Lastly, the proposed theoretical model has far-reaching applications that extend beyond the dynamics of liquid films and drops, and can be adapted for studying the dynamics of various solid-state systems. It's known that similar mechanisms operate in quantum fluids, and this knowledge can be leveraged for developing innovative strategies to control the dynamics of liquid films and drops. Consequently, the proposed theoretical model has the potential to open new avenues for fundamental and applied research in dynamics and condensed matter physics.
